->**Hermetic Philosophy**<-
<note>original: "PHILOSOPHIA · HERMETICA." Hermetic philosophy is an ancient tradition of spiritual and philosophical knowledge attributed to the legendary figure Hermes Trismegistus, often focusing on the relationship between the divine, the cosmos, and the individual, and is deeply linked with the practice of alchemy.</note>

*A circular emblem is displayed here, framed by a golden-yellow border containing the title mentioned above. At the center is a blue oval field. At the top, a golden sun radiates its light downward. Below it, a white pelican is depicted "in its piety"—a classic symbol where the bird nourishes its young with its own blood—perched upon a silver crescent moon. At the base of the image lies a white square block, or ashlar, adorned with four red roses arranged in the shape of a cross.*

<note>The imagery here is rich with Rosicrucian and alchemical symbolism. The pelican represents the process of extraction and revitalizing a substance through sacrifice. The combination of the sun (masculine/gold), the moon (feminine/silver), and the Rose Cross points to the "Great Work" of balancing opposites to achieve spiritual or material perfection.</note>

## To the Reader.

I would be doing something quite unnecessary if I were to write a preface for a book that has already been well-known for so long, in an attempt to win your favor for it. The publisher believes he is performing a helpful service for you by deciding to remedy the recent scarcity of copies <note>In the 18th century, popular books often sold out quickly, and "scarcity of copies" was a common justification for releasing a new edition.</note> by having it translated anew and published. My predecessor <note>This refers to the translator of an earlier German version of this work.</note> sometimes understood neither his text nor the subject matter itself; I flatter myself with the hope that I shall be intelligible; yet—

I ask your forgiveness if I should perhaps not be <note>This continues the thought from the previous page: "I flatter myself with the hope that I shall be intelligible; yet—I ask your forgiveness if I should perhaps not be..."</note> in the chemical articles, even though I consulted an experienced <term>chemist</term> <note>original: "Scheidekünstler," literally a "separation artist," an 18th-century term for a chemist or metallurgist who separates metals.</note> for advice; for one person cannot know everything. Mr. P. Schlegel <note>Likely referring to Johann Heinrich Schlegel (1726–1780), a contemporary scholar and critic.</note> considers this work an **astronomical romance**: <note>In the 18th century, "romance" (Roman) often referred to a work of speculative theory or a narrative that mixed facts with imaginative interpretation.</note> nevertheless, it can serve you for instruction and for pleasure. I no longer recall which modern philosopher called our metaphysics a **romance of the human soul**; and yet one must study it. Even in the histories of this earth, romances are sometimes presented as truths; why would it be a wonder if something not entirely reliable were to slip into the *history of the heavens*. We all fail in many ways; even with the best intentions, this is our lot. If you wish, correct the few noted printing errors and overlook the other unimportant ones; and fare thee well.

->Breslau in April 1764.<-

## Explanation of the Engraved Title Page.

It depicts the philosopher <term>Democritus</term> <note>Democritus (c. 460 – c. 370 BC) was an Ancient Greek philosopher famous for his "atomic" theory—the idea that everything is made of tiny, indivisible particles.</note>, who stayed in his hometown of Abdera among the tombs; he withdrew entirely from human society so that he might contemplate the **structure of the world** without distraction. In his opinion, this world arose from the movement of very small, indivisible parts, which he therefore calls **atoms**, and which must have already existed beforehand. A citizen holds up a tablet before him, on which this verse stands:

->It is not for man to labor on the universe, but rather to till the earth.<-
<note>original Greek: "Οὐ μεν δημοεργειν ἀνθρωπινον, ἀλλα γεωργειν." This quote suggests that humans should focus on practical, earthly work rather than trying to figure out how the cosmos was "built."</note>

The sense of these words is expressed by the latter of these two lines:

->How far, O Democritus, does your confidence soar?<-
->Man should not build the world; the earth he should till.<-

Farmers and travelers who read the saying, or hear it, mock him; one shrugs his shoulders, another laughs aloud; all seem to notice: that we have enough understanding to perceive and organize our own customs and labors; yet we can grasp nothing of what is above us, which has not been entrusted to our care. The truth of this principle is the **intent of this entire work**.

In all times and in all places, this investigation has been conducted: it is the first reflection of a contemplative mind, the first step taken by curiosity. The philosophers of most famous nations have occupied themselves with this matter; and the ancient poets, wishing to embellish their song with a magnificent beginning or an important interlude, were accustomed to treat the creation of the world. *)

However, as eager as we may initially be to listen to those who proclaim this first of all events, their accounts do not deserve equal belief. They are not very consistent with one another, often not very intelligible, and even contradict what is found in nature. One must therefore proceed cautiously and, when studying this history, follow the rules of sound reason and the means that prudence employs every day when it wishes to arrive at the certainty of things about which it seeks instruction.

### Concerning this Work.

Just as French history is a collection and investigation of all that our ancestors have left us regarding the origin and progress of this monarchy: so too is the **History of the Heavens** a collection and investigation of all that those before us have themselves thought, or learned from their fathers, regarding the origin of the heavens and their relationship to the earth.

A prudent historian does not include every collected report in the context of his work: he makes a selection. He rejects everything that is irrelevant or clearly contrary to known history; everything stated without thought, or anything not supported by sufficient evidence, he casts aside. He uses only that which can be connected naturally, accepted with approval, and brought into a coherent whole. Since we are now undertaking to provide the history of the beginning of the heavens and the origin of the names which the various parts of the **celestial sphere** <note>original: "Himmelskugel" — a reference to the imaginary globe surrounding the Earth upon which the stars and planets appear to move.</note> have received, along with the influence <note>This refers to the historical belief in astrology or the physical "influence" of stars on earthly affairs.</note> attributed to them: our foremost concern is to use only that which the most rational persons or nations have thought about it—those who have been most diligent in preserving accounts of the past. To what end should the strange opinions over which other nations argue serve us? Should we collect what the Caribs, Greenlanders, and other savages <note>The author uses the 18th-century term "Wilden" to refer to indigenous peoples, reflecting the Eurocentric scholarly perspective of the era.</note> have...

### Outline

...dreamed, those who, through a long separation from the body of society, have become degraded and have strayed from their kind? We shall therefore adhere solely to that which has been believed and made known regarding the origin of the world and the heavenly powers by those among whom a thread of history has been preserved unbroken; and who, because they have always been a great body of many nations united by the bonds of commerce <note>original: "Handlung" — in this context, it refers to trade and social interaction which allowed for the exchange of knowledge.</note>, have been able to share some of the most ancient records with one another and propagate and preserve them down to our own time.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;However, no matter how much a historian takes care to avoid accepting anything that does not resemble the truth, he nonetheless often finds his material so entangled with well-known and credited fables that he is compelled to dwell upon them and follow them until he can encounter the trace of truth he seeks within them. For example, most French historians have portrayed the Gauls as a people conquered and enslaved by the Franks *), drawing other conclusions from this which are just as fabricated as that victory itself. The learned and astute writer **), who has provided us with a critical history of the establishment of the French monarchy, was thus unable to avoid, for the sake of destroying this— <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the argument on the next page.</note>

He shows us the source of these fables in recent centuries; he goes back to contemporary monuments <note>The author uses "monuments" (Denkmäler) in the 18th-century sense of primary historical records, such as inscriptions, coins, or chronicles.</note> and shows us the kings in **France** in close connection with the **Romans** and the **Gauls** who had become Romanized. He shows us how these princes, long before **Clovis** <note>original: "Chlodoväo." Clovis I (c. 466–511) was the first King of the Franks to unite all the Frankish tribes under one ruler.</note>, had established themselves on this side of the **Rhine**, having served in the most distinguished military roles under the **Romans**, and gradually took advantage of the **Emperors'** weakness to turn themselves from **governors** into their own **masters**: whereby the diversity of our **laws** and **customs** is greatly **illuminated**, which arises simply because the **Gauls**, who were just as free under our **kings** as they were under the **Romans**, were judged according to their **laws**, whereas the **French** were judged according to ours.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;I now find myself under the same necessity to unravel and refute **fables** so that I may firmly establish the **truth**. The most famous **men** who have spoken of the **creation** of **heaven**, the **earth**, and their **relationships** to one another are the pagan **writers**, the **philosophers** <note>original: "Weltweisen" — literally "world-wise ones," a common 18th-century term for philosophers or sages.</note> of all ages, and the **Divine Scriptures**. What the **Egyptians**, **Phoenicians**, **Greeks**, and **Romans** have told us is obscured by fabulous **narratives** and absurd **transformations**. Although they were the most witty and civilized of all **peoples**, they nevertheless conceived such strange **notions** of the go- <meta>catchword: gierung (forming "Regierung" or government/rule)</meta>

<meta>This page continues the author's critique of ancient cosmological theories. # Outline

—governance of the heavens, and its influence on the preservation of the human race, that it is not even necessary to dispute their conclusions, for they refute themselves. However, it is possible to kindle a light in the midst of this terrible darkness. Among all these fables, I find something certain, the clarification of which reveals to us the origin of the fables themselves. It is the key to them. This "certainty" is the meaning of the names and symbols <note>original: "Sinnbilder" — emblems or allegorical images used to represent abstract ideas or natural phenomena.</note> with which, in the most remote antiquity, the sun, moon, and stars were designated according to their various positions. The customs of the ancients and the observation of nature help us discover their meaning; this knowledge immediately shows us how severely the institutions of the first men were misused, and it sheds a great light on the origin of the idolatry of our ancestors.

The second advantage of this investigation is that we may understand how the very same error that populated the heavens with chimerical <note>original: "chimärischen" — referring to the Chimera of myth; used here to mean purely imaginary or illusory.</note> deities also produced a multitude of false opinions regarding the influence of the heavens—errors that still dominate most minds. If our history of the heavens achieved no other benefit than that we discover the error which plunged the human race into shameful delusions, the consequences of which still disturb the peace of society, we could be well satisfied with it.

### On this Work

The greatest error, and one that nearly all of them share, is the belief that a universal matter and a universal motion distributed through this matter are a sufficient explanation for the structure of the world—for they believe these two elements alone are enough to bring it into being. Experience, however, teaches us the opposite and shows us that the general order of the world, the organization of the species <note>original: "Geschlechter," referring here to the distinct kinds or generations of living things</note> *), and the diversity of the elementary natures as we know them, can have as their immediate cause neither a general nor a specific motion. Such things are beyond the power of motion; instead, they require the counsel and will of the Creator, who has ordered every individual part just as He has ordered the whole.

In seeking to explain this principle—the importance of which everyone recognizes—we do not wish to deny in the least that there are general laws of impact and rules of motion which sustain the world. No one denies this, and no one can doubt it. Neither Descartes <note>original: "Cartesius," the Latinized name of the philosopher René Descartes</note> nor <term>Malebranche</term> (Nicolas Malebranche, a 17th-century French philosopher who sought to reconcile Cartesian science with Christian faith), nor our teachers in philosophy have led us into error when they showed us that nature acts according to simple and uniform laws. ### to this work.

My hopes go even further. I have, perhaps with a bit too much vanity, flattered myself that this small attempt could also be of some use to those who teach. I would count myself fortunate if, in their efforts, I have shown them certain perspectives that they can utilize and adapt according to the abilities of their students. It often happens that teachers, even with the best intentions and insights, do not have the time for lengthy investigations. Among those who teach the humanities <note>original: "Humanität," referring to the classical liberal arts</note>, one generally finds that those capable of correct and thorough thinking complain about having to spend many years occupied with absurd or irritating fables <term>Fabeln: In this 18th-century context, "fables" refers to the myths and legends of Greek and Roman antiquity</term>; yet for all the annoyance caused by such ridiculous stories, they do not even have the pleasure of discovering their origins. I trace here all the branches of idolatry <note>original: "Abgötterey"</note> back to a single trunk. I seek to show that one and the same error <note>original: "einerley Irthum"</note> gave rise to gods and goddesses, metamorphoses, prophecies, and oracles. If the fables are placed at their true value in this way, they will provide amusement without danger, and teachers will find themselves comfortable with a principle so simple that even children can grasp it.

The primary fruit I wish to harvest from my work would be to facilitate the learning of natural science <term>Naturlehre: This term encompasses physics and the study of the natural world, often viewed through a theological lens in this period</term> and religion, and to restrict them to what is possible and necessary, for both are still far too extensive.

### The Origin of such Customs which are common to all Nations.

The profound wisdom which provides for the needs of humanity has arranged things so that the increase of the herds, from which man derives his primary nourishment, is made easier by ensuring that the mothers are generally pregnant by the end of autumn. Through this foresight, the rest of winter benefits both the mother and the unborn fruit. If she gives birth <note>original: *wirft*, a term used for animals giving birth.</note> while the weather is still cold, the young animal keeps itself warm under its mother. It later develops with the help of spring, and its tender limbs strengthen themselves against the coming heat. First come the lambs, then the calves, and finally, as a rule, the goats.

In this way, the lambs can follow the ram into the field during the first clear days; calves and goats follow in their own time and increase the herds. One can easily see that antiquity marked the passage of the sun through the three signs of spring with the names of three animals whose new growth is visible throughout the entire spring, and which—because they can be traded—begin to constitute the wealth of society. ### IV.

### Invention of Symbolic Writing and Figurative Language.

These twelve symbolic names, which indicate the twelve parts of both the year and the heavens, were of immensely great use, as they allowed the beginning of sowing, the hay and grain harvests, hunting, and other communal labors to be organized according to them. Since they presented the soul with twelve objects and very sensory <term>figures</term> <note>original: "sinnliche Figuren" – figures that can be perceived by the senses rather than abstract concepts</note>, they were drawn on slate or other stones so that their use would be more convenient. To be sure, these were only crude, linear outlines; however, since such a sketch is the beginning of every painting, these coarse outlines of the twelve celestial signs likely gave rise to the invention of painting. The reader will easily see, however, that such publicly displayed images, intended to announce a certain specific task, or to group two or three of these together...

# On Pictorial Language <note>original: von der Bildersprache</note>

This wind, blowing from North to South around the time the sun passes through Cancer <note>The zodiac sign associated with the summer solstice, around June 21st</note>, drove the vapors toward the south <note>original: Mittag, literally "midday," but used here to mean the South</note> and gathered them in the middle of the country (**) where the Nile originates. Perhaps they did not grasp this chain of effects exactly as we have just presented them. However, without conducting fruitless investigations into the cause and the production of the effect, they nevertheless noticed that the flood always followed the North wind, and that it would be stronger or weaker in proportion to the strength and duration of the wind, which were not the same every year. This wind, which was an infallible sign of the rising water, soon served the inhabitants as a guiding rule <note>original: Richtschnur</note>.

# IB. Poetic Heaven, I C.

The inhabitants, who had fled into their cities upon the warning <note>literally "remembrance"</note> of the Dog Star and the North Wind, remained completely idle for two months and more until the water had fully receded. The successful trial of sowing in autumn or at the beginning of winter and harvesting in March made them long for the subsidence <note>original: Falle</note> of the Nile. The farmer had almost nothing to do until after the water's outflow. Before the flood, the wisdom of the Egyptians therefore consisted in paying attention to the end of the spring winds, the return of the North Winds which began with the summer, and finally the rising of the Dog Star—which circumstance was for them the most important point in the whole sky. # I B. Poetic Heaven, 1 C.

The necessity that made the Egyptians observers and, to some extent, astronomers, also taught them how to paint and write. The observation of the heavens had finally taught them how to organize their agriculture, which—due to the conditions unique to that land and unseen elsewhere—had so often been interrupted and made difficult for them. The custom of assigning the name "Dog" <note>original: Hund; referring to the "Dog Star" or Sirius, whose rising coincided with the Nile's flood</note> to the star that gave them news at such an opportune time, and giving other symbolic names to things that likewise served as a guide, naturally led them to sketch figures in such a way that they could communicate to the entire populace what they should do collectively, as well as the annual events where making a mistake would be dangerous.

The convenience of these signs caused them to multiply; soon, every aspect of the sky, the air, and the agriculture that mattered most to them—and of which their knowledge had to be reliable—was expressed through signs that bore a sensory resemblance to them, primarily through the figures of animals, as these were the most familiar and easiest to sketch.

Initially, efforts were made to invent as many signs as there were rules to observe, ensuring they were easy to grasp and remember, in order to [mark] the
time

---

without a lengthy treatise, to compare the old measurement of the Nile with the newer one.

# Regarding Symbolic Language.

[...not] to miss the time of departure, nor to fail in the manner of sowing according to the degree of the flood. And since the judgment and estimation of the duration of the annual wind and the depth of the Nile, if one had wanted to leave them to the discretion of the common people, would have been very uncertain; so a society of several persons was chosen who were occupied with this sole concern. This society determined and recorded certain signs on a stone which were capable of expressing the various circumstances that changed from one year to another, so that they might give the people a brief and easy instruction on what they had to do.

This is the origin of the priestly order which is so ancient in Egypt, and whose most important occupation has always been to observe the heavens and to note the movement of the winds. This is the origin of the famous tower where this society resided, and where the <term>symbols (Sinnbilder: visual representations of abstract concepts)</term> of the manifold labors and public institutions were carefully drafted: symbols that subsequently, once their meaning had been forgotten, acquired such a mysterious appearance. This dwelling, whose layout and construction were much improved over time, was called then, without any mystery, simply the Labyrinth, that is, the Tower *).

## VIII.

### Closer description of the Egyptian symbols.

If we now wish to discern some of the most common Egyptian <term>symbols (Sinnbilder: visual representations used to convey specific meanings)</term> in a rational manner, it seems to me that we must not seek their interpretation in the concepts of the divine Plato, nor in the <term>doctrine of spirits (Geisterlehre: the study of supernatural beings or demons)</term> of Porphyry or Iamblichus <note>Neoplatonic philosophers who often gave mystical interpretations to Egyptian rites</note>, nor in the metaphysics of certain modern philosophers. Instead, we should consult the practical needs of the Egyptian colonies. It is there that one must naturally seek the meaning of the images that were displayed before the eyes of the entire assembly of the people.

We have just seen that the agriculture of the Egyptians, and their very lives which depended upon it, were very closely tied to the observation of: 1. the winds, 2. the rising of the <term>Dog Star (Hundstern: the star Sirius)</term>, and 3. the increase of the flood. It was to these three circumstances—and not to some incomprehensible metaphysics—that the society of priests and astronomers must have directed the attention of the entire people; for without these observations, Egypt would have found itself without security or bread. But how does one paint the wind? How is one to distinguish the north wind from the south wind? How can one indicate things that cannot be seen?

The hoopoe, on the other hand, travels from South to North. It lives on the small worms that crawl out of the Nile mud in countless numbers **); countless species of gnats, water mosquitoes, and other pests primarily seek out stagnant water—and consequently also the flooded Nile—to lay their eggs, which hatch nowhere better than in the mud heated by the sun after the river has receded back to its banks. The hoopoe then rushes to all the places that the water has only just left; there it diligently observes the time and place where the emerging worms offer it an easy meal, before the winged creature, which is hidden under the skin of the worm and later in the shell of the nymph <note>An archaic term for a pupa or larva in the transitional stage of metamorphosis.</note>, emerges from this covering and flies away to propagate its kind in other places. As soon as the Egyptians saw the hoopoe return—not the natural hoopoe, which was a sign for a completely different matter, but the figurative bird <note>Likely referring to a hieroglyphic or symbolic representation used in a calendar or public monument.</note> that imitates the movement of the hoopoe—they prepared their grain for sowing. As soon as the Egyptians saw the hoopoe return—not the natural hoopoe, which was a sign of something else entirely, but the figurative bird <note>referring to a symbolic or hieroglyphic representation</note> that mimics the movements of the hoopoe—they prepared their grain for sowing. They sought to find the boundaries of their inheritance, which the silt had obscured, through land-surveying <term>Feldmessen</term> <note>Ancient Egyptian geometry was famously developed to re-establish property lines after the annual Nile flood</note> and sowed quickly, so that the winds of April and May would not overtake them and ruin a harvest that was sown too late.

Other secondary images *) which were expressed as so many distinct characteristics on the head of the bird or in its claws could represent the strength of these winds. They showed the people what they should or should not do when the winds were stormy, dry, cold, hot, or damp.

The third circumstance that was highly important to the Egyptian people was the precise knowledge of the river's depth. Initially, they marked the various rises of their river as it overflowed its banks on a column, which was marked with one, two, or three strokes in the form of a cross **) , and where a circle—the symbol of God—was placed on top to indicate the Providence that guided this important event. Instead of the column, which could be used in a stone well where the water only pressed in from below, they more commonly used in their writing a long pole that ended like a T, or was fitted with one or two crossbeams in the shape of a cross.

# ## On Pictographic Writing ##

most important occupation of the **farmer** <note>original: "Landmannes"</note> had to be, because he had to hasten, postpone, or entirely omit the **sowing work** according to the condition of the wind. Quite often we see that the **Canopic jars** <term>Canopic jars: ritual vessels used in ancient Egypt, here interpreted as symbolic agricultural tools</term> end with one or two **crosses**, the meaning of which we have already presented. Very often, various **bird heads** also stand on top of the vessel to indicate the different winds known to them, which either promoted or hindered the growth and the drainage of the water. Sometimes they also placed a **dog’s head** on the Canopic jar to indicate the state of the river at the rising of the **Dog Star** <note>Sirius, whose appearance coincided with the annual Nile flood</note>. At another time, they placed the **head of a maiden** upon it to indicate the level of the Nile under the sign of **Virgo**, and to suggest the approaching drying of the land \*) <note>the receding of the flood waters</note>.

All these conjectures taken together seem to constitute a certainty. One can accept them all the more readily as they are interconnected and all relate to the most important affairs of the colony. We wish, therefore, to continue in this attempt at explanations, because it begins to spread some light over a subject that has been so dark until now, the understanding of which could clarify the meaning of many **monuments of antiquity**.

must have been the most important <note>original: "vornehmste"</note> occupation of the farmer, because he had to hasten, postpone, or completely omit the sowing work according to the nature of the wind. We often see that the **Canopic jars** <note>original: "Kanopen"; these are ritual vessels used in ancient Egypt, though the author here interprets them as tools for agricultural measurement</note> end with one or two **crosses**, the meaning of which we have already explained. Very often, various **bird heads** also stand atop the vessel to indicate the various winds known to them, which either promoted or hindered the growth of crops and the receding of the water. Sometimes they also placed a **dog's head** on the Canopic jar to indicate the state of the river at the rising of the **Dog Star** <note>Sirius, the brightest star in the sky, whose "heliacal rising" coincided with the annual flooding of the Nile</note>. At other times, they placed the **head of a girl** upon it to indicate the level of the Nile under the **sign of Virgo** <note>the Virgin</note>, and to point toward the approaching dry season *).

All these conjectures <note>original: "Muthmaßungen"</note> taken together seem to constitute a certainty. They can be accepted all the more readily because they are interconnected and all relate to the most important affairs of the colony. We will therefore proceed with this attempt at explanation, as it begins to shed some light on a subject hitherto so obscure—one whose understanding could clarify the meaning of many monuments of antiquity.

## IX.

### Continuation of Egyptian Symbols.

The convenience of this language, which one understood through the eyes and which, in a sense, taught animals and even stones to speak, gradually led to its general use.

This symbolic writing soon served for moral instruction as well as for the management of agriculture <note>original: "Erdbau"; the author likely refers to the organization of land cultivation and irrigation systems</note>. It was used among the common people to preserve the knowledge of the most important truths and to impress upon them their primary duties. The places where the Egyptians gathered at the time of the New Moons—like the Chaldeans <note>an ancient people of Mesopotamia known for their early astronomical observations</note> from whom they descended—were soon filled with meaningful figures. These were designed to remind their minds of an **Almighty Being** who rules over all things, who gives life to humans and animals and growth and fertility to plants, and who daily covers the earth with new gifts; a Being that is higher than the sun, the earth, and the industry of man, for it bestows upon the sun its warmth and beauty, upon the earth its fertility, and upon the industry of man the blessing of his labor and the reward for his efforts.

The sign in Egyptian writing intended to signify **God** was not a mere flame, as was customary in the Orient <note>original: "Morgenlande"</note>, but a circle *) or rather a sun, a very simple

# On Hieroglyphic Writing.

These alterations of the images undoubtedly pointed to various circumstances of the day or the year; perhaps the rising and setting sun, the dawn, noon, twilight, cloudy weather, or intense or moderate heat. Obviously, nothing is easier than changing the meaning of one and the same image by adding or removing a component. However, since this writing was grossly misused in subsequent times and its meaning completely perverted—a truth the proof of which will soon unfold—it would perhaps be a futile effort or a daring undertaking to try to explain every detail of these images in the remaining Egyptian monuments; for example, in the **Table of Isis** <note>The *Mensa Isiaca* or Bembine Tablet, a famous bronze tablet with Egyptian-style reliefs that was long studied by European scholars as a key to hieroglyphs before they were deciphered.</note>; because the images upon them are linked together according to the systems of later times, and not according to the original sense, which has been neglected; because this merely symbolic ruler <note>referring back to the solar deity Osiris</note> is viewed as a human who lived on earth, and in the writing remaining on the monuments, is regarded as a god.

Reflective readers will not object here that I am citing the very matter under dispute as proof of my opinion. ### I B. Poetical Heaven, I C.

...suggested another. A charioteer or a king is thus here neither a man nor a god. Lovers of antiquity <note>original: "Alterthum"</note> who take this figure for a god may indeed, I confess, have the very same thoughts that the Egyptians, who had turned to idolatry, once held. However, without wishing to contradict their interpretations in the slightest, I seek to go back to the original sense of this symbol, which, through its name and its accompanying attributes, signifies the solar year or dominion over the earth.

I am very inclined to believe that the ruler, or **Osiris**, with the whip had a much closer relation to the daily motion <note>The sun's daily path across the sky</note>, which is more perceptible; and that with the scepter, he indicates the duration of a solar year; for it is the annual revolution of the sun which regulates everything in all of nature.

The figure of an **Osiris**, or a **sun**—for they are always one and the same—was used to indicate things that reappeared only once every year. In those cases, however, the secondary figure was changed. For example, the Phoenicians and others landed annually at the island of **Pharos** to collect flax, ox hides, fresh oil, legumes, grain, and all sorts of other necessities. The annual return of this fleet was indicated by an Osiris upon a winged horse—the symbol of ships and their sails—or else by an Osiris to whom one gave not a scepter, but a sea-

There was yet another equally famous annual recurrence that likewise required its own sign or symbol: namely, the return of annual days of sacrifice. We see from the funeral procession of **Archemorus** \*) <note>A mythological child whose death, recounted in the *Thebaid* by the Roman poet Statius, led to the institution of the Nemean Games</note>, from the annual memorial of **Anchises** \*\*) <note>The father of the hero Aeneas in Virgil's *Aeneid*; Aeneas honors him with annual games and sacrifices</note>, and from the annual laments of the **Israelite maidens** over the fate of the daughter of **Jephthah**, that it was a general custom in antiquity to weep and pray at the graves of persons dear to the fatherland, and to repeat these assemblies and sacrifices annually. Therefore, **Osiris**—or the image of the annual cycle—could announce an anniversary by the modification of his secondary image. At such times, instead of the whip or the trident, he was given the iron-clad tip of a rudder or an entire oar \*\*\*) in his hand; or a bushel <note>A grain measure</note> was placed upon his head, because during funeral feasts a measure of corn was distributed to every poor person; and perhaps this figure was given the name **Peluta** †) <note>Deliverance or Liberation</note>. ...for the passage <note>The crossing of the water, often symbolizing the journey to the afterlife</note> was the sign of death, and the bushel <note>A dry volume measure for grain</note> the announcement of a distribution on behalf of the deceased; and that in ancient times, the death of the righteous was regarded as a liberation from all evil.

Although one could certainly indicate an annual festival by means of an Osiris <note>The Egyptian god of the afterlife, often used here as a personification of certain natural or religious cycles</note> displayed in the assembly of the people, one nonetheless strictly required another sign alongside it, which indicated the exact season in which the festival was to be held; and whether the assembly should be held at the new moon, the full moon, or on another day of the month.

We proceed, therefore, to the symbol <term>Sinnbild</term> <note>A symbolic image or emblem intended to convey a moral or natural truth</note> which actually determines the holy year and the order of the festival days.

## The Civil Year. Isis.

One could with good reason call the order of festival days the ecclesiastical year <note>original: "Kirchenjahr"</note>, because these festivals were spiritual assemblies in which God was worshipped and His providence was praised. Our investigation into ancient customs and the meaning of ancient writing is visibly restricted to the times before the introduction of idolatry <note>original: "Abgötterey"</note>; however, since this order of festival days or workdays is a law of society, we prefer to call it the civil year <note>original: "bürgerliche Jahr"</note>. It was not quite possible to designate the various festivals of the year in a simpler way than through the symbol of the Earth and

# I B. Poetic Heavens, 1 C.

...the kind of pears which the *Persea* tree bears <note>The *Persea* (likely *Mimusops schimperi*) was a sacred tree in ancient Egypt; its fruit and heart-shaped leaves were often depicted in religious art.</note>, the large leaves of the banana tree, and certain other plants that bloom and bear fruit in different seasons, were used for the finery <note>original: "Puze"; refers to the ceremonial dressing or adornment of a cult statue.</note> of Isis, and could very well make the people understand the special events of the year, or announce this or that feast day to them.

I previously believed that the moon, or the first quarter upon the head of Isis, could be the symbol of Nature, which receives everything from God, just as the moon receives its light from the sun: however, one will likely not be wrong in imagining that Egyptian natural philosophy <term>Natural philosophy (Naturlehre): A historical term for the study of nature and the physical universe, practiced before the development of modern science.</term> was much simpler. It is much more natural to believe that the first quarter on Isis’s head marks the new moons, or the assembly held upon them; that the full moon on her head or breast indicates a feast in the middle of the month; that the quarter or full moon, accompanied by this or that foliage, indicates the gathering at the next new or full moon after a particular harvest; that a radiant star in her headdress announces a sacrifice which was to take place early at the rising of the Dog Star <note>Sirius, or the "Dog Star," was the most important star to the Egyptians, as its appearance coincided with the start of the Nile's annual flood.</note> or a planet; and likewise with other circumstances which serve to distinguish the feast days or seasons. All these changes had their special meaning, and Isis changed her garments just as the Earth does.

# On Pictorial Writing.

If the priests, in the assembly of the people, placed beside [the statue of] Isis—who wore a crescent moon upon her head and held a sickle in her hand—an Osiris with a bushel <note>original German: "Scheffel"; a container used for measuring grain, often depicted as a crown or vessel in Egyptian-style iconography to symbolize fertility</note>; then the poor could conclude that a funeral sacrifice and the annual distribution [of grain] would be held at the next new moon before the harvest. A single example of this symbolic language is enough to understand how easily the interpretation can be changed according to the circumstances and additions to the figure. We do not claim at all that these are strictly the true meanings of all these symbolic women; however, we can be satisfied with the probability of these explanations, since we have proven through the signs in the zodiac and the Sphinx that these figures were intended to designate the various parts of the year.

### XII.

->Agriculture. The Farmer’s Year. Horus.<-

The first teachers of Egypt seem to have focused very little on subtle and profound investigations in their instruction; their greatest purpose was to instill feelings of gratitude toward God in the people and to properly arrange agriculture, upon whose success their entire life depended. A philosopher, full of a physical system or high thoughts about the nature of spirits, will not fail to immediately see his favorite theories within this secret Egyptian pictorial writing <note>The author refers to hieroglyphs as "geheimen Bilderschrift" (secret pictorial writing), reflecting the 18th-century view of them as mystical symbols before they were deciphered by Champollion.</note>

### Concerning Hieroglyphics.

...painted with significant ornaments or tools; thus they expressed in an ingenious way the relationship of successive tasks, the obstacles, and the successes of agriculture.

They gave the child the name *Hores* or *Horus* *), which in Egyptian—presumably just as in Hebrew, Phoenician, and Arabic—signifies the plowman, the artist, agriculture, and diligence; in a word, it means labor. They often abbreviated the symbol by simply depicting a human head, the natural sign of the intellect. And to show how much depended on the labor that provides us with our life's sustenance, they joined this head with the image of a serpent, the emblem of life; or they perhaps even put both figures entirely together: the symbolic serpent and the child beloved by the sun and the earth**). Indeed, so that they might indicate the relationship of these things to agriculture, they often placed both figures upon the instrument used for winnowing grain <note>The author refers to a winnowing fan or sieve used to separate grain from chaff.</note>.

All he can do then is to hold a pole, a square <note>original: "Winkelhaken"; a tool used by masons and surveyors to ensure right angles.</note>, or a compass, and sometimes a weather vane or a staff topped with a hoopoe \*\*), or some other prominent object suitable for catching the wind to indicate its course and direction. In fact, the husbandman, having had much to do in Egypt with harvesting or threshing before the inundation <note>The seasonal flooding of the Nile, essential for Egyptian agriculture.</note>, is almost entirely idle as long as the water stands upon the fields. During this time, he can do nothing more than measure the height of the rise, observe the return of the midday wind—I was almost about to say the flight of the hoopoe—and prepare the necessary tools for the swift measuring and dividing of his land-holdings <note>original: "Erbstücke"; literally "heirlooms" or "inheritances," here referring to the inherited plots of land.</note>, which the remaining silt has made unrecognizable; this is done so that immediately after the division, one can sow, cover the seed with the plow, or even, instead of any preparation, make use of mere pig snouts, as the swine driven into the mud root eagerly with their snouts to seek out roots from the sandy soil lying beneath \*\*\*).

One often finds the head of Horus placed upon the vessel called the Canopic jar <note>original: "Kanope"; a jar used in ancient Egypt to hold internal organs, though here interpreted as a symbol for the river's state.</note>, which indicates the state of the river. If it were appropriate to place a sign in his hand, it would only be one concerning the wind, and usually, he also holds a hawk feather in one hand <note>original: "Sperberfeder." Now that we know the letters of the Egyptian script which have a relationship to agriculture, let us write something ourselves. Let us make an attempt to paint according to the Egyptian taste. In order to bring much together into a small space, we shall make use of the freedom to join various separate parts of several figures into a single body. The connection of these parts will be just as understandable and significant as if we had them all fully before our eyes. This abbreviation will be very convenient; and although these parts are naturally never found together, this novelty will be all the more clever in drawing the people's attention to the meaning hidden beneath it <note>The author is explaining the logic of composite hieroglyphs—the way Egyptian art combines different symbolic elements (like a human body with an animal head) to communicate complex ideas through a single visual "shorthand."</note>.

Does one wish to make the Egyptian people understand that the sign of the Lion <note>The zodiac sign Leo.</note>, with which the harvest begins elsewhere, is for them the time of most perfect rest? Does one want to indicate to them that their inactivity will last from the blowing of the annual north wind <note>original: "Etesiae." Angerona, whom the Romans held to be the goddess of silence because she had her finger on her mouth, was originally nothing other than an imitation of the Egyptian Harpocrates and an encouragement toward peace during the rest of winter. peace one loses everything. The Egyptians were therefore also accustomed, upon seeing this figure, to say: the tongue governs fortune. Well-being and woe depend on the tongue \*): and because the people had a particular need for this teaching, the image of Harpocrates was generally widely reproduced and often simplified. One commonly finds it with one jug instead of three, and with only one goat horn instead of both; or also with a circle and large banana leaves; or also with some other signs which were suited to instill in the people gratitude toward the author of all good things, and to make them civilized through teachings of gentleness and peace.

The Greek sculptors, who found no taste in such monstrous headgear, arranged everything with more decorum. They placed the goat horn in one hand of the figure. They showed fruits emerging from it, and did not forget the gesture of the other hand which teaches the people to be happy by restraining the tongue and anger.

He now sees clearly that these were letters of an ancient alphabet, or public notices, through which it was agreed to inform the people about the state of the heavens, the order of feast days according to the seasons, and the sequence of labor necessary throughout the year.

The subjects and motivations of this mournful custom are much easier to unravel among the Egyptians than among other nations, not only because the Egyptians—having mixed less with foreign peoples—altered their ancient formulas less, but also because their customs were tied precisely to the public, permanent symbols carved in stone and carried about in processions on feast days. When the festivals representing the ancient state of the human race and the progress of industry <note>In the sense of diligent labor or craftsmanship</note> were celebrated, the image of the Earth, as well as the image of Labor, was given different names in different countries. Isis, the image of the Earth as it was transformed after the Great Flood, was called Ceres, Themis, Nemesis, Semele, Mnemosyne, and Adrasteia. Since the harvest is the event that most strongly stirs the spirit of a people, the new moon which fell after the grain harvest must have been one of the most pleasant of all their festivals. 

Hence comes the great solemnity in the regions around **Thebes** upon the entry of the sun into the **Ram** <term>Aries</term>. The barn was full: that says it all. This same reason was why, in Memphis, the course of the sun in the **Bull** <term>Taurus</term>, and in **Mendes**, its entry into the **Goats**, was celebrated with great splendor. Outside of Egypt, the harvest happened—or had already happened—when the sun enters the **Lion** <term>Leo</term>; for this reason, one finds this sign most frequently associated with **Isis**, who announced the great festival at which one [thanked] God...

### Symbolic Customs.

If no accuser stepped forward, or if an accuser who testified against the deceased was proven to be untruthful, the mourning for the dead ceased and a eulogy <note>A "Lobrede" or funeral oration.</note> was delivered for him. *) One praised, for example, his excellent upbringing, his reverence for religion, his fairness, moderation, chastity, and other virtues. However, one never spoke of his birth as an advantage, because it was held that this was the same for all human beings. The entire crowd of bystanders gave their approval to this praise and wished the deceased happiness, that he might now go forth to enjoy eternal rest with other righteous people.

On the shore of the lake <note>Referring to Lake Acherusia, mentioned on the previous page.</note> was a strict and relentless ferryman <note>In Greek mythology, this figure became Charon.</note> who, only upon the express command of the judges and never otherwise, took the dead body into his boat. The Egyptian kings themselves were judged with this same severity and were not taken into the boat without the permission of the judges, who sometimes even denied them burial. The ferryman transported the corpses across the lake to a field that was adorned with meadows, streams, bushes, and every rural delight. This place was called *Elisut*, or the *Elysian Fields*; that is, "Full Abundance" <note>original: "Volle Gnüge."</note>; the seat of rest and joy. As for the earth thrown onto the corpse and the tender farewell of the relatives, this was a natural duty and the most tangible expression of their grief. However, it was not enough for them to pay this honor only in passing by the grave; they placed at the entrance to the burial site and over the door of the deceased the image of the respect and tender love they bore for their departed friend. To express the triple call they made over the grave of the deceased according to the custom—which permitted this honor only to be shown to righteous people—they gave the figure of the dog three heads and three maws. This image, placed by the grave and on the door of the newly buried person, thus signified that the family honored him with their mourning and with the call that friends never failed to give at the grave of one they honored and loved for his good qualities. ### I B. Poetic Heaven, 2 C.

...keys, and by the countless modifications with which every <term>key<note>In early linguistics, a "key" refers to a root sign or radical used to classify symbols; here, the author refers to the overwhelming complexity of adding marks to symbols to change their meaning.</note></term> becomes overwhelmed.

It was found, therefore, in Egypt or elsewhere—and indeed long before the time of **Cadmus** \*), for it was even before the days of **Job** and **Moses**—that a reflective mind, a fortunate spirit driven by God whose name history has not preserved for us, noticed that the number of tones <note>Original: "Töne." He struck upon the idea of representing this small number of sounds with an equal number of signs. Thus it happened that with twenty or twenty-four letters, one could visibly represent the twenty or twenty-four sounds whose mixture is sufficient to form all words or signs for things. Now, with very few signs, one could produce the thoughts of all things that we distinguish through the variety of these sounds.

### I B. Poetic Heaven, 2. C. <note>original: "I B. poetischer Himmel, 2. C." This likely refers to Book 1, Section B, Chapter 2 of the treatise.</note>

...service among the first humans. They came regularly with their sacrifices and bowed their knees before the instructive images <note>In this context, "instructive images" refers to the symbolic or hieroglyphic depictions used before phonetic writing became common.</note> that taught them about God and their duty. The action was laudable, and they found in their religious institutions a multitude of beneficial teachings. But their hearts clung only to the earth and were entirely tethered to their passions. The abundance for which they prayed more than for justice, and their long life, which they viewed with pleasure as the effect and the reward of their piety, were also the driving motives for this devotion. If they celebrated some festivals with more splendor and zeal than others, pious sentiment still had little part in it; rather, it happened merely because of a symbol <term>symbol; from the German *Sinnbild*, referring to a visual emblem or allegorical representation</term> peculiar to their province—primarily the form of the animal in which their wealth consisted, or which indicated the correct time for their harvest. Instead of judging the greatness of their fear of God by their brotherly love, they believed they had done everything if they faithfully maintained the manner of a mechanical and entirely external devotion, the observation of which is not at all difficult in comparison with a change of heart <note>original: "Herzensänderung"; this refers to a fundamental internal moral transformation or repentance.</note>. They strictly adhered to a series of minor exercises in the opinion that they were certain of their merit and assured of its consequences. As a result, they believed God allowed justice to be done to them through their prosperity or their personal small advantages, and they viewed these as a distinguished reward that He must have made His particular concern.

# The Race of Gods <note>original: *das Göttergeschlecht*</note>

With such crude dispositions, it is no wonder that the first humans easily lost sight of the Creator and true piety. What the public symbols <note>original: *Sinnbilder*; these are the visual allegories or hieroglyphs used in early religious instruction.</note> taught them had moved them little, even when their meaning was still understood. And such indifference <note>original: *Kaltsinnigkeit*</note> could not drive them to seek understanding once it began to fall into oblivion.

Now we can draw a conclusion about what kind of impression the symbolic figures must make on the minds of our ignorant or self-seeking worshippers. Those whom their evil inclinations have corrupted abuse everything. The script <note>Likely referring here to symbolic or hieroglyphic writing rather than an alphabet.</note> which was intended to instruct them will, as a consequence of their indifference and as punishment for their malice, lead them from one error to another, becoming for them an occasion for the saddest and most unfortunate transgressions.

Because they looked no further, they missed the true meaning, which was the actual object of this language and the soul <note>original: *Sele*; archaic spelling of *Seele*</note> of this symbolic script. 

There is surely no one who could not easily foresee the strange consequences of this error. One can now see, without further proof, that this was the primary source of the whimsical forms and absurd <note>original: *abgeschmackten*; literally "tasteless" or nonsensical</note> concepts found in universal idolatry. 

However, since the monuments of the ancient Northern and the farthest Oriental peoples have not survived to our time, or have mostly been subjected to constant alteration, we would do well to restrict our detailed investigation to the deities of the Egyptians, Syrians, and Greeks. This is because the likenesses of their gods are known to us; because we are surrounded by their influence; because their idolatry and that of our ancestors has become one and the same; and because it is even, in a certain sense, still our own, since we still grant it such a prominent place in our paintings and in our language today.

## I.

### God, the Sun, and Osiris Confused with One Another.

Everywhere, and especially in the sacred assemblies, the Egyptians saw a circle or the image of the sun. Often this image was placed at the top of every painting intended for their instruction; it was frequently seen upon the heads of birds, serpents, and the most prominent symbolic figures. Since the sun was the body <note>It is customary in the study of symbols to call the physical figure the "body," and the title or interpretation the "soul." —Translator's note</note> of this emblem, they also frequently called it "the Sun." Furthermore, because the Supreme Being is the "soul" or the meaning behind the image, they called that same figure—instead of the Sun—the Essence, the Eternal One, the Father of Life, the Strong One, and the Most High <note>The original text lists these titles as: *Iehova* (the Lord), *Hevoe* (the Self-Existent), *El* (God), *Eloah* (the Adored One), and *Helion* (the Most High).</note>. 

Before this image they knelt, primarily during their sacrifices, and directed their prayers and thanksgivings to the Most High, whom this script was intended to bring to their minds. However, because the eye, the ear, and even the heart were constantly occupied with the sun during this public worship, the common people began to direct all these great names, all their adoration, and all their gratitude toward the sun itself. ### III.

## Isis, the Queen of Heaven.

No image appeared more often in the assemblies of the Egyptians, besides the symbolic king—namely the sun—than Isis, the image of the Earth, or rather the sign of the festivals, which were marked by the various fruits emerging according to the seasons. A crescent or a full moon on the head of Isis or elsewhere could, as we have seen, announce a new moon or even the festival in the middle of the month of the hay harvest, the sowing season, the grain harvest, or any other part of the year, depending on which sign of the season or specific fruit suitable for it was placed alongside. The festivals dedicated to the Most High <note>The author argues that early humans originally worshipped one supreme God, using the moon only as a tool to schedule their services.</note> were placed on the new or full moons, or some other part of its course, simply because its various phases were a natural indicator and a very easy means of gathering people on a certain, agreed-upon, and publicly announced day. They lost sight of the adorable Being, the sole object of these festivals; they came to believe that these were dedicated to the moon itself, and to the imaginary woman who, in their opinion, was supposed to dwell within it and who would be very concerned for their welfare. Even the spots on the moon, through their false resemblance to a human face, helped to confirm this error.

Fieldwork in **Egypt** did not begin until the **Nile** had left the fields. For this reason, the sign for labor was called **Moses** (*Musaeus*), that is: "freed from the water." <note>The author is connecting the Hebrew name Moses—traditionally "drawn from the water"—to a seasonal agricultural symbol.</note> And in its proper place, we shall see that for this same reason, the nine months during which **Horus-Apollo** (representing fieldwork) continued his duties were called the **Nine Muses**.

The custom of announcing political arrangements and the work appropriate to each season through various poses of the "Son of **Osiris**" <note>Here, Osiris represents the sun or the generative power of nature; his "son" Horus serves as a seasonal indicator.</note> led to him being commonly given the name **Menes** <margin>From *Manah*, to count, arrange, or establish.</margin>, which means "Rule for the People" or "Lawgiver." After the **Egyptians** turned this new name into something real and an actual person, they imagined that **Menes** was their first lawgiver and the author of their civil order, and that he had established the calendar and the laws. Consequently, they placed this fictional founder at the head of all the lists of kings in all their various provinces. And because they believed he was legitimately born from the union of **Osiris** (or **Ammon**) and **Isis**, they called him sometimes **Chemmis** <note>original: "Chams Sohn," meaning Son of Ham. See Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*.</note>, and sometimes **Osiris the Younger** <note>Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*.</note>, or even simply Osiris without any addition.

### I B. The Poetic Heaven, 2 C.

Writers whom MARSHAM \*) cites attribute the invention of letters both to Aesculapius and to Thoth. And they do so with good reason, for one is not distinct from the other. Marsham—who held a greater respect and a more particular love for these Egyptian tales than for the Holy Scriptures—rails quite earnestly against those who have so confused matters and falsified history by attributing the honor of an invention to Aesculapius that rightly belongs to Thoth. He reconciles these two opinions as best he can. However, no such reconciliation was necessary here at all, because Aesculapius (or the <term>Dog-Man</term><note>German: "Hundsmann." A personification of the constellation Canis Major</note>) and Thoth (or the <term>Dog-Star</term><note>The star Sirius</note>)—just like Anubis—were merely the names of a symbol that was displayed at the public assemblies to notify the people that the star had been seen rising, and that the flood would soon follow its appearance.

This fourth key to Egyptian writing has produced yet other personages who will also appear in their proper place; and all four together have given rise to entire swarms of gods, from which we shall select only the most famous ones whom our ancestors still worshipped. We do this not only because we have constantly heard these gods spoken of without being able to discover their origin, but primarily because the very events and circumstances that help us toward their discovery [provide a...]

## VI.

### Propagation of the Egyptian Gods: Expansion and Progress of Idolatry.

After we have found—in the misuse of symbolic figures and their confusion with real persons—the origin of those "inhabitants" <note>Referring to the personified gods and constellations</note> whom Egypt devised and placed in the heavens; and if it further appears that the gods of other most famous nations, and the superstitions of which we have not yet spoken, are a mere obvious propagation of Egyptian concepts and customs; then the easy derivation of such varied errors from a single, very simple cause must confirm the correctness of this principle anew, even though it already seems sufficiently proven by what has been cited thus far.

But is it then quite so easy to demonstrate that the Phoenicians, Syrians, Greeks, and all the Westerners <note>German: "Abendländer," referring generally to the peoples of the Mediterranean and Europe</note> whose deities we know, imitated the Egyptians? These people traveled little; since they were satisfied with the abundance they found at home, they did not require foreigners *), and did not seek outside their own country what they gathered at home without difficulty. From this

### VII.

->The Egyptian gods are brought to Asia and Europe by the Phoenicians.<-

Egypt has at all times been the most fertile land in the world and remains so today. An almost reliable harvest, which generally far exceeded the needs of the inhabitants, provided the opportunity to stockpile large reserves of grain there, which served as a refuge for the Arabs, Canaanites, Syrians, and Greeks in years of crop failure. Travelers, drawn there by either curiosity or necessity—but primarily the Phoenicians, who inhabited only a very small coastline at Mount Lebanon and found no safer grain market than Egypt—were all equally astonished by the <term>civil order</term> <note>original: "Policey." In the 18th century, this term referred to the overall administration, public safety, and well-organized governance of a state, rather than just modern law enforcement</note> of such a beautiful country, by the peaceful nature of the inhabitants, and by the mysterious appearance of the customs and feast days, which were celebrated with such great preparation and pomp. Finally, they were also amazed by the abundance, which they regarded as a miracle in a land where it did not rain <note>Egypt’s fertility depends on the annual flooding of the Nile rather than rainfall, a phenomenon that fascinated ancient Mediterranean travelers</note>.

After this language had been divided into different dialects through the lengthening, shortening, or other alteration of the very same words, the children of Noah scattered in hosts, according to the dialect which they could understand. But it is certain that the foundation of the language nevertheless remained, and that the words—although in a different order and with different pronunciation—are found again in Arabic, Syrian, Hebrew, Latin, and even in modern languages. What purpose has it served us, then, to have sought them in the Canaanite language? They might be pronounced according to the Egyptian and Greek manner, and thus they were no longer understood; but if they are taken according to Hebrew, then we understand them. By this means, we still find in them a sense that is in accordance with the intention of the first inventors <note>The "first inventors" refers to the original creators of language or the first post-flood civilizations who established the symbolic systems.</note>. Now, however, this sense almost always relates most closely to the constitutions of society. With the gods and goddesses, on the other hand, the meaning of these words has no relation at all. We are thus on the right path to the truth, and we would do well not to abandon this trail.

Nothing contributed more to humanizing the concept of God, if I may say so (to transform Him into a human being), or rather to directing worship and adoration toward beings who are similar to us.

## VIII.

### The King and the Queen of Heaven,
### the Heavenly Host.

The foreigners did not conduct any extensive investigations into the life and deeds of <term>Ammon</term><note>Ammon (or Amun) was a major Egyptian deity, often identified as the "King of the Gods."</note>, whom the Egyptian people conflated with <term>Osiris</term><note>The god of the afterlife, fertility, and agriculture. The author suggests travelers did not distinguish between these complex figures.</note>. The concept that remained in their minds when they saw this man—the sign of the sun—was simply that he was King, the Lord of Heaven, and the Father of all Good. And if this image had been a part of the ancient <term>Canaanite script</term><note>The author refers to the early pictographic or symbolic communication used by Canaanite peoples, suggesting these religious icons functioned like a shared visual language.</note>, it is no wonder, after he had first become a god in their thoughts, that they also communicated him to other nations, regardless of Osiris or Ammon, which were merely Egyptian names.

<term>Isis</term><note>The mother-goddess and consort of Osiris, associated here with the seasonal calendar.</note> at the side of the great King, the symbol of the festivals according to the seasons, had the appearance and the name of a woman. Her various crowns were a royal ornament. Her beloved son <term>Horus</term> received as many names as he had garments and positions. They <note>Meaning the travelers or the myth-makers.</note> turned these various depictions into just as many distinct persons, serving as an entourage and a courtly household for the King. Travelers brought home the unanimous report of the images and the worship of the King and the Queen of Heaven, and of their numerous entourage. Thus, the kings always went accompanied by the queens and a multitude of friends or an entourage. They were called the <term>Heavenly Host</term><note>Original: *himmlische Heer*. A term often used in the Bible to describe an army of angels; here, the author traces its origin to the visual "court" of Egyptian deities.</note>.

The greatest veneration shown to this mighty celestial body, once it had been transformed into a "King of Heaven," was the practice of dedicating children to it. This was done through an imagined purification ritual, believed to be beneficial to their health, by which the children were made to be permeated by the full power of the Sun's fire. At that time, the concept of a charioteer was not ignoble; rather, in antiquity, it was a highly respectable duty to drive a carriage. This was a common leisure activity for kings and heroes. *) The Greeks, who surpassed other nations in wit and invention, when they adopted the image of the sun, did not find it sufficient to merely place a whip in its hand—which in ancient writing sufficiently denoted the governance of the year—but instead gave it a chariot, fiery horses, and a complete vehicle. **) They depicted the sun, their god, sitting upon a chariot with a radiant face, holding the whip in one hand and the reins in the other, steering four winged horses. This is now a very finely dressed Osiris and Ammon! Even if his Egyptian appearance has been taken away, and though he wears different finery from land to land, he still retains the mark of the ruler, and beneath all that pomp, one still recognizes Osiris. The sign of the sun is always linked with the sign of the Almighty. The Phoenicians also called him Helion, and the Greeks Helios. ***) It is always the same name and blasphemy <note>The author likely uses "blasphemy" to reflect the perspective that these various pagan names were all distortions or "profanations" of the singular divine truth.</note>.

After the Greeks had multiplied their gods—along with the symbols <note>The author uses the term "Sinnbilder" to describe the icons or emblems, like the whip or the sun-disk, which originally had astronomical meanings.</note> which they had adopted without truly understanding—they provided each one with a nearly identical set of attributes, so that they might more easily gain ground and maintain their reputation; they adjusted their finery, attendants, and vehicles according to the prestige of their rank.

The greatest folly among all, however—and it became a general practice—is that they not only confused God with the ruler of heaven and earth (that is, the sun), but they also sought this king and ruler among their own heroes and founders. Thus, the Egyptians found in him their Ammon, the Syrians their Bel, the Cretans their Asterius, and the Arcadians a Jupiter. Because this Jov <note>A variant of Jove or Jupiter.</note> possessed a human form, he was regarded as the king of all the lands where he was worshiped, even though he had actually lived nowhere, for he was merely a symbol of the sun’s path.

## XI.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 194 regarding the Greek transformation of Eastern religious symbols. It moves from the etymology of Aphrodite’s name to the physical evolution of her iconography in sculpture, specifically focusing on how the "horn of plenty" was created through a misunderstanding of seasonal symbols.</meta>

<page-num>195</page-num>
<header>The Lineage of the Gods.</header>

We have already noted that the Greek sculptors could not bear the sight of those terrifying ox or goat horns on their statues. Originally, these horns designated Spring and Winter through the most physical parts of these two figures of the zodiac <note>Taurus the bull and Capricorn the goat</note>. These horns once served as a support for one, or sometimes three, fruit baskets, or for snakes, stalks of grain, and other attached symbolic signs. Their inventors <note>the ancient Egyptians and Phoenicians</note> sought to give the people instructions for their conduct through these shorthand and combined symbols. The Greeks, however, sought only to please by imitating these figures. Thus, the horns and all the strange headdresses had to be removed. Yet they took careful care not to completely strip the goddess of any of her identifying marks. Such a theft would have had dangerous consequences; the least of which would have been a poor harvest and the death of all young livestock. Therefore, none of her ornaments were taken away; rather, they sought only to apply them with more taste and artistry.

They depicted Amaleta <note>likely a variation of Amalthea, the nymph or goat of Greek myth</note>, Aphrodite, the Harvest Queen, such that she grasped a long goat's horn with her left hand, from which stalks of grain, legumes, and tree fruits protruded. In her right hand, she held a sickle or something else. Thus, without any logical reason, they joined the symbol of the approaching harvest with the wild chamois horn <note>the horn of Capricorn</note>, which actually indicated the end of all harvests and the beginning of winter. This is the quite simple origin of the **cornucopia** <term>horn of plenty</term>.

From all these images, various patron gods now emerged. Everyone wanted to have their own. The diverse ornamentation and the many names of the ancient Isis have thus multiplied the status and the beautiful histories of the great mother Rhoea <note>Also known as Rhea, the mother of the Olympian gods.</note>, of Dione the consort of Jupiter, and of his daughter Diana.

Now it is not difficult to guess how this same Diana is sometimes an earthly deity, sometimes the Moon, and sometimes the Queen of Hell. According to her first institution, she belonged to the Earth, for she signified its increase <note>Specifically, the growth of crops and the abundance of nature.</note>. All of pagan antiquity, after conflating the sign of the new moons and the festivals dependent upon them with the celestial body—which, through its various forms (*phases*), ruled the common affairs of men—ascribed to the moon an absolute power over all the fruits of the earth and over all human activities. People were also convinced that the moon knew the future with certainty and never appeared without indicating through sure signs what would befall the farmer, entire families, and whole kingdoms. Even now, this prejudice, which was conceived in ancient times regarding the influence and omens of the moon, has not been entirely abandoned.

If one considers it closely, the moon was certainly placed in the heavens merely so that humans should consult it regarding what they had to do; for the Creator gave it various forms so that it should be a visible measure of time in the sky and a recognizable rule for all activities. With its help, one can precisely determine the length of time that must be applied to every business. However, an error was made therein,

However, the poets are no more in agreement on this point than they are on others, and they tell us many tales of Diana's nightly visits to the shepherd **Endymion**. The origin of this deviation is not obscure. At certain festivals, people celebrated the representation or the memory of the ancient state of the human race. The location for this assembly was a beautiful grotto, a shady forest, or the area surrounding a spring. There, the sign of the new moon was displayed: **Isis** with the moon, and beside her **Horus** <note>In this context, the author refers to the Egyptian deity Horus as a "sign" or symbolic figure used to mark seasons or agricultural cycles.</note>—the symbolic figure required by the season or the specific festival.

If, during this festival of representation, one wished to indicate the rest and security with which God rewards human labor after many hardships, a sleeping Horus was placed in this grotto. This is the source of the scandalous rumors regarding Diana's conduct. The proof of this slander lies in the name of her supposed shepherd; it is simply the name of the place where the sleeping figure was positioned. For **Endymion** signifies, in the Oriental language <note>In 18th-century scholarship, "Oriental language" usually referred to Hebrew, Phoenician, or Syriac.</note>, "the grotto of representation" *).

## XIII.
### Cybele.

This Isis of ours is a maiden of very strict virtue, whose virginity is beyond all suspicion. Let us go into Phrygia <note>An ancient kingdom in the west-central part of Anatolia, in modern-day Turkey.</note>; there, Isis will take on a completely different form according to the pleasure of the people; here she is worshipped as the mother of all the gods. She is carried through the cities in triumph as a model of fertility. The nations rejoice with her that all the gods of the first rank are her children, and that she can embrace a hundred grandchildren *).

The towers which she wears upon her head make her recognizable to us as an Egyptian Isis—as the ancient sign of gratitude which the peoples are obliged to show at their festivals to the one who provides them with food, clothing, and shelter <note>The "towers" refer to the mural crown, a crown representing city walls, which was a standard attribute of Cybele.</note>. The drums or flutes associated with Cybele were the characteristic marks of a festival. And because the most prominent festival of all nations located far from Egypt was that which was celebrated in summer at the beginning of the harvests, it was designated by a key and a lion, because the sun was then in this sign <note>The author refers to the zodiac sign of Leo, which the sun enters in late July, coinciding with harvest times.</note>. This is the origin of the towers, the musical instruments, the key, and the lions, by which Cybele is identified.

# The Race of the Gods.

One might ask me here: who is this Atys who usually accompanies the Phrygian Cybele? He is Osiris under another name. Scholars are in agreement that this word in Phrygia signifies "Lord." One finds monuments where Atys is called "the Highest" <note>original Greek/Latin: "To the mother of all, Rhea, and to Atys the highest." Such a similarity of misfortunes between the husband of Isis and the husband of Cybele would be sufficient to prove that one is the imitation of the other. The rest of their history is a collection of silly and indecent matters that might be well-suited to the crude Phrygians, but which I may surely be permitted to pass over in silence. ## XIV.

### Venus, Ilithyia, Mylitta.

Once Isis had passed through so many different roles and statuses, she took on a new form and became the famous Venus. In antiquity—and still today in the sweet language of our novels and plays—this figure represents two entirely different characters. At times, she is the common, Earthly Venus, the goddess of lust and the mother of pleasure. At other times, she is the Heavenly Venus, who inspires only wisdom and elevates the spirit to profound reflection and spiritual beauty. What could have caused such a strange contrast? Will we find in our Isis the origin of two goddesses whose inclinations and duties are as far apart as heaven and earth? If we recall the secondary symbols or the "finery" of Isis, we shall find the basis for this glittering display.

Isis often wears celestial symbols upon her head, for example: a moon, the Dog Star <note>The star Sirius, which was of great importance to the Egyptian calendar and the flooding of the Nile.</note>, or a sign from the zodiac. This is *Venus Urania*, the Heavenly Venus. Who would not assume that such a figure was occupied with the contemplation of the stars and the highest sciences? The matter is clear: if one is to judge the Heavenly Venus by such marks, then all her thoughts were indeed in the heavens.
