# The Generation of the Gods.

Another version of Isis possessed earthly secondary symbols; for example, various animal heads, many breasts <note>This likely refers to the "multimammia" or many-breasted statues often associated with Artemis/Diana of Ephesus, which the author here connects to Isis.</note>, or a child in her lap. The common people, who no longer understood the meaning of this symbolic language, believed they understood it perfectly. They took this woman to be a fertile mother; and since everything surrounding her related to the procreation and nourishment of humans and animals, they regarded this goddess as the protectress of fertility—a power dedicated to inciting all animals to carnal desire. Although some philosophers revered the first <note>The "Heavenly Venus" or Venus Urania mentioned on the previous page.</note>, the temples of the common and earthly Venus were much more frequently visited. It is incredible how much carnal lust and philosophy have accumulated shameful desires and spiritual (metaphysical) errors by attempting to explain an image that was originally intended only to indicate the seasons and the festivals connected with them.

I do not doubt that the origin of the various roles assigned to Venus will be recognized in the meanings of the adorned Isis, who borrowed her ornaments sometimes from the heavens and sometimes from the earth. But from where did the name Venus originate, which the Latins <note>original: "Lateiner"; the Romans.</note> gave to this supposed goddess of fertility?

I B. Poetic Heaven, 2 C.

When one reads the *Centennial Hymn* <note>original Latin: *Carmen Saeculare*</note> of *Horace* <note>original: *Horatius*</note>, one will wonder how this poet, who so thoroughly understood and observed propriety, could ask *Diana* for something that did not suit the character of the chaste goddess at all. He asks her to assist women in labor; he calls her *Ilithyia* <note>A Greek goddess of childbirth often identified with Artemis/Diana</note>, the *procreative goddess* <note>original Latin: *genitalis diua*</note>, a goddess of generation. He asks her primarily to bless, through successful fertility, the ordinances and laws which the Senate <note>original: *Rath*</note> had enacted to bring the state of marriage into honor. This was a matter for *Venus* or *Juno* rather than for *Diana*. The latter had nothing to do with marriages, for it is said she could not even tolerate the names of "wife" or "mother." How does it happen, then, that these two goddesses have such a great similarity that one can attribute qualities and deeds to one over which the other two would be jealous and protective? These are nothing but difficulties and contradictions if one wishes to settle the dispute by assigning each her own specific office. However, our explanation resolves the dispute if we recognize them all as manifestations of Isis. They are different only because:

> Gently, in the proper way, open the mature births,
> O mild Ilithyia, protect the mothers,
> Whether you prefer the name Lucina,
> Or the Procreative Goddess: bring forth offspring:
> And prosper the decrees of the fathers concerning
> The yoking of women, and the law of marriage
> Prolific with new progeny.
> **HORACE, Centennial Hymn**
> <note>original Latin: *Rite maturos aperire partus / Lenis Ilithya, tuere matres...*</note>

We do not wish to dwell here on the investigation of the origin of the remaining Oriental gods and goddesses. ### Pallas, Pales, Minerva.

The famous Pallas, whom Athens honored, is one and the same as the Pales of the ancient Sabines <note>An ancient Italic tribe living in the central Apennine Mountains</note> and is not distinguished from the Egyptian Isis. But what similarity, scholars might ask, could there be between the Athenian Pallas, the goddess of war and the arts; Pales of the Sabines, the overseer of the festivals of the farmers; and the Egyptian Isis, the Moon and the Queen of Heaven?

That Pallas and the goddess Pales, who was honored at the Palilia <note>An ancient Roman pastoral festival held on April 21st, aimed at cleansing both sheep and shepherds</note>, are one and the same is evident from their similar names and duties. Pales gives laws to the farmers in Italy; Pallas teaches the Athenians advantageous agriculture. Both signify public order. *) The function of Isis was likewise none other than to organize public institutions and to indicate the specific labors for each season through various secondary signs. This equality in customs and the religious worship of both cities has been fully proven by more than one scholar. \*) A similarity in their occupations is just as easy to demonstrate. The Athenians primarily cultivated the olive tree and flax, and these were their most reliable sources of income. They themselves say that Pallas showed them their use, teaching them to make linen and also to plant the olive tree and press out its fruit. ### XVII.
## **M i n o s.**

From the mainland, let us journey to one of the most beautiful islands in the Mediterranean—the first one encountered upon departing from Egypt, namely the island of Crete. Its excellent fruits and vast size attracted a great many inhabitants very early on, who either descended from Egypt or were at least great adherents of the Egyptian religion, for we find among them all the ceremonies and state constitutions of the land of Egypt.

Before we attempt to prove this, let us recall that in the deepest antiquity, it was a general custom to hold festivals at the graves of worthy people in the fatherland and to renew their anniversaries. We find many examples of burials in the lives of the Patriarchs <note>The "Erzväter" or biblical figures like Abraham and Isaac</note> and among secular <term>writers <note>original: "Scribenten"</note></term>. This custom has been passed down from one era to the next. The first Christians, who otherwise carefully avoided any appearance of idolatry, gathered every year at the graves of the martyrs <note>original: "Blutzeugen" or "blood-witnesses"</note> for prayer and held a love-feast <note>Also known as an "Agape feast," a communal meal in early Christianity</note>. Such a custom, which is grounded in the faith of the Patriarchs, is still held in honor among us *) today.

Ever since Egypt adopted the ridiculous misconception that the statues of Osiris, Isis, and Horus were monuments to their founders, and that Osiris had lived in Egypt and was buried there, stories were invented to suit this belief. # I B. Poetic Heaven, 2 C.

If the Egyptian symbols <note>original: "Sinnbilder"</note> brought to Crete all took on a historical appearance there, it was likely because they were taken literally; they looked like monuments of past events, even though they had just as little basis in historical reality in Egypt as anywhere else. This critical point sheds great light on everything preceding it, and it will be well to clarify it further and support it with other circumstances to demonstrate its total certainty.

Because the origins and holy customs of the Cretans were derived from Egypt, they possessed from the very beginning a Labyrinth, or palace, with as many divisions as there are months in the year. In this place, the symbolic images for each month were set up so that the young priests raised there could be taught the order of the heavens and the Egyptian social order <note>original: "Policey," referring here to the organized administration and civic laws of a state</note>. This dwelling of priests and symbols only became "mysteries" <note>Secret religious rites intended only for the initiated</note> over time, once their original true meaning was neglected. This truth is confirmed by the fact that in ancient times, these images and this instruction were displayed and conducted publicly before everyone. This is what DIODORUS SICULUS <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BCE</note> teaches us, and upon this rests everything we have established so far.

### The Dynasty of the Gods.

Furthermore, because the Cretans derived their origins and civic administration <note>original: "Policey," referring to the organized social and political structure of a state</note> from Egypt, they also divided themselves into three classes: the priests, the farmers, and the craftsmen or smiths. These last were the weakest and poorest in the colony. They applied themselves to the mines and the smelting of metals. They lived in forests, primarily in the valleys of Mount Ida, where they found ore in abundance and sufficient wood to refine copper and iron and to forge useful tools for the inhabitants. These workers were called Dactyls *)—that is, the poor of the colony. What *Diodorus Siculus* **) and the Arundel Marbles <note>A collection of ancient Greek inscriptions and sculptures, also known as the Marmora Oxoniensia</note> report of these Dactyls—that they discovered the use of iron, fire, and the hammer—is based merely on their rank in the colony: they were the smiths within it.

—through new hardships, were forced to seek clothing, build huts, and invent arts.

— *Sharpening mortal hearts with cares*
*So that practice, through meditation, might forge various arts.*
<note>original: "Curis acuens mortalia corda / Ut varias usus meditando extunderet artes." This is a quote from Virgil’s *Georgics* (Book I), which describes how the gods introduced struggle to the world to prevent humanity from becoming lazy, thereby sparking the invention of technology and culture.</note>

From the ancient world <note>The world before the Great Flood</note>, the habit remained of lightly covering oneself with a mere animal skin and protecting oneself from the sun’s heat in tents. These tents were composed of skins and had been invented by one of the children of Lamech *). After the Deluge <note>The Great Flood</note>, this defense against heavy rains, severe cold, and violent winds proved too weak. From then on, the entire body was covered with the skins of the animals that provided food, primarily with buck- and goat-skins, which were the most supple. The hunt sometimes provided unusual clothing that also brought honor. Whoever appeared in a lion or tiger skin drew all eyes upon themselves and announced a beneficial victory. Time and experience eventually taught humans to spin sheep’s wool and goat hair, and to make clothes for themselves that were softer and could be easily washed.

Once the arts were invented and improved through new trials, the memory of the harshness of the earliest times remained. The comparison of the labor which the human race initially endured with the comfortable inventions of later times ensured that the rural festivals <note>The author refers to "Landfeste," likely meaning Bacchic or agricultural festivals</note> representing this first state of existence were much more vivid than all others.

## The Race of the Gods.

A significant aspect of these festivals was that people appeared dressed in the skins of bucks *), chamois, tigers, and other tame and wild animals. They stained their faces with blood to carry upon themselves a mark of the dangers they had endured and the victory they had achieved.

Instead of blood, they often applied a light coating of wine dregs <note>The sediment or "lees" left over from winemaking</note> or mulberry juice, which was not as disgusting as animal blood on the face of the performing person and was more aesthetically pleasing. *She paints her forehead and temples with blood-red mulberries* **). <note>original: "Sanguineis frontem moris et tempora pingit"</note>

This is the makeup of the most prominent figure in the Bacchanalia <note>Festivals held in honor of Bacchus, the god of wine and theater</note> whom Virgil introduces. However, because the wine dregs were easier to obtain at the beginning of winter, when the festival was celebrated, they were used by everyone who represented the retinue in the Bacchic procession; and subsequently by all actors ***); for comedy was, after all, a consequence or an extension of the Bacchic festivals, the institution of which also aimed at the representation of the past.

Everything then transformed into masquerade, roaming about, howling, and nonsense, and people vied with one another to commit follies. They no longer merely wore buck and goat skins, but rather preferred to disguise themselves entirely as bucks and tigers, putting on goat or deer horns.

### I B. Poetic Heaven, 2 C.

The performances of these women, who sought to outdo one another in the laments and poses authorized by custom, were therefore called **Maniae** <note>The author connects this to "Manes," which he previously defined as ritual regulations, though it also evokes the Greek word for madness</note>. They were also called **Thyades** *), that is, roamers, when they scattered across the mountains like hunters; and **Bassarides** **), that is, vintagers, because these festivals were celebrated after the grape harvest, when the new wine could be enjoyed.

Behind all this swarm and procession, an old man finally came riding slowly and calmly on a donkey ***), offering wine to the weary youths and exhorting everyone to rest a little. Who might this figure be, who brings the procession to a close? Judging from the man upon the peaceable beast of burden, from the jug hanging from his arm †), from his encouraging words to the hunters, and finally from the name **Silenus**—which signifies health, rest, and an encouragement to stillness—one can clearly see that in this representation, he is meant to represent the state of the elderly, who are exempt from this roaming about due to their age; or else he represents that quiet rest which is the reward for all field work and for the hunts completed against the wild animals in the area.

### I B. The Poetic Heaven, etc.

I will not repeat what has already been said; however, I must necessarily remind you that **Menes** <note>traditionally considered the first human king of Egypt</note>, the symbol of civil constitution, became a teacher of the human race—namely, the legislator **Bacchus** <gloss>Lawgiver, Shepherd, legislator <note>original Greek and Latin: "Νομοθετης , Νομευς, legislator"</note></gloss>. **Horace** <note>the leading Roman lyric poet during the time of Augustus</note>, who was very pleased by his teachings <gloss>I saw Bacchus on remote rocks teaching songs—believe it, posterity! <note>original Latin: "Bacchum in remotis carmina rupibus Vidi docentem, Credite posteri." In all seriousness, within the ridiculous wonders that the poets attribute to **Bacchus**, one can still find all the praises of agriculture. And this provides new proof that these symbols were eventually transformed into real historical persons.

It is agriculture, and not **Bacchus**—for he is but an empty sound and a thought—that learned to provide for the flooding of rivers and the powerful surges of water; agriculture laid reins upon the streams or set up dams against them, researched the height of the silt buildup, and kept the inhabitants safe by means of sufficiently constructed mounds <gloss>You turn the rivers, you turn the barbarian sea <note>original Latin: "Tu flectis amnes, tu mare barbarum." The symbol of agriculture, rather than a man transformed into a god after death, for a long time indicated various tasks necessary for life and the means to sustain all generations through its festivals. This was signified during the festivals of **Bacchus** by carrying a golden snake and casting it toward the onlookers †) . This was meant to show that no sustenance or harvest could be expected if they did not strictly observe everything ordained for them from one season to the next. However, this snake, once a simple image of life <term>image of life</term> <note>Ancient Mediterranean cultures often used the serpent as a symbol of renewal or vital force due to its shedding of skin</note>, took on a wondrous appearance through the work of ever-inventive poets. It became a sign of **Bacchus's** power and authority. Everyone at the festival could play with it without danger; women even used it as a ribbon to bind their hair.

### XIX.

->Apollo, Belenus, Latona.<-

One sometimes sees images of Anubis and Isis with a tortoise, a duck, or a lizard. <note>original German: "Eydere" and "Eidex," archaic forms of "Eidechse" (lizard).</note> \*) These animals have the characteristic of living sometimes in the water and sometimes on the land, as they require both, and as the water rises, they always seek out the heights. Such a lizard in Isis’s hand, or an image that was half-woman and half-lizard, signaled that it was time to reach the high ground and to stock up on olives, dried figs, flour, malt, and other non-perishable foodstuffs, so that one could survive as long as the flood <note>Specifically referring to the annual inundation of the Nile in Egypt.</note> remained. I immediately surmised that this was the interpretation of the sign carried by the Egyptian Isis during the impending flood, and that she was then given the name *Leto* or *Latona*, for that was the name of this lizard \*\*). My conjecture became a certainty when I encountered this Isis in ancient monuments with the head and shoulders of a woman and the body, feet, and tail of a lizard \*\*\*).

<header>The Generations of the Gods.</header>

<margin>Q 3</margin>

When the Nile water receded from the fields early enough, leaving time a month before the Sun entered Sagittarius, the Egyptian farmer was assured that he could measure the boundaries of his fields at leisure and sow before winter, and that he need not worry until the harvest. This was called "forcing the Nile." This was called obtaining a complete victory over the enemy. \*) This circumstance, so pleasant for Egypt, was represented by a Horus armed with arrows, conquering Python. Horus was thereafter indiscriminately called the Farmer, the Victor, or the Destroyer. \*\*) Isis was given the name Dione, or Diana (meaning Abundance), and a quail was placed in her hand, the name of which also signified welfare or security. \*\*\*) One could not paint "security" itself; instead, an object was shown whose name prompted the thought.

When these images were brought to the island of Delos by some stranger, they presumably gave rise to the fable of Latona. It was claimed she was pursued by a cruel enemy and enclosed in the sea:

We have already seen how the Egyptian figures take on new forms in Crete, Boeotia, Africa, Phrygia, and elsewhere, transforming into unique local histories. When Isis and Horus were brought to the island of Delos and to Ionia, they inspired the stories of the birth of Apollo and Diana on that island and in Ephesus. The victory of Horus—that is, the husbandman <note>original: *Landmannes*; here used to represent the agriculturalist who drains the land and overcomes the chaotic swamp</note>—over the hostile dragon gave rise to well-founded celebrations in Egypt. In Delos and throughout all of Greece, however, these festivals were also celebrated, as if this victory had been particularly beneficial to those lands as well. Everywhere, the festival of the Pythian Apollo was observed with the greatest solemnity; and I am not certain whether the skin of the terrible dragon was not displayed somewhere as an irrefutable monument to the service Apollo had rendered to the human race by slaying the dragon (Python). Such proofs were not even necessary to rouse the people; there was singing, dancing, and theatrical performances at the Pythian festivals, and that was sufficient to maintain their strict observance.

The sea monster, the monstrous dragon slain by Horus, had previously harmed Osiris and driven him away for a time; however, Osiris eventually returned and gained the upper hand. In Greece, Horus was conflated with Osiris, and they knew only of a defeated Python. Osiris’s struggle with the Python referred to the Great Deluge <note>original: *Sündfluth*; the author interprets the "dragon" or "Python" as a personification of the muddy, destructive waters of a great flood</note>. One did not exactly forget that Osiris was the Sun; yet this led to Apollo being confused with Osiris—the original vanquisher of the Python—and thus Apollo also became the Sun, while never ceasing to be the son of Jupiter. Necessarily, this figure now had to have a different realm. Jupiter was left with the scepter and the dominion over heaven and earth; but the chariot, the whip, and the reins were given to Apollo. This is the reason why one so often encounters the <term>attributes</term> <note>original: *Merkzeichen*; the symbolic objects or icons identifying a deity</note> of one god associated with another.

Horus Apollo, who originally related solely to the agricultural year and the arrangement of labor, was all the more readily mistaken for the Sun—the regent of nature—because the whip and the other symbols of the Sun were placed into Horus's hands. This was done to represent the characteristics of the solar year and the labors associated with it in a concise form. Thus, Horus became one and the same as the Moloch of the Ammonites, the Adonis of Byblos, the Bel of other cities in Phoenicia, and the radiant Belenus <note>A Celtic sun god often equated with Apollo</note> whom Gaul worshipped. This charioteer upon the wagon that illuminates the world is the son of Jupiter. Now Osiris, Horus, Apollo, Bacchus, and the Sun are all conflated. The Egyptians were, among all peoples, those who believed they knew antiquity best, yet knew it the least. They took the symbols to be actual human beings who had ruled over them. ### Hercules.

Whenever predatory animals multiplied greatly, or when some raging beast or even a powerful highwayman made the land unsafe, they did not send a whole army, nor did they call up the common people, but only the most tried-and-tested in warfare <term>Kriegswesen: the art, conduct, and systems of military activity</term>, those who had particularly distinguished themselves, and perhaps even volunteers who offered themselves for such an undertaking. # The Lineage of the Gods.

I do not wish to deny that in Greece, shortly before the Trojan War, there may have been a more famous adventurer, a conqueror of the strong, and a destroyer of robbers, to whom—out of honor—all the previously known deeds of so many imaginary Hercules figures were simultaneously attributed. It seems this Hercules left behind descendants who established themselves several times in the Peloponnese. However, it is the same with most of his deeds as it is with his genealogy, which is nothing more than a Phoenician plaything <note>original: "Spielwerk," suggesting a clever but trivial fabrication or a linguistic trick</note>. They called their Hercules *Ben Alcum* or *Ben Alcmen* *), the invincible son. This is presumably the reason why the Greek Hercules was passed off as a son of Alcmene. His history is full of things whose wondrous nature likewise boils down to the interpretation of several ambiguous Phoenician words, serving as proof that most of his adventures have no basis in history. I believe I have sufficiently convinced the reader of this. Without tiring him with individual examples, we would rather see the gods arise one after another and judge from their fictitious origins how little weight should be given to their deeds.

# I B. Poetic Heavens, 2 C.

### XXII.

#### Vulcan, Hephaestus, Mulciber.

How should we make use of this strange figure? A hideous man, one of whose legs is dislocated and much shorter than the other? He holds in his hand a hammer, tongs, or some other smithing tool. He is made the husband of Venus and is called Vulcan, Hephaestus, and Mulciber <note>Mulciber likely comes from the Latin "mulcere," meaning to soften, referring to how fire softens metal</note>. The people of Lemnos <note>an island in the northern Aegean Sea</note> called him Jupiter's son and recounted: His mother Juno was dissatisfied with his appearance and pushed him out of heaven by one foot; it is said he fell for three whole days before reaching the earth, and on their island, he broke a leg from the violent fall. They add that he compensated for his ugliness through extraordinary diligence and made his peace with his exile by devoting himself to the smelting of metals and the manufacture of all kinds of tools in the caves of Mount Mosychlus. The Sicilians and the inhabitants of the Liparian island of Strongoli <note>modern-day Stromboli, famous for its active volcano</note> boast, as do those of Lemnos, that this god resided there, claiming he chose their fire-spewing mountain as his preferred workshop. The same was said of the chasms of Mount Ida in Crete, and of another mountain in Phrygia.

We should not doubt that Horus, with the signs we indicated in the previous sections, referred to the labors of the husbandman <note>Landmann: a farmer or tiller of the soil</note>. ### XXIII.
## Atlas.

Might there also have been a special symbol for the priests, just as there were for the peasants and the smiths? This sign, intended for the instruction of the priests, was presumably not displayed in public gatherings, but was instead set up in a tower or a labyrinth <note>the author suggests these locations were private centers for study and ritual rather than public spaces</note>. If we can find another Horus figure with attributes that clearly aim at the instruction of the priesthood, then our conjectures gain new strength through this entire context.

We know from the reports of Herodotus, Diodorus, Plutarch, and other ancients that contemplation was the primary occupation of the Egyptian priests, who led a very secluded life. They applied themselves to the knowledge of the stars, the course of the celestial bodies and the year, the movement of the air, the return of certain winds, the rising of the Nile, and the ebb and flow of the Arabian Gulf <note>referring to the Red Sea</note>. They also studied the geography of the mainland and the islands, as well as remote lakes and lands; they focused on the calendar of festivals, the lunar cycle, eclipses, the aspects of the planets and stars, geometry, and especially land surveying <term>Feldmessen: the practice of measuring land, crucial in Egypt for re-establishing boundaries after the annual Nile floods</term>. In a word, their occupation was a diligent and laborious

### Proteus.

According to the fable, Proteus held the office of tending the seals <note>The original German uses *Meerkälber*, literally "sea-calves," a historical term for seals.</note> or sea-horses that pull Neptune’s chariot. In truth, Proteus is the sign <note>The author continues his "Euhemerist" approach, suggesting that myths are actually misunderstood historical records or public symbols used in antiquity.</note> which signifies the trade of Egyptian produce in exchange for servants, livestock, metal, wine, and other goods that were brought from Phoenicia to Pharos, the only accessible harbor at that time. The ships collected their necessary grain, flax, and other fruits of this land there. One can also believe that the fable had its basis in the figures of the slave, the horse, the cask, and other signs that were displayed in Egyptian assemblies to show what the fleet primarily brought in; and which were therefore called *Proteus*, that is, the exchange of the fruits of the earth.

### XXV.
### Proteus.

According to the fable, Proteus had the duty of tending the seals <note>original: "Meerkälber" or sea-calves</note> or seahorses that pull Neptune’s chariot. He held a muster of them at the island of Pharos; and he provided them all with fodder; and if someone approached him, he transformed himself into a man, a woman, a sheep, a horse, and took whatever shape he wished.

Now we have encountered a large number of famous men and women who, in my opinion, we can strike entirely from history. ### I B. Poetic Heaven, 2. C.

<meta>catchword: Ben</meta>

In later times, it pleased them to seek something miraculous and mysterious in everything in this manner. The calculations we have seen, and some others they received from the priests who were their predecessors, were uncommonly simple things. However, they were afterwards taken for the duration of the reigns of their kings, whom they placed in the **Dog Star** <note>The star Sirius, which signaled the flooding of the Nile.</note> and other celestial bodies. One lived for 1,460 years <note>This refers to the Sothic cycle, the time it takes for the Egyptian solar calendar to realign with the rising of the star Sirius.</note>, and another even longer. 

Astronomical calculations, based on various hypotheses and announcements of the periodic orbits of the planets, were the priests' primary occupation. Because these calculations were always found in the journals of the most diligent scholars under men's names—for example, Anubis, Thoth, Menes, Osiris, and others who had been placed among the stars—they were mistaken for the duration of the earthly lives of these gods. This is the origin of this ancient Egyptian history, which is traced back so very far into the past. 

Their ancient kings are the names of celestial bodies, and their years of life are the calculation of the time in which a planet completes its orbit around the heavens. In this way, astronomical calculation as well as **pictorial writing** <note>hieroglyphics</note> were grossly misused; and it is now clear that if one subtracts from Egyptian wisdom a little <term>astronomy</term> <note>original: "Sternkunde"</note>, <term>geometry</term>, and a great taste and talent for architecture, then all their remaining learning falls into history and religion, and degenerates into foolishness.

### Where does the staff of *Mercury* likely get the name *Caduceus*?

In the Orient, every person of high standing and dignity carried a scepter *) or staff of honor; and many-

---

*) The proof of this custom is found in the Holy Scriptures on several occasions. When the prophetess Deborah, in her song of praise, blesses the leaders of the half-tribe of Manasseh who lived beyond the Jordan for coming to the aid of God’s people, she presents them to us with a staff of command in their hands. When the tribes grumbled because the priesthood was to remain solely with Aaron’s family, their leaders received the command to bring their staffs into the Tabernacle. By the next morning, Levi’s staff, which Aaron carried, had blossomed; and the Scripture notes that every other leader took his staff back again. This sign of distinction was so closely associated with the head of every great family that, in the languages of the East, a tribe has no name other than "scepter"; therefore, the twelve (scepter) staffs of Jacob signify the twelve tribes of Israel; and if one wanted to say "the tribe of Levi" or "the tribe of Judah," it could only be said as "the scepter of Levi" or "the staff of Judah." When the Scripture wishes to indicate the two excellent craftsmen whom Moses employed in the construction of the Tabernacle, it says of Oholiab <note>Original: "Halialib"</note> (Exodus <note>Original: "2 B. Moſ." (Second Book of Moses)</note> 31) that he was of the scepter of Dan, and of Bezalel, that he was of the staff of Judah. Here, my reader will permit me to make a digression that should prove useful to him. In connection with this staff of honor, I wish to note that the famous prophecy regarding the scepter of Judah has been completely obscured because the staff in question has been mistaken for a royal scepter— <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; the author is likely referring to Genesis 49:10 and arguing that "scepter" refers to tribal identity rather than kingship.</note>

...the fourth year a whole day, and after eight by two days too early, and if one continues in this manner, the beginning of the year recedes through the entire calendar <note>The author is describing the "Sothic cycle" or the "Vague Year" of the Egyptians, which consisted of 365 days and lacked a leap year, causing the calendar to shift one day every four years.</note>. However, the custom was always observed, during the solemn procession of Isis—which was the first festival of the year—to send the god Anubis, the gatekeeper of the festival, ahead. From this, it can be seen that everything was more astronomical than historical. This is evidently the same as Janus in Latium <note>Latium: The region of central-western Italy in which the city of Rome was founded.</note>, who, along with the title of gatekeeper, also possessed his characteristics. And the genealogy of Mercury confirms everything we have said. He is the son of the beautiful Maia, and the grandson of Atlas. Maia refers to the Pleiades, that small cluster of stars in the constellation Taurus <note>the Bull</note> so well known even to the common people; the peoples of the East called these stars *Maah*, that is, "a hundred," or a multitude. The Greeks partly retained the first name, Maia; and partly translated it as *Pleiades* or *Pleione*, which also signify a multitude. Since these highly noticeable stars were convenient for the establishment of astronomy, and were the first to catch the eye before the rising of the Dog Star <note>Sirius</note>; great effort was made to first introduce these "forerunners of the Dog"—alongside the Hyades—to the apprentices of the Egyptian priests within the "Sphere of Atlas" <note>Atlas was often depicted as holding the celestial globe, representing the study of the heavens</note>. Because this sign was treated as a god, all these instructions were likewise turned into history; these stars, through which the knowledge of other stars was made easy, became the "beloved daughters" of the teaching Atlas. Maia withdrew from the rays of the sun when it was in Gemini <note>the Twins</note>, that is, in May, and this may well have given rise to the name of that month. ...be able to understand the reason why a **Dog** or a **Capricorn** was placed beside him *), especially when he held a **full pouch** in his hand? It is undoubtedly certain that the later Greeks and Romans arranged these symbols according to the erroneous concepts of their **mythology** <note>German: *Fabellehre*</note>, and applied everything to the ridiculous stories attributed to him. Regarding the **full pouch** in his hand—the **symbol of trade** <term>Handelszeichen; Mercury's traditional money bag</term>—ancient monuments often include the head of a **Capricorn**. This quite naturally indicated the period for the sale of summer and autumn harvests, lasting until the sun entered the constellation of Capricorn, which occurs in **December**. However, once Anubis was transformed from a celestial sign into a **god of trade and deception**, these simple images were distorted into mythological events, superstitions, and wretched allegorical references. Anyone with an interest in such things can find them everywhere in the works of **Natalis Comes** <note>Natale Conti (1520–1582), a famous Italian mythologist</note> and **Cantari** <note>likely Vincenzo Cartari (1531–1569), author of a famous book on the images of the gods</note>.

If, according to the fable, *Daedalus* fled from *Crete* to *Sicily*; if the Cretan King *Minos*, angry with him, pursued him to this island and built the city of *Minoa* there for amusement: it does not follow that there must be a monument of *Minos’s* journey there or anywhere else; for he is just as much a non-entity <note>original: "Unding," referring to a fictional or mythological construct</note> as *Daedalus*. Instead, because people found the same names and signs in *Crete* and *Sicily*, they sought to bring a connection into the

...to bring things into a **whole**. In both Crete and Sicily, people were familiar with the *Manes* <note>The author here defines the Latin term "Manes"—traditionally referring to ancestral spirits—as "feast days and ordinances"</note>, that is, festival days and regulations. At these festivals, the same words were used, even if they were no longer understood. They were part of the ceremony, and people were accustomed to them. New cities were given their names based on these festivals and the most pleasant celebrations associated with them; and because these names were found in entirely different locations, people invented histories and journeys from one place to another in order to bring a connection to things that did not actually belong together.

In Attica <note>original: "Attien"</note> and the islands of the Archipelago <note>The Aegean Sea</note>, Icarus was well known, but in a completely different way than in Crete. On these islands, it was remembered that Icarus was a farmer; however, the knowledge had become confused, specifically that *Mera* <note>The dog of Icarus in myth; here linked to the star Sirius</note> referred to the Dog Star when no wind blew at its rising, and the pitiful state of *Erigone* <note>The daughter of Icarus, associated with the constellation Virgo</note> during the "fall" of *Anubis*. That is, the sadness associated with the sign of the Virgin <note>The constellation Virgo</note> when the north wind failed to swell the Nile during the Dog Days. Since people understood nothing of all this—which was only intelligible in Egypt—the following story arose from the combination of these well-understood and misunderstood parts:

## The Generation of Gods.

Our Horus, motionless and without feet, was the natural sign of the inactivity in which all Egypt remained from the rising of Anubis <note>referring to the Dog Star, Sirius</note> until the time of the land measurements. This inactivity lasted until the end of the year if the water had not reached a sufficient height. However, after the "flight of Daedalus"—that is, when Anubis, through many days of sustained north winds, had provided a sufficient depth of water—the images of Isis and Horus were presented in a freer posture. The countryman saw that he once again had eyes, hands, and feet. Here we find the origin of our celebrated sculptor <note>the Greek myth of Daedalus describes him as the first to create statues with open eyes and separated legs, a concept the author traces back to Egyptian seasonal symbols</note>. It is true that, in time, the Egyptians—who no longer understood the meaning of the signs that reappeared at every festival according to ancient custom—sought great mysteries beneath them. They especially replicated these swaddled figures because of their wondrous appearance; hence, they are found everywhere *). However, it follows from their very abundance that they date from later periods, and that they do not in the least prove the historical truth of the story of Daedalus. Whatever the Egyptian imagination might have associated with these bandages and wrappings concerns us little. They were mere trifles regarding their invented mythology, and empty, newly devised allegories.

---

*) See the *Isis Tablet* <note>original Latin: *Tabulam Isidis*</note> and the *Collection* <note>original French: *le Recueil*</note> of MONTFAUCON.

One could with good reason complain about my silence if I did not wish to answer the objection taken from the famous statue of Memnon, which, according to the account of Philostratus <note>Flavius Philostratus (c. 170–250 AD), a Greek scholar who wrote about the life of Apollonius of Tyana</note>, had its feet together and produced a sound at the rising of the sun. But who does not see that it is an image of Horus with the surname Menes or Menoph, whom Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist and author</note> also calls Menon, and whom people considered a legislator of Egypt because this statue served as a rule <note>a standard or guide</note> for the people? It has been said that this image directed itself exactly according to the sun: because Horus was in truth nothing other than an indication of what the countryman had to do every day of the year. In regard to the night, he had nothing to say to them. His teachings were meant solely to determine what should be done at every sunrise according to the season. Therefore, one took the opportunity—initially as a joke, which was later accepted in earnest—to say it was a speaking image that let its voice be heard with the rising of the sun.

There they were called *Cabiri* <note>original footnote: derived from the Hebrew/Phoenician "Cabbirim," meaning "the powerful ones"</note>, that is, powerful gods; and the Phoenician name *Cabiri* was as common in Egypt as in Phoenicia itself. This demonstrates a constant mixture of Phoenician words within the Egyptian language, even where the underlying roots are not entirely the same.

Since the figures of these gods—created by joining together various parts that are not usually found together—originally had a specific, intended meaning, they necessarily took on a strange, even ridiculous appearance once their interpretation was no longer understood. These branches, horns, wings, and spheres upon the heads of an *Osiris*, a *Horus*, and an *Isis* must have seemed wondrous and laughable to those who were not accustomed to them. **HERODOTVS** <note>referring to Book 3 (Thalia), section 37; the text notes section 77, likely a citation error or different edition</note> also notes that Cambyses <note>the Persian King who conquered Egypt in 525 BC</note> was forced to laugh heartily at the *Cabiri* and the limping *Vulcan* <note>the Roman name for the Greek Hephaestus, the smith-god</note> when he entered their temple and that of the smith-god.

I B. Poetic Heaven, 2 C.

One could reasonably complain about my silence if I did not wish to answer the objection taken from the famous **Pillar of Memnon**, which, according to the account of **Philostratus** <note>Flavius Philostratus (c. 170–250 AD), a Greek sophist who described the statue in his "Life of Apollonius of Tyana"</note>, had its feet together and emitted a sound at the rising of the sun. But who does not see that it is an image of **Horus** <note>the Egyptian sky god, often associated with the sun</note> with the surnames **Menes** or **Menoph**, whom **Pliny** <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, Roman author of "Natural History"</note> also calls **Menon**, and who was considered a legislator of the land of Egypt because this pillar served as a rule for the people? It has been said that this image directed itself precisely according to the sun, because **Horus** was in truth nothing other than an indicator of what the farmer had to do every day of the year. In regard to the night, he had nothing to say to them. His teachings were intended solely to determine what should be done at every sunrise according to the season. Therefore, people took the opportunity to say—at first as a joke, but later accepted in earnest—that it was a speaking image that made its voice heard at the rising of the sun.

ness, nevertheless, refers precisely to these. Namely, the division into three Graces, three Furies, three Fates <note>original: "Parcen," referring to the Parcae or Moirai who spin the thread of life.</note>, and three Harpies. These twelve peculiar images are, in fact, the sequence of the Egyptian months designated according to the seasons.

The Charites, or Graces, are, as we have seen, the months of *) July, August, and September.

The Furies, or Eumenides <note>original: "Eumenides," a Greek euphemism meaning "the kindly ones," used to avoid invoking the Furies' wrath.</note>, with snakes upon their heads and torches in their hands **) were considered by the Greeks to be fit for nothing else than to torture the godless (in the underworld) in Tartarus <note>The deep abyss in Greek mythology used as a dungeon of torment for the wicked.</note>: the poets assign them this task whenever they do not occasionally let them depart to instigate some evil undertaking or to drive a nation into a frenzy.

All these fables have their basis in the visual figure; however, the intention of the original institution was quite different. These images are one and the same as the Gorgons and Medusa, and they designated the three autumn months, which are, so to speak, the providers for the Egyptians, because during these months beer was brewed, and wine, olives, and fruit were pressed. The meaning of the snake is well known <note>Likely referring to the Egyptian symbol of the uraeus or the serpent as a guardian of sacred cycles.</note>. The torches were the sign of a sacrifice. Two quails—that is, safety and salvation—fully demonstrate the purpose of the image. The names of these three months refer to the beverages that Egypt obtained during them. The

The name **Furies** \*) signifies "winepresses," and **Eumenides** \*\*) signifies "nurturers."

The **Fates** <note>original: "Parcen," referring to the Parcae or Moirai</note> are the three months of January, February, and March; these were the three "spinning months" in Egypt and Greece. They are depicted with a weaver's beam, a distaff, a spindle, scissors, and other tools for spinning and weaving, as these activities were most common during these three months. For this reason, they bear the name **Parc**, which signifies linen, a veil, or a sail \*\*\*).

Since the Greeks understood nothing of the actual labor represented by these three goddesses, they reimagined them as spinning the lives of men. According to their fables, whichever name was drawn from the Urn of Fate—in which all our names are constantly shaken together—the goddesses would let that person’s thread...

...brought refreshments and healthy food to the coasts in Lycia. Bellerophon signifies, according to the letters of the name, healthy nourishment, or a store for the inhabitants to restore health *).

The story of Perseus and Andromeda is likewise a common expression from which a fable has been made. In the Hebrew and Phoenician languages, it is very common to call cities and lands "daughters" of rocks, deserts, rivers, and other frequently occurring things. Thus, Jerusalem is often called the Daughter of Zion—that is, the daughter of dryness; or likewise, the daughter of the parched hills upon which she lay. According to Strabo's report **), the actual Palestine was a long-stretched coastline full of rocks and sandy regions. From Joppa <note>modern-day Jaffa</note>, which is almost the only harbor, all the way to Gaza, it is surrounded by rocks and steep shores. On the other side, if one went from the borders of stony Arabia to the Sirbonian Lake <note>original: "See Sirbonides"; a lagoon on the Mediterranean coast of Egypt</note> and Mount Casius, it was, according to the same Strabo, an infertile land covered with sand ***), where the flood covering all of Egypt ceased and lost itself in this sand. ## XXXIII.

### The Argonauts.

The inhabitants of *Colchis* <note>An ancient region on the coast of the Black Sea, in modern-day Georgia</note> are said to have been an ancient Egyptian family. Almost all writers agree on this \*), and one finds proof in **HERODOTUS** \*\*) that they are still similar in various ways. They were dark-skinned and had curly hair like the Egyptians. Presumably, they had adopted circumcision since the times of *Joseph*, because his family was still freshly remembered by them, and Egypt owed its prosperity to him; or they were *Ishmaelites*. I would most prefer to believe that the introduction of this custom in *Colchis* came from the ten tribes of *Israel* who were initially scattered in these regions and then throughout the entire North. The Colchians had the same language and customs as the Egyptians; and like them, they applied themselves primarily to linen weaving. **Strabo** \*\*\*) gives these same marks of their origin and adds this circumstance, remarkable for us, that their land †) produced much flax, hemp, wax, and pitch; that their linen weaving was very famous, and their

Moreover, it is well known to everyone that the River **Phasis** <note>The modern-day Rioni River in Georgia</note> carries gold grains or gold flakes as it flows through **Colchis**; these are caught on the banks using sheepskins or coarse (hairy) fabrics, as is still done to this day, because these grains become entangled in the wool and stick to it. We need nothing more than this specific circumstance, unique to Colchis, to explain the famous fable of the **Argonauts** <note>In Greek mythology, a band of heroes who sailed with Jason to retrieve the Golden Fleece</note>.

Since the Colchians shared the same customs as the Egyptians, they likely announced their collective tasks through public signs in order to determine their beginning and duration. Their river did not fertilize the fields, as the Nile does in Egypt; however, in its season, it brought gold grains, the gathering of which made the inhabitants wealthy and supported their livelihood. When the time for this <term>gold-harvest</term> <note>original: "Goldlese"; referring to the seasonal collection of gold from the river</note> arrived, they certainly could not allow this precious treasure to reach the sea. They had to scatter themselves far enough along the banks of the **Phasis**, placing sheepskins with their wool intact against the rocks, the roots of strong trees, and at the bends of the river to catch the grains. Thus, they marked the beginning of such an important labor with a public sign: a pole upon which a skin was attached with a loop. The sign of a fleece was quite natural for this occasion. They

When the <term>gold-harvest</term> <note>original: "Goldlese"; the seasonal collection of gold grains from the river</note> was finished, and the people had to be called back to an even more necessary business—namely, spinning flax and making linen—the signs were changed. **Isis**, who signified the beginning of linen weaving, carried a weaver’s shuttle and bore the name **Argonioth**, which means shuttle-work **).

When the Greeks, who came to **Colchis** to purchase rope or linen, tried to pronounce this word, they said *Argonaus*, which means the ship **Argo**. When they asked what the "little ship" in Isis's hand meant (for the weaver’s shuttle truly has the shape and name of a "little ship" <note>In German, a weaver's shuttle is called a *Weberschiffchen* or "little weaver-ship"</note>), the Colchians presumably said that this little ship was an instruction for the people, that everyone should consult it and learn from it what they had to do. Here we have the first foundation of the fable of the ship **Argo**, which gave answers to all who questioned it. These first basic strokes are enough for us. The embellishments that poetic wit and idle sailors have added to it no longer concern our matter.

### XXXIV.
## Argus.

The explanation of the preceding fable suggests another to us; as childish as it is, it has often occupied the greatest poets and the most skilled painters. It is the fable of **Argus**.

**Juno** became jealous of her husband’s <note>Jupiter's</note> behavior, stole his beautiful **Isis**, transformed her into a cow, and gave her to **Argus** to guard. Argus had a hundred eyes, some of which were always awake while the others rested. However, **Mercury**, who wanted to steal the cow from Argus, used songs to lull all hundred eyes to sleep and carried **Isis** away. Now, what is the meaning behind this fable? If I am not mistaken, it arose in this way.

**Weaving** was in vogue in **Athens**, on the island of **Amorgus** *), in **Colchis**, as well as in **Egypt**; however, the time for work was not the same in these countries. In Egypt, people were busy cleaning ditches, making hay, harvesting grain, and threshing in the months of February, March, May, and April. In contrast, in Athens, Amorgus, and Colchis, during these months they continued with spinning thread and weaving linen, which they had already begun before the winter. They laid the distaff—

If the inhabitants of **Colchis** then had the same customs as the **Egyptians**, then **Isis**—the festival sign—whenever she indicated the new moons and other winter or spring festivals, must have had a **Horus** with her who indicated a labor that was to last for six months in succession. This figure was completely covered with open eyes to designate a work at which one must be very vigilant <note>meaning: "always watchful"</note>. When Isis laid aside the horns of the wild goat—the sign of winter—she took the sign of the cow in spring; for during the sun's passage through the constellation of **Taurus** <note>the Bull</note>, this is the most beautiful weather in the temperate zones. Thus, Isis in the spring—the beautiful cow—remained for several months before the eyes of Argus, that is, at the side of the Horus with the open eyes, until he was taken away and the cow abducted by **Mercury** was put in its place; that is, until watching, spinning, and weaving came to an end with the rising of the **Dog Star**, **Anubis**. ### XXXV.
## Circe.

When **Isis**, along with her auxiliary symbols, arrived in Italy, she provided the material for a fable of a completely different nature. There, she was transformed into the sorceress **Circe**, who with her wand changed men into lions, snakes, birds, pigs, and other animals according to her whim. What sort of idea could have prompted such a story? The mythologists believe she is a symbol of lust, which reduces humans to an animal state. It was difficult to provide a better explanation for this as long as one could not trace the invention back to its true origin. **Circe** is none other than the **Egyptian Isis** *) who appeared in all public announcements, appearing specifically at times with a measuring rod for the Nile, at others with a spindle or a distaff, and sometimes with a lance. Beside her was **Horus** and other figures that changed from one moon to the next, even from one day to the next. She was the central figure—

---

—and *climmah* <note>original: "climmah"; likely from the Hebrew root *hammah*, meaning heat or sun</note>, Child of Heat, inspired the thought; that the son of the **Sun** and **Clymene** had ventured to drive the solar chariot and incited a general conflagration. The proper name of this sign, **Phaethon**, means "the linen-arrangement" <term>original: "Leinwandordnung"; referring to the systematic layout of fabric for bleaching</term>. It is derived from the word *pha*, meaning "speech" or "proclamation" <note>original Latin equivalents: "os, sermo, indictio"</note>, and *eton*, meaning "linen" or "linen-work" <note>original Latin: "linum, opera lintearia"</note>; just as *pheob* signifies the announcement of the flood.

# The Dynasty of the Gods

...of a riddle, to which all other pieces were related. She herself was found everywhere; on the other hand, she had beside her and under her rod <note>likely referring to a scepter or wand of authority</note> now a man with a dog’s head <note>Anubis</note>, now a lion, then a snake or turtle, sometimes a complete child, at other times a child’s head on a serpent’s body, and gradually all the signs of the Zodiac, or others which referred to various types of field labor. Further. Isis probably received the name **Circe** from the *circus* <note>original: "Circo"</note>, the sun-circle, which she commonly wore upon her head. This circle is the sign of the Supreme Being, whose feast days Isis announced. But why was this sun called **Circus**, the riddle? Because God could not be painted, and the solar disk was the (image) riddle of God. This was the great riddle *par excellence*. The place in Italy where this Isis, with the circle upon her head, was carried about and honored in ancient times is still called today **Monte Circello** <note>Mount Circeo</note>, the Circle Mountain. ## XXXVII.
### **Transformations and Apparitions.**

From the examples of these fables—which clearly originated partly from Egyptian and Syrian figures, and partly from common legends, puns, and proverbs triggered by the sight of these figures—we are entitled to assert generally that from this very same source, transformations, ghostly apparitions, and prophecies have also flowed.

All Egyptian figures were intended to announce future festival days and labor. When they were eventually transformed into gods, these deities also acquired the privilege of foretelling the future. Alongside the cleaning of the houses, the month of February had two other highly important tasks to announce. One was to clean the canals of the Nile and to make use of the time when the river is at its lowest and almost dry to cut through the areas filled with silt, so that after the flood, the water might soon return to its bed.

The other and most important duty of all, the greatest ornament of spring, which occurred just before the harvest, was the assembly of the judges as they administered justice. The priests appeared little in public throughout the rest of the year, except during the time of divine service. In the spring, however—that is, in February—they went out and assembled, settling the disputes of the inhabitants so that the people could thereafter remain undisturbed in their work. Since these priests were maintained at public expense \*) in the Labyrinth <note>A massive complex of buildings in ancient Egypt, described by Herodotus as surpassing even the Pyramids; it served as both a religious and administrative center.</note>, they had no self-interest, ambition, or other connections, and they judged the people fairly and impartially.

The cleaning of the trenches and canals was announced in the New Moon assemblies by an **Isis** who bore the name **Tite** or **Tetis** \*\*), and by a **Horus** called **Titan**, that is, mud—the clearing away of the earth.

### the Lineage of the Gods. ###
X 4

Alongside the cleaning of houses, the month of February had two other highly important tasks to announce. One was to clean the canals of the Nile, taking advantage of the time when the river is at its lowest and almost dry to cut through the areas filled with silt, so that the water might soon return to its bed after the flood.

The other and most important duty of all, the greatest ornament of spring, which took place immediately before the harvest, was the assembly of the judges as they administered justice. The priests appeared in public very little throughout the rest of the year, except during times of divine service. In the spring, however—that is, in February—they went out and gathered together to settle the disputes of the inhabitants, so that the people might thereafter remain unhindered in their labors. Since these priests were maintained at public expense \*) in the **Labyrinth** <note>A vast ancient Egyptian funerary complex and temple located near Lake Moeris, famously described by Herodotus as surpassing the Pyramids in scale.</note>, they were free from self-interest, ambition, or other obligations, and judged the people fairly and impartially.

The cleaning of the ditches and canals was announced in the assemblies of the new moon by an **Isis** who bore the name **Tite**, or **Tetis** \*\*), and by a **Horus** who was called **Titan**—that is, Red, or the clearing away of the earth.

The assembly of the priests who were to judge the people was signaled by a

# The Race of the Gods #

While the people were occupied with threshing, the sessions of the judges continued, and they regulated all the needs of the state through issued general orders; and because these assemblies lasted throughout the entire year until the rising of the **Dog Star** <note>The "Dog Star" refers to Sirius; its heliacal rising signaled the beginning of the Nile flood and the Egyptian New Year.</note> in June or July, the sign of the courts—an old man with a sickle—remained in its place until a new Osiris arose, that is, until the new year. We will hear strange stories that this circumstance gave rise to.

Gradually, the meaning of these simple images, festival icons, and names was lost, although all the customs remained unchanging. Common writing caused the interpretation to be lost; and nothing promoted this forgetfulness more than the habit of no longer precisely determining the sacred year, but instead shifting its beginning back by one day every four years. <note>The author is describing the "Vague Year" of the Egyptian calendar, which consisted of exactly 365 days. Without a leap year, the calendar seasons rotated through the actual solar year over a period of 1,460 years, known as the Sothic Cycle.</note> As a result, the summer festivals eventually fell in the winter, and so on, and people no longer understood what all of this was supposed to mean. After the images were transformed into men and women whose deification was celebrated, a genealogy was created for them that fit the order of the festivals. **Osiris** and **Isis**, who began the year, were the two great deities of the first rank, from whom the gods and goddesses of the second rank—whom we have already discussed—descended. But from whom do Osiris and Isis themselves descend—that is, Jupiter and his consort? These are, like their brother Neptune...

### Saturn.

I find proof of this truth in the observations that the myth of Saturn naturally provides to me.

Instead of his usual depiction with a sickle—which was meant to indicate the sessions of the judges during the harvest time—one sometimes finds him depicted with eyes on both the front and back of his head <note>original: "vorn und hinten mit Augen"</note>, where some are awake and others are closed. ## XL.

### Origin of the Sacred Animals and the Transmigration of Souls.

That I seek the origin of Western idolatry <term>idolatry: the worship of physical images or idols as if they were gods</term> primarily in the misuse of Egyptian writing is driven by more than just the fact that it is remarkably easy for an unlearned people to take a man, a woman, a child, or an old man at face value. It was natural for them to accept what the images presented to the eye and call them King **Osiris**, or the god **Ammon**, the Queen or "the Lady," the beloved son, or the lawgiver of Egypt. Beyond this, I have been particularly struck by how noticeable the connection is between these first missteps and the other unique circumstances of the Egyptian people. Their monstrous opinions and strange customs <note>The author is likely referring to the Egyptian practice of animal worship and the belief in metempsychosis (the soul moving into new bodies after death).</note> are a visible consequence of the false meaning they attributed to their ancient script.

<summary>The author argues that pagan mythology and Egyptian "idolatry" arose not from intentional invention, but from a literal and confused misunderstanding of ancient symbolic writing and icons of justice.</summary>

Every day it was said—in the ancient astronomical language, which was perfectly identical to the characters of Holy Scripture—it was said, namely: the ruler of the earth <margin>Osiris, the sun.</margin> has left the **Ram** to enter the **Bull**; and thereafter he would betake himself into the **Goats**, into the **Crab**, into the **Lion**, and further into the other signs of the **Zodiac**. Since they accepted this man historically as their founding father, they took everything else said about him to be literal history. They imagined that the stars beneath which the sun passed were given these various names specifically to preserve the memory of so many extraordinary events that had befallen their ruler before he was taken up into the sun.

When his soul, they said, left the mortal body, it initially entered a **Ram**; afterward, it dwelled in a **Bull**; then in a **Goat**, and so it went from one animal into the other until it took possession of the sun, where it now reigns and casts its benevolent gaze over Egypt. <note>This explains the origin of the belief in metempsychosis, or the transmigration of souls, suggesting it began as a literal reading of astronomical metaphors.</note>

## XLII.

### The Origin of Apis and Mnevis.

In **Memphis**, a calf was once found by chance that had a spot in the shape of a circle or a half-moon: a highly regarded sign! This accidental mark was nothing in itself, and deserved just as little attention as a white spot on the head of a horse or anywhere else; nevertheless, it was held to be the sign of **Osiris** and **Isis**, which had been impressed upon this animal so pleasing to their gods. It occurred to a hypochondriacal mind <note>The author uses "hypochondriacal" in an archaic sense to describe someone with a melancholic, obsessive, or overly imaginative temperament.</note> to persuade himself and others that this was a manifestation of their ruler, and that the protective god of **Egypt** was visiting them in grace. This wonderful calf served first primarily for the festive procession, and afterwards it was maintained in a magnificent house in **Memphis**. Its dwelling became a temple. In all its movements, people found something prophetic, and the entire populace ran to it and brought their offerings. It received the beautiful name **Apis**, the strong and mighty god **).

# The Race of the Gods.

In this way, this strange veneration continued; and to this was added a powerful reason: it was profitable.

The inhabitants of Heliopolis <note>Ancient Greek for "City of the Sun," known in Egyptian as Iunu; a major religious center.</note>, whose government or dynasty was distinct from that of Memphis, believed themselves to be so close to the Sun (from which the city takes its name) that they too should share in the divine visitations of the Sun and his son. Therefore, they soon had their own sacred bull, just like those in Memphis. He was given the name Menaphis or Mnephis, which means "the strong Minos," much like Menophis <insert>*</insert>; and since they gave him his own name, they also devised other characteristics and special duties for him, which won him the devotion of the people.

As soon as the Egyptians had forgotten the only Being worthy of worship, and the worship in spirit that He demands, and had "changed His glory into the image of an ox that eats grass" <insert>**</insert>, then all the animals that frequently appeared in the hieroglyphic figures began to share in this veneration. Egypt and Libya knelt before the ram <note>A reference to the god Amun, often depicted with ram's horns.</note>. The worship of the bull became universal. The goats, which [represent] the third sign <note>The author is likely referring to the zodiac sign of Capricorn or possibly Gemini, which in some ancient systems was associated with goats or kids.</note>...

### XLIII.

### Proofs of the Veneration and Worship of these Strange Deities.

I cannot well deny, it will be said, that the sight of all these symbolic animals—the interpretation of which was no longer known—and moreover the constant habit of saying "Osiris and Horus proceed into the Ram <note>Aries</note>, into the Bull <note>Taurus</note>, and further through the Zodiac" <note>original: "Thierkreise"</note>, may have confused people’s heads and given rise to extravagant tales. To carve images, or to cast them in molds, was not entirely forbidden to the Hebrews; for the interior of the Tabernacle <note>original: "Stiftshütte," the portable earthly dwelling place of Yahweh used by the Israelites</note> and the lid of the Ark of the Covenant <note>original: "Bundeslade," the gold-covered wooden chest containing the Stone Tablets of the Ten Commandments</note>, wherein the Law lay, were decorated with many winged figures—images of heavenly spirits, signs of adoration and obedience toward the Highest Being. These figures, however, were not replicas of Egyptian deities, as some scholars have believed, because Moses consistently calls their animals and images "abominations." Rather, it was an innocent and clever application of the ancient **picture-writing** <term>Bilderschrift: the use of symbolic images to convey complex ideas, similar to hieroglyphics</term>; it was a teaching through signs \*). These figures were not an imitation of what Egypt worshipped, but rather encouragements toward the worship of the Highest, representing to the soul the deepest humility, self-abasement, and swift obedience. Carving was only forbidden to the Hebrew if the image was offensive and could lead the people into idolatry.

Why then, we might ask, did the **Brazen Sea** <note>original: "eherne Meer," a large bronze basin in the Temple of Solomon used by priests for ritual washing</note>—that is, the great cauldron in the forecourt of Solomon’s Temple, from which the priests washed their hands and feet when they wished to offer sacrifices—stand upon the backs of metallic oxen? This evidence becomes even stronger through the customs of the **Passover**. The sacrifice of the **Passover lamb** and all the sacrifices in the Law certainly have their important connection to a much greater sacrifice <note>The author is referring to the Christian theological view that Old Testament sacrifices foreshadowed the sacrifice of Jesus</note>. Another particular circumstance in the regulations of the Jewish **Passover lamb** <term>Osterlamm; the lamb sacrificed during the Jewish festival of Pesach/Passover</term> is the prohibition against boiling the lamb’s meat or eating it raw. What difference did it make to the Jewish service whether the sacrificial animal was roasted or boiled; and why was the eating of raw meat forbidden first, something for which one already has a natural disgust? We can draw a conclusion about the customs of the Egyptians from those of the Athenians, for the latter had originated from the former. When these [Athenians] sacrificed to Horus, or the **Horae** <term>Horis; the Greek goddesses of the seasons and the natural order of time</term>—that is, the seasons—deities who certainly came from Egypt, they had the instruction to boil the meat but not to roast it *). In Athens, the Egyptian custom was retained during the worship of clearly Egyptian idols: and the Hebrews were commanded the opposite, so that they might have no fellowship with idolatrous acts and customs.

The prohibition against eating any part of the lamb, for example the entrails, without cooking everything first, was based on the strange custom in which, in honor of **Bacchus** <note>Also known as Dionysus, the god of wine and ritual madness.</note>, the meat and especially the entrails of goats and other sacrifices were eaten raw **). So, we have, along with the proof of the deepest wisdom in the **laws of Moses** <term>Mosis; the religious and civil laws of the Torah</term>, which always run directly contrary to the Egyptian ones, simultaneously the proof of the extravagant errors of the Egyptians, according to which they began to believe more than three thousand years ago that the names of the **Zodiac** <term>Thierkreises; the belt of constellations through which the sun, moon, and planets move</term>, and the images of their script or festive customs, were important, mysterious things, or even venerable evidence,

## Python or Typhon.

The very same self-love that led the **Egyptians** to find **Ham** <note>original: "Cham"; the biblical son of Noah, often associated by early scholars with the Egyptian god Amun or the founder of the Egyptian race</note>, his wife and sons, **Menes** <note>traditionally the first human king of Egypt</note>, and **Thoth** <note>original: "Thot"; the Egyptian god of wisdom and writing</note> within the most distinguished images of their ancient script, also caused them to seek an ancient enemy of their colony and of **Osiris** in the sea monster which they called **Ob** <note>likely a reference to "Ob" or "Aub," a Hebrew and Near Eastern term for a familiar spirit or serpent</note>. This custom of placing a bridle on the enemy’s power, and hanging the captive *Typhon* <note>Typhon was the Greek name for Set, the Egyptian god of chaos and storms; here, the author refers to the practice of wearing symbols that "bound" this dangerous force to protect the wearer</note> around the necks of children, the sick, and the deceased, seemed so important and so beneficial that it also emerged among other nations. Such a reprehensible arrangement necessarily resulted in even greater ignorance. And indeed, everything degenerated more and more. The testing of students and the sworn promise of **inviolable silence** were customs that held great prestige and were maintained very strictly. Ceremonies are easily preserved in all religions; they tend to increase rather than decrease, for they do not act upon the passions, but rather leave them entirely at peace—where they are not sometimes even conducive to them. It was quite different with truth and instruction than with the ceremonial. This brief passage tells us everything we desire to know; it not only opens the barriers for us but even pulls away the final curtain that covered the entrance to the mysteries <note>The "mysteries" refers to secret religious rites of antiquity, such as those at Eleusis, which were restricted to initiated members.</note>. Now everything is as clear as day. These customs did not concern the gods at all; for the gods arose much later; and they are secrets only because it required reliable people to whom one could explain what all of this meant in ancient times. From others, this was hidden with an inviolable silence, because in these mysteries, the figures transformed by the common people into gods meant something entirely different than deities, and such a confession could lead to dangerous consequences <note>The author suggests that "gods" were originally just symbols for tools or laws; revealing this to the public might have been seen as atheism or subversion of state religion.</note>.

The festival in memory of the original human state was celebrated in Egypt, Phoenicia, and Sicily. It arrived in Greece with all its particulars. Noah and the patriarchs <note>referring to the biblical ancestors of humanity following the Great Flood</note> recommended sincerity, love for labor, thrift, abstinence, and peace to their kin. Approaching the time of a festival, they exhorted peace of mind, fasting, and abstinence from all even otherwise permitted merrymaking. This was so that when they observed the festival, they might possess sentiments through which virtue would be awakened within them and their conduct of life made more perfect. This preparation and these teachings were preserved in the great festivals and have come down to us. However, the love for God (the essence of religion) which had awakened them was lost among most peoples; they became ceremonies without spirit. # The Lineage of the Gods.

These articles of faith <term>Glaubensartikel: fundamental tenets of belief</term>, by which their lives were organized, were not destroyed and abolished; rather, they have been distorted through the addition of many new opinions and foolish habits.

The service of the heart, worship in spirit and in truth <note>The author uses language echoing the New Testament (John 4:24) to describe what he believes was the "pure" original form of ancient religion</note>, was transformed by worldly desire into an entirely carnal religion, which strives more for the goods of this earth than for righteousness. Out of ignorance, they converted the signs of the sun, the weather, the festivals, and the symbolic humans and animals into gods; and their imagination assigned them dwellings in the heavens. From a new error, they turned these supposed heavenly persons into people who had formerly made themselves famous on earth and were relocated to heaven after death <note>This refers to the historical theory of "Euhemerism," which suggests that gods were originally historical heroes who became deified through storytelling</note>. # The Race of the Gods

With such a vast number of tutelary deities <term>tutelary deities: "Schutzgötter," guardian spirits or patron gods assigned to protect a specific place, person, or nation</term>, one could take their pick, and everyone could find something to their taste. Every land had its own patron gods whose histories were invented and whose monuments were displayed. These were local, gracious gods upon whom one could rely. Thus, it was natural that they were given the highest rank. 

However, this affection did not go so far that foreign gods were completely rejected because of it. No one wanted to offend any of these powers; one was accepted into the company of another; often gods were found together who descended from a single original image, yet appeared in such a procession and with such duties as if they had sprung from different families and countries. Sometimes a dispute arose among them regarding precedence. Their nobility and status were often difficult to determine, for they consisted—as is still the case with many gods of this earth—merely in the imagination. 

The Greek chroniclers took the trouble to draft their genealogical tables as best they could. One can find in the treatises of Plutarch and especially of Eusebius <note>original: "in Praepar. Euangel." — referring to the *Preparation for the Gospel* by Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century work that preserved many fragments of older, lost histories of mythology</note>, a great variety in the events and duties that the Africans, Phoenicians, and Phrygians attribute to the same gods. The heavenly court was different in Egypt than in Greece. There, Osiris had to enlighten the world; here, Jupiter was relieved of this burden, and instead left with the scepter and thunderbolts.

<summary>The author explains how ancient peoples preferred local "tutelary" gods but frequently adopted foreign ones, leading to a crowded and contradictory divine hierarchy. He notes that the same original deities were assigned different roles and genealogies as they moved between cultures like Egypt and Greece.</summary>

The chariot for the day’s journey, however, was assigned to Horus or Apollo, who, as the personification of agricultural labor <term>agricultural labor: "Ackerarbeit," referring here to the seasonal work of tilling the fields, which was originally represented by symbols that later became the attributes of gods</term>, also possessed the signs of the sun’s position or the seasons for the sake of brevity.
