But Jupiter could not do everything, nor could he be everywhere at once. Therefore, he was given his governors <term>governors: "Statthalter," meaning deputies or provincial administrators acting on behalf of a higher power</term> in divided provinces. Everything now took on a structured form; the deeds and adventures of the gods were organized and categorized; everything that each nation claimed about them in its own way was attributed to their names. Added to this were the chronicles of the priests in the temples and of the kings who had established their worship. Most notably, the indiscretions <note>original: "Ausschweifungen," here referring to the moral lapses or sexual escapades often found in classical mythology</note> of the female sex were excused by the supposed transformations of the gods who had become enamored with them. From this arose these vast mythologies (fabular teachings), where it is no surprise if one finds neither logic nor consistency, no order in time or place, and no regard for reason or morality.

Although the majority of these fabulous tales are nonsensical, people in all ages have nonetheless made an effort to discover their true origin, as they form a part of the peculiar theology of our forefathers. I have also dared to offer my own conjectures on the matter, as they seemed to me to come quite close to the truth, and allowed everything to be explained with propriety and utility. ## Of the Poetic Heaven
### Third Chapter.
### Divination. <note>original: "Die Wahrsagerey"; refers to the practice of seeking knowledge of the future or the unknown by supernatural means.</note>

Every part of the ancient script spoke a language, and spoke, in a manner of speaking, for they each had their own meanings. Just enough of these ancient letters <note>The author likely refers to hieroglyphs or early symbolic characters which he views as a "script" of nature or history.</note> had been preserved to provide people with instruction for their needs; and if understood correctly, this is indeed the truth. However, as soon as people began to believe that stone, metal, elements, and stars actually spoke with humans, or could in all seriousness send them messengers and news about the future, the human race became darkened. Humanity clung to trifles and grew accustomed to various superstitions.

Because the most prominent signs of the astronomical and secret script were transformed—through ignorance of their true interpretation—into so many powers that ruled all parts of the world and sought to instruct mankind on what concerned them; so too did the secondary figures, by which the meaning of the primary keys <term>Hauptschlüssel: the core symbols or characters used to decode hidden meanings in ancient scripts</term> was more closely determined,

In ancient times, when these **symbols** <term>Sinnbilder: meaningful images or allegories used to represent concepts.</term> were first introduced, people would say before setting sail, sowing, or planting: "Let us first look at the birds"; and this was entirely understandable*); people were glad that they had paid attention to them, and often regretted having neglected to do so. For these birds were actually the winds, and their observed migration decided the success of the undertaking and the beneficial effect of this caution. 

In later times, however, people turned in all seriousness to the birds themselves. A farmer or a traveler was meant to pay attention to the movement of the East, West, North, and South winds, which were indicated to him by the images of the **dove**, **ibis**, **sparrowhawk**, and **hoopoe**; but eventually, he waited in full confidence for his undertaking upon the appearance of the bird itself. The variety, the number, the migration—even the smallest details in the flight of these "citizens of the air"—became omens of future events. What kind of advice must such prophets have given?

Such gods were more pleasant to them than a God who looks into the heart, who demands sincere service in spirit and in truth <note>A reference to the Gospel of John 4:24, contrasting the inner moral requirements of monotheism with the external rituals of pagan divination.</note>. The desire to know the future had now been introduced among the people and confirmed through common speech and the apparent interpretation of ceremonies which, in their opinion, were supposed to reveal how their ventures would turn out; and thus everything else was accepted and interpreted in the same manner.

Isis or Juno, as a symbol, did indeed give them important information, and for this reason, the Latins of old called her *Moneta*, the Counselor <note>original: "Moneta, die Rathgeberinn." Thus, a mere calendar—which could do no harm and whose entire capacity consisted of determining the times for assembly—was transformed into a source whose influences extended to everything; an error that a great many people even now refuse to let themselves be talked out of.

According to their belief, the moon causes hair to grow, causes oysters and crabs to become full, ensures that seeds and plants thrive, and causes illnesses to subside and medicines to take effect. Even if they saw lead turn pale, stones flake away, and towers lean noticeably, they would very easily find the cause for it in the constant alternation of heat, winds, and the great downpours that always come from one side, where they deposit such thick moss that it splits the stone through its roots and gradually softens the mortise holes <note>original: "Zappenlöcher." ### III.

->Interpretation of Sacrifices. Prophecy from the Entrails.*)<-

Propriety <note>original: "Wohlstand." In this context, it refers to a sense of decorum or what is fitting for a religious rite.</note> had from the beginning established the custom of bringing only fat and choice sacrifices to the Lord God within the community. For this reason, everything defective was carefully inspected, and the best was chosen. This precaution, which through excessive ritual <term>ceremonialism|the strict adherence to external forms and rites</term> had degenerated into trivialities, appeared to be an important matter commanded by God himself. The choice of the most beautiful specimen for sacrifice was originally based on the reverence required during the offering, and the proper respect one had to show to the community. Once people had convinced themselves that nothing could be obtained from the gods if the sacrifice were not perfect, then the selection and care became extravagantly exaggerated. This deity required a white sacrificial animal, that one a black, and a third a red one.

These ignorant people sought their entire expertise in a precise knowledge of the rules according to which the examination and selection of a sacrificial animal had to be determined. Their principle was that the good or bad condition of the animal’s exterior and interior was a sign of consent or displeasure from the gods. Thus, every detail gave cause for observation. Everything seemed important and highly significant regarding the animals to be slaughtered, just as it did with the birds flying in the air. Every movement of an ox being led to the altar was prophetic. If it walked quietly, straight ahead, and without resistance, it was an omen of a successful undertaking. Its stubbornness, its evasion, or its fall resulted in various good or bad interpretations. Everything was deemed important—whether due to some meager resemblance or even a mere whim—and judged as either bad or good.

## Serpent Divination. *)

# V.

## Enchantments. *)

The selection and binding together of various plants and herbs, intended to mark certain circumstances, gave rise to the idea that these collected herbs—even if they were not even used as medicine—must nevertheless have a great influence on health. And since people saw no logical connection between the binding of a few plants and the recovery or the successful harvest that was supposed to result from it, they could find no other way out than to seek the primary power in the ancestral and incomprehensible words which the priests said or sang when they solemnly presented them to the people. The matter was quite understandable: the leaves and the spoken formula originally announced a truth, a festival, or a communal task to the community. Eventually, neither the sign nor the words were understood anymore, but they were nonetheless carefully maintained; and now, the combination of certain plants and certain words was regarded as mysterious customs which the ancestors had found to be effective, and which one had to imitate exactly in every detail if one did not want to ruin everything. These customs were collected and turned into an art, through which one could help oneself almost infallibly in all situations. The connection of these and those old for-

## VI.

### Astrology.

A seemingly not unreasonable desire to have reliable medicines and to penetrate into the future by means of certain sacred acts gave rise to another art just as deceptive as the previous ones: namely, **astrology** <note>literally "star-interpreting" (German: Sterndeutung)</note>. I could cite a multitude of astrological prophecies or planetary alignments *) to which the outcome contradicted them in every respect. **) We should rather treat astrology as we did idolatry, augury <note>the interpretation of bird flight patterns</note>, and sorcery, and look back at its origin. The history of the beginning of this supposed art is at the same time its refutation: for all astrology is, at its core, nothing more than a false explanation of misunderstood symbols.

The **Egyptians** once viewed the names of the signs in the **Zodiac** and others as mnemonic symbols of what had happened to their forefather, their foremother, and other heroes of their land—whose history took on a different form elsewhere. The veneration of the Great King, the Queen, and the heavenly host probably traveled from Egypt to **Phoenicia**, and from there

Anyone who desires to know how far the foolish conclusions of the astrologers <note>literally "star-interpreters"</note> go, need only take in hand the poem of **Manilius** <note>Marcus Manilius, author of the 1st-century poem *Astronomica*</note>, or **Censorinus’s** little book, or the *Astronomica* <note>English: *Mathesis* or *The Books of Knowledge*</note> of **Julius Firmicus**. I would rather direct the readers there themselves than copy a single page from them. The fantasies of a dreamer have more coherence than the reasons and conclusions of these people.

But that is not the greatest evil that astrology has brought about—that it feeds people with vain hopes, useless labors, and groundless influences. As great as the error was, the consequences were even more unfortunate. As soon as one regarded the heavenly signs, or the points in the sky—which indicated certain regular effects of the seasons with a certain name—as the **cause** of these effects, this miserable error found great approval. This was because people believed they had found the cause of every thing and the means to escape an evil with which they were threatened. One chose this month, this day, this hour, this **aspect** <note>the angular relationship between planets</note> to begin a journey, a day's work, or a piece of fabric. ### VII.
### Influence of the Planets.

In all of astrology, nothing is made into a greater matter than the **influence of the planets**. One speaks there constantly of the benign influence of the **Moon**, when it stands in **conjunction** <term>Conjunction: an astronomical event where two planets or celestial bodies appear close to each other in the sky</term> with **Jupiter**; and of the harmful influence in its meeting with **Saturn**. Every planetary position has its own particular good and evil, which one must observe with special caution or avoid. However, two remarks will tear the entire astrological system apart.

First: the peculiar virtues of each planet are based on the character of the **hero** or **god** who dwells therein.

The fact that the **Egyptians**—despite the great multitude of their ridiculous dogmas—agree with us on feast and prayer days, in the hope of another life, and in funeral ceremonies, does not occur because we received these articles of faith from them and merely purified them of the strange additions mixed in. Rather, it occurs because all of us who are on Earth—**Egyptians**, **Gentiles**, **Jews**, and **Christians**—have retained the first foundation of the **Noahic faith** <term>Noahic faith</term><note>A theological concept referring to the "Laws of Noah," which many Enlightenment-era scholars believed constituted a "natural religion" or a universal moral code shared by all humanity before the rise of specific cultural paganisms.</note>. Would it be correctly concluded if I said: we have our water from our neighbors, and have only purified it for ourselves? No; it is pure because we have it directly from the primary source. They <note>Referring to the ancient Romans.</note> had three types of special days in each month: Calends, Nones, and Ides. <term>Calends</term><note>original: *Calendae*. The first day of the Roman month, from which the English word "calendar" is derived.</note>, the assembly at the New Moon, was the first day of the month. The <term>Nones</term><note>Falling on the 5th or 7th day, these roughly marked the moon's first quarter.</note> fell on the fifth day, but in March, May, July, and October, they fell on the seventh day instead. The **Athenians** also maintained the custom, even after **Meton's** <note>Meton of Athens was a 5th-century BCE astronomer who introduced a 19-year cycle to align solar and lunar years.</note> improvement of their calendar, of counting the first month from the beginning of the year with the longest day <note>The Summer Solstice.</note>; a custom they received from their fathers, the **Egyptians**.

### IX.

### The Origin and Baselessness of the Sibyls.

The Sibylline oracles arose from another notable error in astronomy, or rather from the habit of consulting certain stars. The harvest has always been the greatest wish and expectation of all nations. In order that they might properly manage the improvement of their lands, agriculture, sowing, and other affairs upon which the entire community depended, they always kept their eyes fixed on the Maiden <note>The constellation Virgo</note>, who carries the ear of grain and serves as the sign of the harvest time. They watched how far the sun was distant from her; and the habit of "consulting the Maiden" regarding this became universal—an expression that was just as sensible as the action it described. Initially, this constellation was given the name *Shibul Ergona* <note>original: *Shibul Ergona*</note>\*), the red ear of grain; for one must wait for this specific condition during the harvest, and the harvest ripens when the sun approaches this constellation.

Afterward, however, she was called sometimes *Shibul*, and sometimes *Erigone*. The name Erigone meant in Gree— <note>The text breaks off mid-word; the catchword indicates it continues as "Greek"</note>

### X.
### Origin and Power of Talismans.

Errors lead one another by the hand, just like truths; and one follows after the other. Once the veneration of celestial signs and the planets was established, many such images were produced so that they might assist the devotion of the people and yield a profit from them. These images were made by casting or hammering, often in the style of a coin or a small disc, which was pierced in order to hang them around the necks of children, the sick, and the dead by means of a ring. In the cabinets of antiquities collectors <note>original: *Liebhaber der Alterthümer* — literally "lovers of antiquities," referring to early archaeologists or hobbyists</note>, one finds many such plates or amulets upon which a **T** <note>The letter T often represented the Tau cross, an ancient symbol of life or protection</note> is stamped, or the sun, the moon, another planet, and various signs of the zodiac. In the East <note>original: *Morgenlande* — literally "the morning lands," referring to the Orient or Levant</note>, these figures were called **Tselamim**, which means **images** <margin>From *Zelem*, *Tselamim* <note>Hebrew: *tselem* (image, idol, or shadow)</note></margin>; and among us, they are called **talismans**. "Talisman" is still a significant word that misleads many because it is not understood.

The arts of sculpture and painting, which were invented for the instruction of mankind and the support of devotion, have also contributed much to their corruption. Self-interest and greed attributed an altogether too great a value to these small figures of the planets and the stars. Anyone who carried them could not doubt, if he recovered from an illness, that he owed them his heal— <note>The text breaks mid-word; the catchword indicates the full word is *Gesundheit*, or "health."</note>

### XI.
#### Influence of the Climacteric Years.

The human mind—which finds it much easier to derive logical consequences from false principles than to satisfy itself of the truth of its principles—had scarcely devised this foolish correspondence between metals and planets, based merely on the character of the indwelling deity, when it discovered that one metal was abundant in one land and another in a different region. From this, it reached the "logical" conclusion that the planet which favored the creation of that metal must hold dominion over that entire land. Now, every country was assigned its ruling planet, and its influence extended to plants, animals, and even the temperaments of men. In one country, everything was lead; in another, everything was mercury. Gradually, the planetary system served as the explanation for everything. All things became subject to one of the seven **wandering stars** <term>Irrsterne</term> <note>The traditional term for planets, referring to their movement against the "fixed" stars</note>. Every limb of the human body had its protective planets, and every hour of the day was assigned one. The number seven decided everything. Years, months, days, hours—everything recurred in cycles of seven. Every seventh year, every seventh day, every seventh hour was of great significance. However, seven times seven is a dangerous number; the forty-ninth year <note>commonly called the great climacteric year <note>original Latin: *annus climactericus*</note>, from the Greek word for ladder or staircase <note>original Greek: *κλιμαξ*</note></note> is even

### XII.
### Origin of Alchemy.

Once people had convinced themselves that each planet produced its own metal, they went further and said: because one planet is more powerful than another, the base metal produced by the weaker planet must, through the influence of the stronger, be transformed into a nobler one. Consequently, lead—which is a true and just as perfect a metal as any other—is, in the eyes of the astrologers, merely a "half-metal," a deficient and imperfect effect of the weak Saturn. They believe it must transform itself into copper under the aspects of Venus, into silver under the gazes of the Moon, and finally, under certain solar—

# Divination

In the ancient festivals, everything was quite simple. People gathered on a high place; they dug a small trench around it to burn the entrails of the sacrificial animals; they also let the blood flow into it. A portion of the meat was given to the sacrificial priests; the rest was boiled, and the people sat around the hearth and consumed it. Gradually, they departed from this simplicity, primarily after the emergence of idolatry <term>Abgötterey</term>. The images which provided the occasion for this were eye-catching because of their beauty or their particular form; a taste for ornamentation emerged and became more powerful day by day. Instead of sitting on the grass, people sat on skins, on carpets, and finally on magnificently decorated beds <note>This refers to the ancient custom of reclining on couches, or *lecti*, during formal banquets and religious feasts</note>. Instead of a hearth dug into the earth, they set up a table and called it an altar, or at least a large vessel on a magnificent tripod <note>A three-legged stand or bowl, often made of bronze, used in religious rites</note>, under which a fire could be made and a portion of the sacrifice could be placed along with a handful of incense <term>Weyhrauch</term>, which was intended to dispel the foul odor of the burning blood and fat. Bit by bit, every festival acquired its own special manner, special processions, and its own unique altar. This altar was surrounded with foliage; they varied these leaves just as they did the form of the altar or the symbols <term>Sinnbildern</term> themselves. At this festival, they had to surround it with oak leaves, and at that one with myrtle branches

There, they believed they were dealing with friendly gods who, because of the interest they still took in the welfare of their families, could not fail to reveal everything to them, both the useful and the harmful. Thus, all <term>funerary arrangements<note>original: "Todtenanstalten"</note></term> were interpreted just like other solemn matters, and everything was transformed into means and ways for prophecies.

The <term>customs for the dead<note>original: "Todtengebräuche"</note></term>, although they merely followed the style of the earliest gatherings, were nonetheless distinct in every respect from what was observed at other festivals; therefore, they were considered various ways of interacting with the deceased and learning from them what one desired to know. Who could then still doubt that this was why people sat around the <term>pit<note>original: "Grube"; referring to a ritual trench or "bothros" used in antiquity to communicate with spirits of the underworld</note></term>, into which oil, flour, and the blood of animals slaughtered in their honor had been poured, so that they might commune intimately with their old friends? Could one doubt that the pit, instead of an altar raised toward heaven, was a very fitting and pleasing manner for the dead?

I B. Poetic Heaven, 3 C.

...friends whom they wished to **honor**. The dead necessarily had to find pleasure in these meals, especially in what was poured into the <term>pit<note>original: "Grube"; refers to the ritual trench used in necromancy</note></term> for them. They undoubtedly came up and consumed the honey and the other liquids, for these disappeared, and people were content to offer only <term>liquid sacrifices<note>original: "nassen Opfern" or "Liqueurs"</note></term> because solid food was not considered suitable for the dead. Thus, they flattered themselves with the foolish thought that the <term>shades<note>original: "Schatten"; a classical term for the spirits of the departed</note></term> came and greedily drank these offerings while their relatives consumed the remainder of the sacrifice at the edge of the trench.

After the communal meal between the living and the dead came the inquiry: the specific <term>summoning<note>original: "Beschwörung"</note></term> of the soul to whom the sacrifice was dedicated, and who was now expected to explain themselves. Anyone can see that an inconvenient circumstance prevailed during this ceremony; namely, that all the shades might come and take part in the pouring out of the liquids—which were so pleasant to them—and leave nothing for the beloved shade to whom the festival was sacred. However, a remedy was found. The relatives made two pits; into one, they poured wine, honey, water, and flour for the dead in general; into the other, they poured the blood of the sacrifice, which they intended to eat together. They sat around this second pit, keeping their swords beside them, and by this sight, they scared away the common dead, who cared little for their business. On the other hand, they invited the specific deceased person whom they...

# Divination

...to **honor** or question specifically, and invited him to come forth. The other dead, who did not consider themselves safe there, gathered in crowds around the first <term>pit<note>original: "Grube"; the ritual trench described on the previous page</note></term> where they were free to go, and willingly left the other to the spirit who had a right to the sacrifice and knowledge of those things about which he was to be consulted.

The questions of the living were certainly clear and easy to understand; but the answers, though reliable, were nonetheless not so immediate, and not so easy to explain. However, the priests, who in their labyrinth <note>original: "Labyrinthe"; here referring to the complex and convoluted systems of occult knowledge</note> learned to understand the voices of the gods, the response of the planets, the language of birds, of snakes, and of mute and lifeless things, soon reached a point where they could also perceive the dead and interpret their meaning.

They turned this into an art, of which the most necessary and most suitable main conditions for the dead were darkness and silence. They retreated into deep caves, fasted, and lay upon the skins of the slaughtered sacrifice. When they awoke—or rather, after a period of waking that was more likely to confuse the mind than to discover hidden things—they offered the thought that most struck them, or the most vivid dream they had experienced, as an answer. They also opened a book dedicated to this purpose, and the first words that caught the eye upon opening it contained the requested answer. Indeed, the priest—sometimes even the person asking the question—listened

...listened upon exiting the cave for the first words they might hear anywhere, and these served as them as an answer. These words, of course, could likely have no precise relation to the question; however, they twisted them so much and so often that they eventually had to fit to some extent. But it was also not uncommon for a seemingly logical sense to be found. Often, instead of the aforementioned methods, **lots** were used; that is, they wrote all sorts of words as they came to mind, as well as verses—both well-known and newly composed—on small slips of paper. These were thrown into a vessel and stirred together; the first one pulled out was given to the worried family for their reassurance.

The means of <term>prophesying<note>original: "weissagen"; the act of foretelling the future through supernatural means</note></term> were truly endless. Almost the entire religious service became nothing but methods for recognizing the future. Some places became more famous for this than others, and that is the origin of the **oracles** \*). This subject has been sufficiently dealt with by scholars and is unnecessary to repeat here.

It is quite clear, one might say, that such customs are very well-suited to spreading the **foolish delusion**, which still clings to the common people, that one can interact with the dead and that they often come to teach us. However, what proof does one have that such strange customs were once in use?

# Divination.

If I can provide my readers with the evidence of this habit, or rather this perverse misuse of **funeral rites**; then it seems to me that I have sufficiently proven: the opinions of men regarding the gods, the dead, and the answers they provided are nothing more than a crude and literal interpretation of simple **symbols** and such customs that once indicated certain truths or commanded certain duties.

Because all nations ran in great numbers to the heights to pour the blood of sacrificial animals into the pit, to commune with the dead, and to ward off others by brandishing swords; God often and emphatically forbade the Israelites from gathering on the heights; or, which says the same thing, to eat nothing with blood; that is, to hold assemblies near the blood, and to eat around the pit moistened with the blood of the sacrifice *).

The practice of using a sword during sacrifices for the dead to rid oneself of unwanted spirits is confirmed by *Ezekiel*, who reproaches the Hebrews: You have [eaten] blood

*) *You shall not eat with the blood* <note>original Hebrew: "Lo thocelu al haddam"</note>, *you shall not eat beside the blood, or upon the blood, or perhaps around the pit sprinkled with the blood of victims* <note>original Latin: "non comedetis iuxta sanguinem, s. super sanguine, f. circa fossam victimarum sanguine conspersam"</note>. For eating and sacrificing are one and the same here.

**Homer** **), who is even older than **Ezekiel**, shows us these same customs among the Western peoples <note>The Greeks</note> and serves as an interpreter of the Scripture. When **Ulysses** <note>Odysseus</note> wishes to consult the spirit of **Tiresias**, who was said to be far more enlightened than other mortals, regarding his return journey to **Ithaca**, he first begins by pouring honey, wine, water, and flour into a pit in honor of the spirits in general; this is done so they might occupy themselves there and leave him alone. This spirit is specifically summoned and finally arrives; he begs the hero to move away from the pit and to put away the sword of which he is afraid, so that he may drink from the blood shed in his honor and afterward deliver a prophecy to Ulysses *).

# Divination.

This prophecy <note>The author uses "Weissagung" (prophecy) here to refer to the general practice of divination</note> was based, like all others, on the false interpretation of simple and initially innocent ceremonies. These later became so many idolatrous acts, or at least provided a close opportunity for <term>idolatry</term> <note>the worship of physical objects or symbols as gods</note>, because they were given an incorrect interpretation. The authority these ceremonies gained in the minds of the people is thus a fresh proof of the crude manner in which they transformed symbols into persons and gods. It follows from everything we have seen so far: that idolatry, <term>astrology</term> <note>predicting the future by stars</note>, <term>star-gazing</term>, divination, conjuration, and sorcery are nothing but absurd and deceitful habits. These were caused by a false explanation of ceremonial rites, sustained the desires of the common people, were accepted by general consensus without investigation, and supported the greed of the priests. Perhaps the priests themselves believed their prophecies were true and correct, as they might have appeared to be fulfilled from time to time. It is believable that when the outcome contradicted them, they were themselves misled by the many summoned powers that always seek to confuse everything in the world; and that they sincerely valued an art through which they fared well.

From Homer’s Odyssey, Book 11, where the ghost of Tiresias speaks to Odysseus.</note>

### Book 1, Poetic Heavens. Chapter 3: Divination.

While I here characterize <term>idolatry</term> <note>the worship of idols</note> and <term>divination</term> <note>the practice of seeking knowledge of the future by supernatural means</note>, which have so greatly dishonored human reason, as mere delusions of ignorance and wicked desires; let it be far from me to think that evil spirits do not exercise upon mankind the measure of power that God, according to His inscrutable purpose and always adorable wisdom, grants them. I am, on the contrary, fully convinced of their existence and their efforts toward our destruction, especially of the plagues they are permitted to inflict upon the bodies of the possessed to reveal the mighty grace of our Savior. I also grant that God sometimes allows the spirits of darkness to answer the questions of sorcerers and the misled people through apparent ambiguity. Yet, what He permitted for such punishable desires occurred as their punishment. All these arts are nonetheless deceptive *), false, and groundless, for they have their origin in the forgotten true meaning of the first instructions given to mankind concerning the course of the sun and the moon, agriculture, and the constitution of the commonwealth, as well as the gratitude they owe to the Author of all good.

*) *Scripture itself gives us evidence of the impotence of idols and the deceit of priests, in the story of the priests of Baal in Daniel.* <note>The author likely refers to the story of Bel and the Dragon from the Book of Daniel, where the prophet Daniel exposes the fraud of priests who secretly ate the food offerings left for an idol.</note>

# Book I: The Poetic Heaven. Part 3: Divination.

While I here declare idolatry and <term>divination</term><note>The practice of seeking knowledge of the future or the unknown by supernatural means.</note>, which have so greatly disgraced human reason, to be nothing but the vain deceit of ignorance and evil desires; far be it from me to think that the evil spirits should not exercise upon mankind that measure of power which God, according to His inscrutable purpose and ever-adorable wisdom, has granted them. I am, on the contrary, highly convinced of their existence and their efforts toward our perdition, especially regarding the plagues they are permitted to inflict upon the bodies of the possessed for the revelation of the mighty grace of our Savior. I also admit that God sometimes permits the spirits of darkness to answer the questions of sorcerers and the deluded people through apparent ambiguity. But what He permitted to such sinful desires occurred for their punishment. Nevertheless, all these arts are deceptive \*), false, and groundless, for they have their origin in the forgotten true meaning of the first instructions given to mankind concerning the course of the sun and the moon, agriculture, the constitution of the commonwealth, and the gratitude they owe to the Author of all good.

\*) Scripture itself gives us proofs of the impotence of idols and the deceit of the priests in the story of the priests of Baal in <note>original: "Daniel"</note> Daniel. <note>This likely refers to the story of Bel and the Dragon in the extended Book of Daniel, where the prophet Daniel exposes the fraud of the priests who were secretly consuming food offered to the idol.</note>

->End of the First Part.<-

# The History of the Heavens,
## Book Two.
### The Structure of the World, or the Creation of Heaven and Earth according to the Opinions of the Philosophers.

**D**he investigation into the origin of the **poetic heavens** <note>The "poetic heavens" refers to the mythological and allegorical interpretations of the stars and gods used by ancient poets, as opposed to physical astronomy.</note> and **pagan religions** has not been nearly as unpleasant as we had believed. We have seen how much a person allows themselves to be deceived and misled by error when their heart is not guided by a love for truth and justice. We have been able to profitably observe how so many perverse and harmful opinions have arisen, from which many people even to this day cannot be dissuaded; finally, we have also begun to sense the excellence and the inestimable advantage of the **Mosaic account** <note>original: "mosaischen Erzählung." This refers to the creation story in the Book of Genesis, traditionally attributed to Moses.</note>: for we have, in the midst of the multitude of fables which in later times to the

## II B. The Structure of the World.

old traditions, even in paganism we have found the same historical basis, the same customs, and indeed even the same fundamental truths as those contained in the **Mosaic account** <note>The "Mosaic account" refers to the narrative of creation and early history found in the Book of Genesis, traditionally attributed to Moses.</note>. Long before the Law was given in the wilderness, we encountered—on both sides—sacrifices, new moons, monuments and altars sanctified by oil and water, funeral processions, the hope for a better life, and a universal belief in a justice that will judge everyone according to their works. In Egypt, there were visible signs of the dwellings of **Ham** <note>original: "Chams." In the biblical tradition, Ham was one of the sons of Noah, whose descendants were said to have settled in Egypt and Africa.</note>. In the opinions of the Eastern peoples regarding the origin of the gods, there are traces from the histories of **Abraham** and **Noah**; the memory of the earth divided among the three sons of the latter; the knowledge of the restoration of agriculture by a man saved from the **Great Flood** <note>original: "Sündfluth."</note>; the memory of the **Ark**; a clear report of the different states of nature and humanity before and after this event; and finally, which is well worth noting and of which one can be convinced by the *Metamorphoses* of **Ovid** <note>original: "Ovidius." Referring to the Roman poet Ovid, whose work *Metamorphoses* details the mythical creation and transformation of the world.</note>, the dual origin of man, which paganism as well as the Holy Scripture derives simultaneously from earth and heaven; from earth mixed with water, that is, from germs <note>The author uses "germs" (Keimen) to mean the "seeds" or fundamental biological building blocks of the physical body.</note>, for he lives in a body whose primary material consists of earthly elements; and from heaven, for from it he possesses life, soul, and intellect.

<summary>This page discusses the cultural and historical parallels between pagan traditions and the biblical narrative, focusing on shared memories of the Great Flood and the dual physical and spiritual nature of humanity.</summary>
<keywords>paganism, Mosaic account, Noah, Ham, Great Flood, Ark, Ovid, Metamorphoses, human origins, soul and body</keywords>

--- Page 627 ---
<meta>This page continues the comparison between ancient pagan traditions and the biblical (Mosaic) account, transitioning from general cultural parallels to the specific concept of "Chaos" or the state of the universe before creation.</meta>

->Chaos. II<-

My readers might justifiably complain if I did not ascend to that formless mass (*chaos*) <note>original: "wüsten Klumpen (*chaos*)"</note> of which both the poets and Moses make mention. Poets as well as philosophers <note>original: "Weltweise," literally "world-wise ones," referring to sages or natural philosophers.</note>, civilized nations, and barbarians alike have preserved the memory of a state of night and confusion that existed before the arrangement of this visible world; and we cannot deny that this magnificent remnant of the history of a created world—despite the secondary notions that each nation and each philosopher has gradually attached to it—is a universal testimony to the truth of the Mosaic narrative. However, when we compare the Chaos as we have received it from the Hebrews with the Chaos of the poets and philosophers, we find in the former nothing but truth and correctness, and in the latter nothing but error, and false, often dangerous conclusions.

...is scant. Iron is scattered within the womb of the earth from one end to the other for the benefit of mankind; and water carries small particles of this metal everywhere, perhaps to perform important services for us, even though we have little or no knowledge of them.

Water carries into the bodies of plants and animals a multitude of small iron particles, just as it supplies them with tiny air bubbles, droplets of oil, grains of salt, and other basic substances. I do not mean to say that this iron is intended to give stiffness and strength to the bark or the wood, in the way that iron rods provide it to the beams in our buildings. I also do not wish to claim that these iron particles are necessary, or even merely useful, for the opening of clogged vessels <note>The author refers to the 18th-century medical theory that iron's physical weight helped "force" open blockages in the human circulatory or digestive systems.</note> in plants or living bodies; yet this path is not unworthy of the wisdom of the Creator; for it is precisely through this that <term>mineral waters <note>original: *mineralische Wasser*. Specifically referring to chalybeate or iron-rich springs, which were popular for their perceived healing properties.</note></term> become healthful, because they clear blockages through their weight. 

Our conjecture on this is confirmed by the small pieces of iron and hard pebbles found in the stomachs of many animals. Without establishing anything specific regarding the utility of this iron—which is not known to us through sufficient experience—we can nevertheless generally assert that iron is everywhere useful and necessary, because God has distributed it everywhere, and because it is indeed found everywhere. ## II B. The Structure of the World.

...specific provinces; however, iron reaches everywhere; it distributes itself in the sap-conducting vessels of plants and in the bowels of the earth wherever water flows. This fact can be proven by the magnet. If you hold it, or a magnetic needle, against wood ash, or ash from meat, hair, or animal blood, iron particles will attach themselves to it. Often the needle is entirely covered with them.

The very same water that brings iron particles into the bodies of plants and animals also carries and eventually collects them, after much time, at the bottom of an exhausted mine, where one might suspect all sorts of slag and <term>hammer scale <note>original: *Hammerschlag*. These are the iron oxide flakes that fly off red-hot iron when it is forged; they were often discarded as waste but still contained high concentrations of metal.</note></term> from furnaces and smithy hearths have been discarded. Under this rubble, there can still be enough metal to unite with the new material brought by the water, eventually forming a new mine. 

However, the master smiths who fill their ditches with such slag and find some new iron there after twenty or thirty years should not boast that they caused its generation. Nor should they attribute to nature an imagined creation or a transformation of <term>glassy slag <note>original: *Glasschlacken*. The vitrified waste product from smelting ore, which 18th-century observers sometimes mistakenly thought could "regrow" into iron.</note></term>—a process that does not actually occur. Sand and earth do not transform, nor does the sun melt them. It is certainly the water, which moves through the <term>ore veins <note>original: *Erzgängen*. Fissures in the rock where minerals are deposited over time.</note></term> and gradually gathers new particles of this metal there, carrying them down from higher regions into the depths. Thus, it gives to one place what it [takes from] the other...

Transpositions and various changes occur only in **organic** or **mixed bodies**. However, in those bodies which we have called **simple**, no actual change occurs except for the increase or decrease of their mass.

We wish to begin with the investigation of fire. In the *Spectacle of Nature* <note>original: "Schauplatze der Natur"; referring to *Le Spectacle de la Nature* by Abbé Pluche, a popular 18th-century work that explained the natural world through a theological and teleological lens.</note> *) we have presented a multitude of experiences and proofs regarding this element, through which, as a whole, this truth is established: fire may well have various natural causes for its increase; but no natural cause for its existence. We can grasp it where it is, unite its parts, and animate the whole. And so we light a fire, but we cannot create it. Thus we can distribute this swift element here and there and let it break out. We can, by means of a fan <term>Windfächer</term> <note>Literally a "wind-fan." We do not destroy this fire, however, even if we scatter it. We may likewise extinguish it in our fireplace <term>Camine</term> <note>A term for a domestic hearth or chimney.</note>, yet we by no means annihilate it. In classical philosophy, the "efficient cause" is the primary agent or force that brings something into being.</note> of "Red" neither in the degree of light's movement nor in the bodies it touches: we must confess that its essence and concept are beyond our understanding; and it must be even less possible for us to state the cause from which light originates. All that we know of this from experience is that light and its primary colors are as immutable in their essence as the Will which created them.

It will consequently be a dangerous undertaking to seek, alongside the philosophers, the natural cause and the mechanical laws which produced light from hard or soft, round dust particles driven in a vortex <note>A critique of mechanistic theories of light, particularly those of René Descartes, who imagined light as the pressure of small particles moving in "vortices" or whirlpools of subtle matter.</note>; and moreover, we must first know what light actually is. On the contrary, it will be a reliable and wise natural philosophy <note>original: "Naturlehre"</note> if we attribute the so wondrous, perpetual effects of light to the almighty Will of Him who commanded light to be, to illuminate the inhabitants of the earth, and to distinguish all things from one another so that they would be immediately recognizable. This physics is at least understandable, and one cannot follow this school of thought without improving oneself.

One might stop me here and refuse to accept the opinion which assumes original and immutable rays of light, because it was difficult for a certain Mariotte <note>Edmé Mariotte (c. 1620–1684) was a French physicist who famously had difficulty replicating Isaac Newton's experiments with prisms, leading him to doubt the immutability of individual colors.</note> to prove the constant nature of the light ray.

But in all these experiments, one element does not become another. It seems, for example, that the air which has penetrated common water has become water; it no longer shows any sign of its presence, and one might almost be tempted to believe it has been transformed or blended, because it can no longer be compressed while inside. A tin sphere full of water cannot be made smaller, contract, or be flattened under the blows of a hammer without driving the water out through every pore. If the air within the water were still in its natural or essential state—since it is capable of great expansion—it seems that it should also allow itself to be compressed. The water could thus obtain from the air the space it needs as the air contracts; but this does not happen. Should one therefore believe that the air is transformed or annihilated? ## II B. The Structure of the World ##

...we have. <note>The text continues from the previous page: "We have [enclosed the air]..."</note> However, although a drop of water is eight hundred and fifty times heavier than an equally large drop of air, these enclosed air particles will immediately exert their <term>spring-force</term> <note>original: "Federkraft." A historical term for elasticity or atmospheric pressure; the "spring of the air" was a common 18th-century concept.</note>, push away the masses of water, and reveal their existence as soon as the pressure of the external air is removed by the <term>air pump</term> <note>original: "Luftpumpe." A device used to create a vacuum in a glass chamber to study physical properties in the absence of air.</note>. Thus, the air is not lost within the liquid, and it always remains therein what it was.

Here is yet another experiment that likewise proves that air mixed into water does not become water, because water without air acts quite differently than it does in its combination with it. When one shakes water in a long glass tube, the agitated air causes it to foam; and as the air settles between the water and the bottom of the tube when the water drops, it causes the water to fall gently and with little noise. 

If, however, you use the pump to remove as much air as possible from both the water and the tube, and quickly seal the upper part with a <term>melting lamp</term> <note>original: "Schmelzlampe." A blowpipe or lamp used to melt glass in order to create a hermetic (air-tight) seal.</note> so that air cannot get back inside, and then shake the tube, almost no air can place itself between the water and the bottom as it falls. The water thus strikes the bottom with its entire dense surface and produces such a strong, silvery tone, as a golden or marble ball would produce when falling. <note>This describes the "water hammer" effect, where water in a vacuum behaves like a solid mass because there is no air to cushion the impact.</note> Water can therefore strike, separate, enclose, and retain air, and even expand along with it, but it does not transform the air into its own essence. One can have the air back whenever one wishes.

Let us put the air to a still more rigorous test. Keep it locked away in a narrow space for many years in a row, and let us see if this imprisonment and all this torment can have any effect upon it. The <term>air gun</term> <note>original: "Windbüchse." A weapon that uses compressed air rather than gunpowder to propel projectiles. In the 18th century, these were high-precision instruments used for both hunting and scientific demonstration.</note> has been invented; by its means, the air is pressed so tightly together with a plug that it can hurl ten or eleven equally deadly bullets. The small amount of trapped air is released in ten or eleven equal parts, little by little, by pulling the trigger as many times. If one keeps the air locked inside for ten, fifteen, or even more years—this experiment *) was conducted in Paris and London. What was the result? Has its <term>spring-force</term> <note>original: "Federkraft." A historical scientific term for elasticity; natural philosophers like Robert Boyle famously described the "spring of the air" to explain how it resists compression and seeks to expand.</note> been weakened, as happens with all other <term>elastic forces</term> <note>original: "Schnellkräfte." Physical forces characterized by rapid expansion or tension, such as a tensed bowstring.</note> that are kept under tension for too long? Other bodies seem only to have borrowed this force, which can be changed by various accidents. But air and fire, which are perhaps the foundation of all other elastic forces, always retain their power; and the air gun fired after fifteen years penetrates a wooden board just as well as it would have done on the first day.

To be sure, expanded air no longer possesses the same force and effect, because it acts within a larger space and upon more points; however, it is still the same, even if it is more distributed. Bring it back into a narrow space, and it will once again have its former effectiveness.

### II B. The Structure of the World. ###

It is therefore clear that light, fire, and air, even though they are always found together, nonetheless do not mix. They are <term>substances</term> <note>In 18th-century natural philosophy, a "substance" refers to a fundamental, irreducible building block of reality that maintains its identity even when interacting with others.</note> that act upon one another, and through their mutual interaction, they grant each other greater or lesser speed and new directions; yet one cannot become the other. They cannot impart their essence and properties to one another. We judge them so because even in the most intimate mixture, we still find them to be of the same kind. However, their wonderful structure is not as easy to perceive as their effects and existence; it is therefore a daring and almost dangerous undertaking when one pretends, as our <term>philosophers</term> <note>original: "Philosophen." At this time, the term referred to "Natural Philosophers," the precursors to modern scientists, who sought to explain the laws of nature through reason and observation.</note> do, that one only needs this or that to bring about light, air, or fire. Since we do not know the nature of the primary things from which the world consists, how then do we dare to judge the whole? Who would think to send a proposal for the materials to restore the Imperial Palace in Peking from Paris to China, when we are not acquainted with those materials at all here? <note>This analogy emphasizes the "scientific humility" common in certain 18th-century circles, suggesting that humans are too far removed from the "divine" or "true" nature of matter to dictate how it works.</note>

Water, which has often been presented to us as if it arose from thickened air, and were itself a fertile cause of many effects whereby it loses its essence and gains a completely new one, is at all times and in all bodies with which it mixes nothing other than water. It only seems to change, for its nature is immutable. When fire ceases to give it movement and fluidity, it is ice. ## II B. The Structure of the World.

[...rendered] volatile and withdrawn from the eye, but not transformed into another essence.

If this vapor is driven higher, does it not come back down as rain? When the rain penetrates into plants and fruits, it disappears once more. There it carries away with it salts, oils, and other elements; it is the mixture and quantity of these that cause the fruit to become sour, ripe, stale, or rotten. To be convinced that the water within is not lost, one simply needs to proceed to a decomposition in a <term>retort</term> <note>original: "Kolben". A glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used in early chemistry and alchemy for distillation and the breaking down of substances.</note>, which faithfully yields it back. The nature of water, therefore, does not depend at all on its surroundings—on what dilutes, carries away, conceals, or mixes with it. No power can create or destroy it; and no intellect can fundamentally flatter itself with the thought of truly knowing it. How then could anyone be capable of providing a rule for how water is to be made? <note>In the mid-18th century, before Lavoisier's discovery that water is composed of hydrogen and oxygen, water was considered a primary, indivisible element that could not be synthesized by humans.</note>

Let us now examine oil. This too is a work of providence which surely lay within the counsel of eternal wisdom, but was within no natural capability. This diversity, however, is merely a change of positions, and not a creation of things that did not previously exist, nor an internal (that is, essential) altered positioning of the components, nor the transformation of one substance into another. ### II B. The Structure of the World.

This learned man <note>Referring to Herman Boerhaave (1668–1738), the Dutch physician and chemist discussed on the previous page.</note> had initially fallen into bad company, that is, he consorted with **alchemists**; and although he gradually recognized how deceptive their principles and opinions are, it happened to him, once he had come to true **knowledge**, as it does to converted sinners, from whose mouths certain expressions still escape from time to time that testify to their former disorder.

Meanwhile, after all these experiences and confirmations, a correct conclusion follows: it is within man’s **power** alone to separate or to combine something, but not to produce or create anything new. His intellect can list the **fundamental substances** of that which he can dissolve into various natures. However, it is imprudent when he attempts to specify the **constituent parts** of **simple natures** <note>In 18th-century natural philosophy, "simple natures" or "simple substances" were the basic building blocks of matter (like pure elements) that could not be further subdivided or altered.</note>, which he can neither change, destroy, nor distinguish the slightest bit within.

Now, if an experience even stronger than these reasons proves to us that **motion** can effect nothing new, and that our intellect can never reach an understanding of the essence of any **element**; then we have all the less justification to assume that the world could arise from a **moving chaos**, or that this or that is the **cause** of an element, since **cause** and **effect** are equally foreign to us. Thus, it is all over for the **philosophy** that takes its refuge in general laws, or that seeks to derive a world-structure from the general pressure of motion; since experience, when one takes it to coun- <note>The text cuts off mid-word ("Rath" or "counsel") and continues on the next page.</note>

## IV.

## The Fundamental Substance (the <term>prime matter</term> <note>original Latin: *materia prima*; in Aristotelian philosophy, this refers to the formless, pure potentiality from which all physical things are created</note>) of the Greek Sages.

All the massive volumes that the ancient and modern sages have written regarding the manner in which one should imagine the initial construction of the heavens and the earth can be quite comfortably distilled into these four famous verses by La Fontaine <note>Jean de La Fontaine (1621–1695), a French fabulist. The quote is from his fable "The Sculptor and the Statue of Jupiter."</note>.

> *A block of marble was so fine* <note>original French: "Un bloc de marbre étoit si beau / Qu’un statuaire en fit l’emplette. / Qu’en fera, dit-il, mon ciseau? / Sera-t-il Dieu, table ou cuvette?"</note>

Shatter this stone God: what remains for you? Pieces of *marble*. Smash the table or trough, it is still *marble*; everywhere the same. These things are different only in their outward form. Take *clay* instead of *marble*. What came from the hand of the potter as a plate will become a cup as soon as he wishes. And everything that the *philosophers* say about a (homogeneous) *matter* from which everything can be formed comes down to this. 

The concept of a universal *matter* for all *bodies* is a true <term>cornerstone</term> <note>original: *Eckstein*; here the author uses a play on words, as "cornerstone" also implies a "stumbling block" (*Stolperstein*) because the sages "tripped" over it</note>, against which almost all <term>sages</term> <note>original: *Weltweisen*; literally "world-wise ones," referring to philosophers</note> have stumbled, one after another. When they investigated the work of the creation of this world, they all fell into the habit of comparing it to the action of a human being making a piece of work. That is the source of the false *philosophy* which has seduced many souls into <term>atheism</term> <note>original: *Atheisterey*; an archaic, disparaging term for atheistic belief</note>. 

A man’s work comes from a *matter* already made; all the skill of the *master* consists in the arrangement of the *parts* which already have their specific *nature*, but did not receive it from him. If two men make a *watch*, one from *wood* and the other from *iron*; the assembly requires the same skill. Their difference consists in the chosen *matter*, which for one is poor and fragile, and for the other good and durable. The quality of the *matter* thus constitutes the main value of the *work*. Likewise, as beautiful as the arrangement of the world may be, the primary feature of this great *work* rests upon the excellence of the various *elements* that serve as its foundation,

Anaxagoras was led to this by the observation that a drop of water always remained water, no matter how much it was divided or evaporated; that a grain of gold, even if divided into ten thousand parts, remained just as much gold as it was in the whole. Anaxagoras glimpsed the truth from a distance. Had he, with his intellect, stopped at those simple natures which experience shows us to be indestructible, he could have rightly claimed that they could merely be separated or joined for a time, but never created anew.

His first error was this: that he extended his principle to mixed bodies. Blood is not constituted in the same way as water. Our philosopher <note>original: *Weltweiser*, literally "world-wise one"</note> draws conclusions about the origin of mixed and organic bodies like someone who, finding some resemblance between a cat and a tiger, might say: A tiger is composed of several small cats joined together so that a large one might result. Since <term>Homeomeria</term> <note>The theory that substances are composed of minute parts (seeds) that are identical in nature to the whole; for example, that gold is made of tiny bits of gold.</note>, like many other even newer systems, is nothing more than a means of speaking learnedly about a thing that one does not understand, we shall let Anaxagoras’s world go and examine the one built by his teacher.

Thales, the founder of the Ionian school, had learned from the Phoenicians what they knew through tradition or from their neighbors, the Hebrews: that there was a state of imperfection before the final completion of heaven and earth. They have, however, distorted this belief and devised a <term>Chaos</term> <note>The formless, void-like state preceding the creation of the universe in Greek mythology and philosophy.</note> of universal matter, out of which everyone brought forth a world according to their own whim. This thought of a presumed matter—which is nonetheless common to everything that exists—passed from one school to another; and we shall see how one philosopher delivers it to the next from hand to hand, always indeed with new coverings, but fundamentally little changed.

<page-num>100</page-num>
## II B. The Structure of the Universe.

Thales, who conducted actual observations, was not satisfied with a far-fetched <note>original: *weitschweifigen*, meaning rambling or overly broad</note> explanation that he could not possibly demonstrate. He came to believe that water was the primordial substance <term>Grundstoff</term> <note>Literally "ground-stuff"; the fundamental material from which all things are composed.</note> and the universal matter from which everything was made. This philosophy was held in high regard in Ionia and Greece for a long time. It was the fashionable system of the day. Everyone spoke of water; everything was explained by means of water. Pindar says at the beginning of an ode: "Water is the most excellent element" <note>The author refers to Pindar’s *First Olympian Ode*, which begins with the famous Greek phrase *Ariston men hydor* ("Greatest of all is water").</note>; however ridiculous and absurd this statement may seem to us today, it appeared quite learned back then and showed that the poet was a philosopher.

Thales had some degree of probability on his side. Does not everything that decays and is scattered pass away in vapors? Do these vapors not thicken into dew and rain? Does rain not become the basis <insert>substance</insert> for a thousand new creations? This transformation of water into other beings, and these back again into water, was later asserted by Helmont <note>Jan Baptist van Helmont (1580–1644), a Flemish chemist and physician who performed a famous "willow tree experiment" to prove that plants grew from water alone.</note> in Brussels. He intended to create a balsam <note>In this context, a medicinal elixir or alchemical "universal medicine" believed to restore health and prolong life.</note> from this generative and changeable water, with which one could live for centuries and provide his students with as much money as was required for a comfortable life. But he was scarcely sixty years old when he left his family—who were carried off at one moment by burning fevers, at another by rashes, and even by the plague—and a world that was not worthy of such a man and his balsam.

We do not wish to investigate the reasons here that he, as well as PARACELSUS *) might have had for passing away so young without any mercy, and without doing anything for his family, who during his life and after his death were neither wealthy nor healthy; we merely wish to consider the means he employed to justify his promises.

If one wishes to make gold, he said, one needs nothing but water. For from water, one can make trees, animals, and indeed an entire world. He did not see fit to prove his proposition by going into his workshop and creating a tree. Instead, he relied on an experiment <note>original: *Erfahrung*, which in this period denotes both a lived experience and a controlled empirical observation</note> for which he required a tree already in existence. It was a small willow **) weighing five pounds, which he planted in two hundred pounds of lye-treated soil <note>original: *Laugenerde*, soil that has been washed or treated to remove soluble nutrients, emphasizing the "purity" of the test</note> and covered with a lead plate. In five years, this willow weighed one hundred and sixty-four pounds, not counting the leaves that fell annually. The soil in which it stood had also been weighed five years prior and had lost none of its weight. This small tree, however, obtained from mere watering with water not only its entire weight but also the oil, water, salt, air, and earth [of which it was composed],

So, let us begin another way. If you consider the nature of a plant and investigate why God gave it flowers, fruits, and seeds, you do not think at that moment of a pear tree, nor of a rose bush, nor of a nutmeg shrub. You think of plants, flowers, and seeds as a general concept, without thinking of a specific genus. 

But if God wants to create a flower, it will not be merely "a flower." For a flower in general is nothing, or at most a mere thought. God would make an anemone, a tuberose, a narcissus, or some other specific flower. In the same way, we can certainly form a general concept of "spirit" and imagine it as a thinking being in general. ## II B. The Structure of the World.

What then will become of the three worlds we intend to design—namely, the worlds of Aristotle, Epicurus, and Descartes <note>original: *Cartesius*; the Latinized name of René Descartes (1596–1650), who proposed that the physical world was made of a single, uniform substance called "extension."</note>? It is already clear that they are all constructed from a single type of matter, of which they spoke but which they never truly knew, and which can be found nowhere in nature.

Such a universal matter that has no form may well be useful to a logician <term>Categorist</term> <note>A scholar focused on Aristotle’s "Categories," the basic ways things can be described.</note>, and a body extended in length, width, and depth may be useful to a geometer in his reflections; and a substance consisting of parts placed side by side fits the explanations of a Cartesian. They all believe they are saying something different; however, they all present a wavering and abstract concept, and say nothing that exists more really or truly than a "flower" in the abstract, which is nowhere to be found. I do not mean to criticize the method by which one considers some properties of things alone and without the others. One can say much that is good regarding the use of roots, stems, stamens, leaves, and other parts of a flower. But a "flower" simply as such—a universal substance—is as little real as a "universal intellect" (an intellect in the abstract).

->II B. The Structure of the World.<-

What will now become of the three worlds we intend to outline—namely, the worlds of Aristotle, Epicurus, and Descartes? One can already foresee that they are all constructed from a single "matter" of which they spoke but did not truly know, and which is to be found nowhere in nature.

Such a universal matter, devoid of form, may well be useful to a categorist <note>A philosopher who organizes reality into the strict categories defined by Aristotle.</note> in his reflections, just as a body extended in length, breadth, and depth is useful to a geometer; and a substance consisting of parts placed side by side suits the explanations of a Cartesian <note>A follower of the physics and philosophy of René Descartes.</note>. They all believe they are saying something different; yet they all offer a vague and abstract concept, and they describe nothing that exists more really or truly than a "flower as such," which is nowhere to be found. By this, I do not mean to criticize the method by which one considers certain properties of things in isolation from others. Much good can be said regarding the use of the roots, the stem, the stamens, leaves, and other parts of a flower. However, a "flower as such"—a universal substance—is as little real as a "universal intellect" (an intellect in the abstract).

Philosophers have always maintained the habit of believing they have discovered a new thing whenever they have invented a new word; and they assume that whatever they have ordered in their thoughts must also be found thus in nature. However, neither the authority of Aristotle and other teachers, nor their refined concepts, nor the supposed clarity of their conclusions can ever provide us with anything real. Nature can be entirely different from them. Pure experience alone entitles us to say: "this is" and "this is not." But if one holds this experience up against the world of the Peripatetics; it is an edifice that crumbles into dust.

**Form** determines **matter** to be this or that; and it is either *accidental* or *essential*. It is *accidental* when it merely concerns the exterior of the matter—for example, whether it should become round or angular. It is *essential* when it affects a part of the matter internally and determines it, for example, to be gold rather than earth or mercury.

For if, for example, a lemon is to be made, then nature must work on something that was not a lemon.

# The World of the Peripatetics <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle. In the 18th century, they were often caricatured by Enlightenment writers as clinging to outdated, "scholastic" explanations of nature rather than observing the world as it truly is.</note>.

A legion of caterpillars is devouring the foliage in the gardens this year. Your philosophy grows anxious over this; people fear they must perish from misery before summer even arrives. Who knows whether the grain seeds might not serve as food for these pests <note>Original: *Geschmeiß*. A derogatory term for swarming insects or vermin.</note>, which persist in the land from one year to the next and threaten to devastate everything? You "great philosophers," who claim you can construct a world from three or four elements and create living animals out of a bit of mud <note>A critique of "spontaneous generation," the then-common belief that life could arise spontaneously from non-living matter like mud or decaying meat—a theory the author rejects in favor of divine design.</note>, why then, from this entire world already completed, can you not find a remedy to hold back the armies of caterpillars sent against your fields? Do not be troubled. Both the affliction and its remedy rest in the hand of Providence <term>Vorsicht (Providence)</term> alone. She calls to the wind, and it will carry the butterflies and their eggs to another region, where they will cause no more harm than she has specifically determined and measured out.

A philosopher who has not witnessed the arrival or the migration of these insects near his home will be greatly astonished to suddenly find certain plant species covered in insects that are entirely foreign to him, or that had not been seen in previous years. He will certainly seek refuge in theories of fermentation, of "foul air," or in the "mixture of the warm and the moist." <note>These were standard explanations in pre-modern science for the sudden appearance of pests, often used by those who did not understand that insects laid eggs or migrated.</note> He will claim it was a mist or a wind that produced the caterpillars all at once and caused them to fall from the sky. These words are just as contrary to experience and just as incomprehensible as saying: "Chaos gave birth to the world," or "The mixture of elements formed the globe."

# The World of the Peripatetics <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle’s philosophy; here, the term is used to critique traditional academic scholars who prioritize abstract logic over practical observation.</note>

The attacks of these enemies <note>Referring to the pests and insects mentioned on the previous page.</note> are thus beneficial messages regarding the danger in which you find yourselves. And when you wage constant war against them, you eliminate or avoid the uncleanness <note>Original: *Unreinigkeit*. This refers to the filth or decay that the author believes attracts or necessitates the presence of such creatures.</note>, which is more harmful to you than to them.

In this manner, the learned have always sought in their natural philosophies to avoid occupying themselves with the counsel and the benefits of God, to accept them, to recognize His intentions, and to praise Him for them. And yet this occupation could have contributed the most to their happiness and was the ultimate purpose of the reason they had received. On the other hand, they have applied this measure of their knowledge in such a way that they sought to comprehend and explain the structure of the world, which God has nonetheless not revealed to them. 

But for so many centuries, while these system-makers <term>Systemschmiede (system-makers)</term> <note>A pejorative term used to describe philosophers who "forge" elaborate, often unfounded theoretical systems to explain the universe.</note> spoke of nothing but science, conviction, and insights, they find themselves incessantly hindered by thorns that God has intentionally scattered in their path. They see only a false glimmer and heap up confusion and dispute without end, because they consider their reason to be the only rule and guide for what they should think and believe. And yet, from time to time, they owe new observations and new clarity only to those who stick to the sheer simplicity of experience <note>In this context, "experience" refers to what we would now call empirical observation or experimental science.</note>, and who are satisfied to apply for themselves and others the magnificent benefits and truths that God reveals to them, even though He declines <note>Original: *verzeucht*, an archaic form of *verzieht*, meaning to withhold or delay.</note> to make them fully comprehensible to them.

Is it really possible, my readers will say, that people have made a name for themselves in the world, and in the modern world at that, by asserting such follies? Descartes <term>Cartesius</term> <note>René Descartes (1596–1650), often referred to by his Latinized name Cartesius, was a French philosopher, mathematician, and scientist.</note> explains himself more extensively in his *Meditations* <note>Referring to his 1641 work *Meditations on First Philosophy*.</note> as well as in the section on the *Method* <note>Referring to the *Discourse on the Method* (1637).</note>, to prove that he cannot think without existing; and so that this first principle may not be disputed, he addresses everything that could be objected against him, and always finds that he thinks, and that if he thinks, he also exists—whether he be awake or dreaming, or whether a higher spirit or a powerful deity <note>This refers to Descartes' "Evil Demon" or "Deceiving God" thought experiment, where he imagines an all-powerful being trying to trick his senses.</note> might seek to deceive him. ## II B. The Structure of the World.

He does not claim, like *Descartes* <note>original: "Cartesius"</note>, that a single principle will lead him to the most distant truths and that none will escape him. In order to always move one step further, he proceeds geometrically as far as it can be done. However, he does not flatter man with the hope that he will bring all scattered knowledge into a single whole, or that he will present natural science <term>Naturlehre</term> <note>The study of the laws of nature, encompassing what we now call physics and biology.</note> just like geometry. Rather, he admits *) with certain conviction the opposite.

Why then is *Mariotte's* method more valuable than that of *Descartes*? It is because the former is supported by experience, while the latter is abandoned by it. *Mariotte's* method is, in truth, not a new invention; it consists of telling the reader what has succeeded in all previous centuries.

If natural science has made some progress from time to time, and made some useful discoveries, it did not happen through the effort to know everything and to explain it from first principles: but rather to know a little more than was known before, and primarily to make science useful—if not through total clarity, then at least through sensory certainty <note>The idea that knowledge is valid if it can be confirmed by the physical senses.</note>. And where the first causes are lacking, which are always hidden, one should use as principles and guides all those reliable effects which have been recognized and confirmed through remarks, experiments, and the testimony of the senses.

If this is the case, one might say that the perfection of natural science <term>Naturlehre</term> <note>In the 18th century, "Naturlehre" referred to the study of the physical world, encompassing what we now call physics and natural philosophy.</note> consists in collecting what the senses teach us about nature, rather than what reason says of it. Does this not mean reversing the order of the sciences?

No? This does not mean reversing the order, but rather establishing it. Scientific disciplines will never be better organized than when experience goes first, while sound reason follows behind, making use of what experience reveals through the application of the intellect, arithmetic, geometry, and all other faculties. We are not, therefore, without rules and principles; for the more reliable the experiences that guide us are, the more certain our principles become, leading us ever further. Even if our science does not reach so far as to explain the nature of the bodies around us through geometry alone, it nonetheless collects the impressions they make and carries the proof far enough to suffice for determining our conduct wisely. For this purpose, a few general concepts in the intellect and various types of sensory knowledge under the guidance of reason are sufficient. Our human condition requires no more; and experience shows us that this is where God’s order, or His conduct toward us, lies.

### II B. The Structure of the World.

...take things as they are; without wasting time on refuting **Pyrrhonian** <note>Named after Pyrrho of Elis, the founder of Greek skepticism, who argued that one should withhold judgment on all things because nothing can be known for certain.</note> or **sophistical** <note>Referring to "sophistry"—reasoning that sounds clever but is actually false or intended to deceive.</note> brooding.
