Without a doubt, we must be satisfied with that which, in its successful application, is justified by the total reliability of the resulting effects.

1. There are things that we recognize clearly from their concept alone, or from a necessary consequence that the understanding cannot deny. Such are numbers, and measure, and all truths that are proven in mathematics. The proof of the existence of a **First Being** <note>A philosophical term for God, often used in the 18th century to describe the ultimate cause of the universe.</note> can be given with the same geometric rigor as everything else that is irrefutable in mathematics. Just as easily as God has made it for us to establish certain mathematical truths and derive others from them, He has made it just as easy for us to find certain principles of **equity** <note>original: *Billigkeit*; refers to natural fairness and moral justice.</note> and to apply them correctly. We all begin from the very same principle, and it is easy for us to convict those of error who deceive themselves in their conclusions. Thus, **moral philosophy** <note>original: *Sittenlehre*</note> is, for great and attentive souls, almost as clear and convincing as geometry.

# The World of Descartes.

There is yet a third kind of knowledge: the reports that our senses provide about the world outside ourselves. This is the experience of the quality and usefulness of things, whether they are near or far. This final category of knowledge encompasses **natural science** <term>natural science|Historically termed 'Naturlehre,' this refers to the study of the physical world and the laws of nature before the modern specialization of physics and biology.</term>, the arts, history, and religion. 

The objects themselves, as we perceive them through our senses or feel them within us, may be quite obscure; however, the evidence that forces us to form a judgment about them can be clear and distinct. This clarity comes from repeated sensory perception—experience—which confirms for us the actual existence and purpose of things. There is nothing to stop us from calling this new kind of clear knowledge a **conviction** <margin>Self-evidence <note>original: "Evidenz"</note></margin>. Indeed, nothing affects us more deeply than that which is convincing in this manner, or the knowledge provided by our senses. 

It is easy to see that **God** leads us back to the simple testimony of our senses at every turn, so that He might assist us in the confusion and uncertainty of our **rational deductions** <term>rational deductions|Logical arguments or conclusions based purely on reason (Vernunftschlüsse), which the author implies can be fallible or overly complex without sensory confirmation.</term>. This sensory testimony provides reliability and certainty in social life, in natural science, and in the rules of faith and morality. We might certainly wish for a deeper and more perfect light regarding the true **essence** <term>essence|The fundamental, internal nature of a thing, as opposed to its outward appearance or properties.</term> of things, rather than just the common properties our senses reveal. However, if one intends to strive for this higher light, it is only prudent to first determine whether one is not **vain-**

### The World of Descartes.

<note>original: *Cartesius*. The Latinized name of René Descartes (1596–1650).</note>
From these originally diverse and unevenly moved parts of matter, which are equally capable of becoming everything and anything, Descartes first sees three elements arise; from these, all other things that are perpetually maintained in the world are formed. First, all the corners, angles, and edges of these particles are broken unevenly through friction and collision. The finest particles <insert>resulting from this wear</insert> are the matter he calls the **first element**. The small bodies rounded off by the motion are the **second element** or **light**; and the coarse and strong ones, which retain the most corners, are finally the **third element**, or the matter for the **earth** and the **planets**.

When all these elements are in motion, and meet and resist one another, they compel each other to move not in a straight line but in a curved one, and to oscillate in **vortices** <note>original: *Wirbeln*. Descartes imagined the universe as a series of massive whirlpools of fluid matter that carry the planets along.</note> that swing around these and other common centers. And since they nevertheless retain their endeavor to continue in a straight line, they constantly strive

...distance decreases; thus it ceases at a certain range. One can therefore divide the light, from the Sun outward to this distance, into many layers, through which the unequal speed continually decreases from one layer to the next. Further out, the round matter <note>Descartes’ "second element," which he believed filled the heavens and transmitted light</note> which occupies the rest of the immense space of the solar vortex no longer receives a greater speed from the Sun. And since this remaining matter consists of larger and stronger **globules** <note>original: *Küglein*</note>, its efficacy always increases from the point where the speed originating from the Sun ends, until it strikes against one of the neighboring vortices. 

If, therefore, some dense bodies are carried into these round elements between the boundary of the Sun's influence and the impact with the next vortex, they must plunge into the nearby vortex with constantly increasing speed; likewise, others coming out of neighboring vortices and into our own round matter could fall downward within it toward the Sun.

There are, however, such small vortices that can move within the large ones, and these do not consist solely of a spherical matter and fine dust which, collected around a center, forms small suns; they can also contain or absorb many parts of the coarser dust—the material knocked off the corners [of particles]—which I have called the **third element** <note>Descartes identified the third element as the heavy, opaque matter that forms planets, comets, and Earthly objects</note>. Here, **Descartes** <note>original: *Cartesius*</note> allows them to remain; and this is quite convenient. He does not allow them to proceed further with their deviating force, nor to be carried away by the impact of the matter from the larger vortex; instead, they darken the sun of the smaller vortex. Indeed, they gradually form a **crust** <note>original: *Rinde*</note> around it; and from this crust, thickened all around, a dark body is formed: a planet, a habitable Earth. In this way, suns are formed from the fine dust masses, and planets and comets from the coarse dust masses.

When these planets enter the first <insert>*) <gloss>i.e., the one nearest to the sun</gloss></insert> half of the spherical matter, they roll onward with continually decreasing speed. However, the dark masses that are pushed into the other half travel as far as the nearest vortices, while others pass by the neighboring vortices and descend into the one near the Sun. The very same dense dust that formed the Earth, planets, and comets, also gathers into other forms by the power of motion, creating for us water, vapor, air, metals, stones, plants, and animals. In a word: all general and specific organic things, and everything else we encounter in our world.

# The World of Descartes. <note>original: *Cartesius*</note>

There are still many points in Descartes' structural system to consider; however, what we have already seen of it consists of parts that do not hold together, and anyone can see, without even looking further, that such a work cannot possibly endure.

1. Right from the start, it is strange to hear: God could not create and join angular bodies unless he had something to fill the gaps. By what authority does one dare to restrict omnipotence <note>The quality of having unlimited power</note> in this way!

2. But suppose Descartes knew why God has such an aversion to empty space <note>original: *leeren Raum*; Descartes famously argued for a "plenum," where a vacuum or void is impossible</note>, and that free movement takes place in a completely full space; indeed, he may even have proven its actual necessity. So be it. I simply want to hold him to the requirement that empty space is impossible. Yet, even by his own premise, it is not impossible. For if he wishes to fill all his gaps, he must have tiny particles of dust of every size and shape, which press into the openings at the right time. These, however, form gradually, for the little spheres <note>Descartes' "second element" of matter consists of rounded globules</note> do not round themselves all at once; the large corners are struck off sooner than the small ones; and after long friction, we can collect enough of this fine dust so that everything can be filled. But all of this happens only gradually. Therefore, at the first moment when God sets the parts of the original matter in motion, the dust is not yet formed. God strikes the points away;

# The World of Descartes.

...part the disciples from their master. Descartes <note>original: "Cartesius"</note>, who allows all things—general and specific, animals and plants—to arise from his three elements <term>three elements: Descartes' physics proposed that all matter was composed of three types of particles distinguished by their size and motion.</term>, even wants to derive the sea and the fish within it from them. However, his disciples abandon him and answer me that when it comes to living, organic things, one must assume a different foundation and appeal to specific designs and an explicit will. I am pleased that you reject the master's erroneous concept and willingly admit that the purpose or command which called the massive whale into being, and gives it only one calf each year, is distinct from the one that placed the snail in two small shells and granted it a numerous offspring every year.

Nowadays, you all unanimously admit that a specific purpose placed the pollen <term>Fruchtstaub: literally "fruit dust," a period term for pollen.</term> and the seed-grain on a single stem in most plants, because they are immobile and fixed in the earth; whereas another purpose separated the two sources of fertilization in animals because they can move and unite. You can observe yet another plan in those solitary animals, such as oysters, which always remain in one spot. One can believe that both substances of fertilization are found within every individual; for they all give birth, and the water drawn from them in summer is always full of tiny oysters that can be recognized through the microscope.

# The World of Descartes.

If they see even smaller tiny animals moving through a magnifying glass, they must also attribute a heart and vessels for fluids to them. They are certainly justified in doing so by <term>Analogy: The scientific and philosophical practice of inferring that if two things are similar in some respects, they are likely similar in others.</term>. But when you draw conclusions from the giant spheres of Saturn, the Earth, and the Moon regarding the "planets" in your invisible water-vortices, you have no rule to justify inferring such a similarity. Between spheres millions of miles in diameter and your invisible droplets, there ought to be vortices of a thousand miles, droplets several cubits in diameter, planets the size of a foot, earths an inch wide, and tiny earths the size of a line <note>original: "Linie". A historical unit of measurement, approximately 1/12th of an inch.</note>; there should be at least some little vortices visible through the <term>Microscope: At the time of writing, the microscope was a relatively new tool that was revolutionizing the understanding of biology by revealing "animalcules."</term>. Instead, you leap all at once from the infinitely large to the infinitely small, without any gradual reduction to establish a similarity between the two extremes.

You have, therefore, neither an analogical chain of reasoning nor the evidence of your eyes to support you. Assign your "moist spheres" whatever laws of motion you please, but do not speak of them with too much certainty; and above all, do not populate them with planets, moons, or <term>Satellites: Referred to in the text as "Trabanten," these are smaller celestial bodies orbiting a larger planet.</term>. You see that I by no means [accept] your method of using analogy to infer God’s behavior in one work from what He does in others—

Descartes did us an important service by habituating us to a mathematical order and way of thinking; however, one must not push it too far or attempt to apply it to everything. One pushes it too far when one attempts to reduce all our knowledge—which is as diverse as the sensations of our senses—to a single universal principle through a series of uninterrupted logical conclusions. And it is promising more from geometry and calculation than they can deliver if one believes they understand nature simply because they have calculated a few proportions within it. I might say with equal reason that one could set ancient <term>chronology: "Zeitrechnung," the historical science of determining the dates of past events.</term> in order all at once, without regard for historical monuments, if one only [took] the average number between the longest and shortest lives of those who lived before Christ...

## II B. The Structure of the World.

If the sea had occupied all lands foot by foot, and had covered and then left all plains and mountains; then one would surely have to find, among that which the water swept away, countless traces of human dwellings, vessels, worked metal <note>original: "gearbeitet Erz." Refers to smelted or manufactured metal objects.</note>, buildings, and even whole cities. Everywhere, one would have to encounter monuments that would differ according to the lands they were in, and which would possess all kinds of distinguishing marks, as major changes would have occurred during this immeasurably long eternity. But one finds nothing of the sort. Most of the traces of fruits and land animals that were thought to be found among the debris carried off by the sea are, upon closer examination, something else entirely. What have been presented in natural history collections as serpent tongues <note>original: "Schlangenzungen." These are glossopetrae, or fossilized shark teeth, which were historically believed to be the petrified tongues of snakes.</note> are visibly the teeth of the great sea-dog <note>original: "Seehund." While this usually means "seal" today, in this historical context it often referred to sharks or other large marine predators.</note>. Fruits which were thought to be olives turned to stone belong to a sea urchin <note>original: "Meerigel." Literally "sea-hedgehog," the standard German term for a sea urchin.</note>; they cover its entire shell and move like so many arms upon its back. The large bones that are often dug out of the earth and held to be elephant bones belong to the skeleton of a sea-horse <note>original: "Meerpferd." Likely referring to a walrus or perhaps a hippopotamus ("river-horse"), whose fossils were often misidentified as those of land giants or elephants.</note>. In a word: one finds traces of the sea everywhere, and nowhere the flooded dwellings that one ought to find everywhere.

### Newton’s World.

God can, for example, create six unequal spheres, and bring the three large ones together and the three small ones together as well. In both cases, an empty space <term>vacuum<note>original: "leerer Raum." The author is arguing against the "plenist" view—held by thinkers like Descartes—which claimed that a vacuum was logically impossible because space and matter were the same thing.</note></term> arises between them. However, it is larger in the former case than in the latter. There is, therefore, a vacuum—both a large vacuum and a small vacuum—depending on how the bodies touch each other.

The possibility of a vacuum can be proven even more easily. One assumes that God saw fit to create a single hollow sphere—or is creating it even now—such that it has absolutely no pores <note>In 18th-century science, "pores" were microscopic gaps within a material. If a material was "pore-less," nothing could leak through it.</note> or interstitial spaces, and no foreign body can enter it; is a vacuum within it not possible and necessary? Imagine also two surfaces of two elements without pores, lying tightly against one another. Imagine in these small surfaces a center point **c**, nearby points **bb**, and the outer points **aa**. If one wants to separate these surfaces, it cannot happen by introducing foreign matter between them through pores, for they have none; rather, one would have to bring it in from the edge. The movement of this matter, however, happens gradually. Once it is between the edges, at edge **a**, it is not yet at **b**; and even less so at **c**. Therefore, the vacuum is possible.

The second Newtonian law is: the effect is governed by the cause, and the former changes proportionally according to the latter, so that, for example, a single, double, or triple cause produces a single, double, or triple effect. There is nothing here to explain or to note.

The third law consists in this: that everywhere an action or an impact suffers a counter-action <note>original: "Gegenwirkung" — this is the classic "To every action there is always opposed an equal reaction."</note> equal to the impact. That is, when one body acts upon another, the second takes from the first a part of its motion; and <term>Newton</term> <note>Sir Isaac Newton (1642–1726), whose laws of motion laid the groundwork for classical mechanics.</note> understands it such that the second acts upon the first with all the force that it takes from it. For example: when one body meets another, it either stops it entirely or is itself stopped, depending on the case. However, it always loses what it communicates to the other, and is stopped only with a force perfectly equal to what it has lost; and this is the force that the other exerts upon it. One ball strikes another that was moving more slowly; this second ball now moves faster. The speed which the second receives, the first loses. Thus, whatever is added to the second acts upon the first, for it pushes it back—or, what is the same thing, it makes the first that much slower.

## Part II, Section B: The Structure of the World.
<meta>catchword: bent</meta>

If one applies these propositions to the moon, which moves around the earth, one finds that the same cause that brings a stone thrown into the air back down also leads the moon back toward the earth. The thrown stone has a force to distance itself from the center; with this, it moves away from the earth. However, at the same time, it obeys a stronger force that acts toward the center, and this brings it back down. Likewise, the moon strives, through the motion it has received, to distance itself from the earth in a straight line; and according to the first law, it would recede from us forever without end, if another force were not present at the same time to pull it back toward the earth. 

One of these two forces restricts the other. If the moon were left to its **deviating force** <note>original: "abweichenden Kraft" — what modern physics calls centrifugal force, or the tendency of an object to fly outward from the center of its rotation.</note>, it would leave its circular orbit around the earth and continue in a straight line, which would be the **tangent** <note>A straight line that touches a curve at a single point; this describes the path an object would take if the force keeping it in orbit suddenly vanished.</note> at the point of the circle where it left its path. On the other hand, if it were left to its **central force** <note>original: "Centralkraft" — centripetal force, which in this context is the pull of gravity toward the center of the earth.</note>, that is, the **attractive force** which drives it toward the center, it would crash down onto the earth. 

But these two forces combined keep it in its orbit. From this, one sees that the straight line along which the moon seeks to distance itself by virtue of the deviating force is bent or curved by the attractive force; and that the next tangent toward which it strives to turn anew is, in that very moment, again bent—

If now the Moon, at the distance of the sixtieth radius <note>original: "Halbmesser" — the distance from the center of the Earth to its surface.</note>, travels fifteen feet in one minute, it must—if it were sixty times lower, that is, quite close to the Earth—travel 3600 times 15 feet in one minute; for the square of 60 is sixty times sixty, or three thousand six hundred.

However, according to the experiments of Galileo <note>Galileo Galilei (1564–1642), who first formulated the law of falling bodies.</note>, the <term>distances<note>original: "Spatien" from the Latin *spatia*, referring to the space or distance traversed by an object.</note></term> that heavy bodies traverse relate to each other as the squares of the times. By the end of one minute, the stone has therefore fallen fifteen times 3600 feet; that is, through fifty-four thousand feet.

One finds, accordingly, that both the Moon and a stone near the Earth travel 54,000 feet in one minute; but if one were to place the stone into the orbit of the Moon and then let it fall, it would, with a 3600-times weaker force, travel no more than fifteen feet in one minute.

### Assessment of this Newtonian Physics.

Since the natural philosophy of Aristotle was nowhere sufficient, the promises of Descartes <note>original: "Cartesius" — the Latinized name for René Descartes, whose "vortex theory" was the primary rival to Newton's gravity.</note> were eagerly listened to. They were astonished by the accuracy of the geometry in the Newtonian propositions, and gradually overcame their resistance to the obscure concept of attraction <note>original: "Attraction" — many contemporary scientists initially criticized gravity as an "occult" or hidden force because Newton could not explain *how* it worked, only *that* it worked.</note> through its exact agreement with the events of the heavens. ...orbits around the sun, Kepler hit upon the idea that the bodies of the planets were composed of fibers, like feathered arrows, which all lay down and became smooth if they turned their tips from one side toward the sun, but conversely stood up and became ruffled if the other side were turned toward it. <note>Kepler proposed a "magnetic" theory in which planetary bodies contained "fibers" that reacted to the sun’s influence, explaining why they moved in ellipses rather than perfect circles.</note>

When the planets turned the smooth side toward the sun, that was the friendly side, and it caused an attraction toward it; but if the rough side was turned that way, it was the hostile side, and this orientation caused a repulsion. In one case, the interval <note>original: "Intervall." In this context, it refers to the variable distance or gap between the planet and the sun.</note> drew them toward the sun, and in the other, it moved them away. Astronomers have retained Kepler’s rules and everything he specified according to his observations; nevertheless, sensible men have expressed pity for all these hypotheses of smooth and ruffled fibers, and for his attraction and repulsion, even though they were presented in magnificent words and with all the pomp of geometry.

The attractive, repulsive, dead, and immaterial forces which Newton uses so extensively originally come from Kepler. Newton’s observations, his geometry, and the calculations added to them far surpass those of Kepler: but do all these forces possess more truth and reality than before, simply because he allows them to appear in better company? <note>The author is skeptical, suggesting that while Newton’s mathematics ("better company") are superior, the underlying "forces" he describes might be just as hypothetical as Kepler’s "fibers."</note>

The Newtonians find a certain distaste for the peculiar notion that light refracts in empty space and turns toward where it finds matter. We do not, however, wish to offer a defense of their school through this new **fear of the empty** <note>original: "horror vacui." Rather, it rebounds from the pores because it makes no difference whether the pores are extremely narrow or if they are completely closed; or because a fluid substance, just as fine as light itself, pushes it back out of the pores even before it touches the surface upon which that fluid itself surges or is agitated more than elsewhere.

It is then a mere hypothesis, which is unsuccessful in a thousand cases, where they at least have the pleasure of applying some rules of proportion and measuring certain ratios, without actually knowing what the thing is they are dealing with. Everything one gains from it—when one wants to apply measure, weight, and calculation everywhere: to the heavens, to light, to the pressure of fluid bodies—is that one can give oneself a very learned appearance, even if one is truly wandering around in the deepest darkness.

Do not expect, say the **Newtonians**, that we will ever again accept your spheres of vapor or your **vortices** <note>Referring to René Descartes’ "tourbillons," the theory that planets are carried around the sun by massive whirlpools of subtle matter.</note>. <header>### Third Book</header>

### Book III.

...bell tower to my ear, no one will likely conclude that the air travels away from the tower and comes to me; rather, that the air moved in the tower pushes against the nearest air, and this further along, so that the air remains in its place, but the impact <term>Stoß</term> <note>In 18th-century physics, this "impact" or "shove" refers to the mechanical transmission of energy through a medium.</note> alone is propagated far away.

Air and light, however, are not outflows of the bell or the sun that stir them. One does not concern the other. The air is present before the trumpet excites it and sounds; and the light is present before it is disturbed in its equilibrium by the flame of the fire and shines.

It is exactly the same with the origin of all created things. A gnat or a flea does not leave the egg until the proper warmth stirs within the membranes of which its body consists. That is true. However, warmth did not, for that reason, animate the seed or prepare the nourishment enclosed within the egg for it.

The Creator has indeed placed constant laws into nature, according to which bodies come together, collide, and part from one another again. The theater of nature changes and renews itself without ceasing. But why is it always the same despite all these changes?

A chemist skillfully brings together some materials that do not cost much and forms from them a kind of metal that is as beautiful as gold and does not smell as unpleasantly as brass. He searches for a fine name for this mixture. He will call it Tombac <note>An alloy of copper and zinc, often used to imitate gold in clockmaking and jewelry.</note>, Prince’s Metal <note>Also known as Prince Rupert's Metal; a form of brass with a high copper content used as a gold substitute.</note>, or Pure Gold *) <note>original: "Schiergold."</note>. "Pure Gold" is a word that can bring this new invention into popular acceptance. He gains a following. However, has this name increased the number of metals? Has he brought forth a new essence? Ask the humblest of his fellow tradesmen about it. He will name for you, piece by piece, everything he took to make it. This material is the main component; that one gives it more hardness; a third is added to create the bond. Our chemist has thus created nothing nor transformed anything; instead, he has merely combined already finished things with artful skill.

As a necessary consequence of God’s intentions for humanity, He brought light into the world so that everything might become visible; He created the air that man should breathe, and the fire that was meant to sustain him. From this very same <term>design: Entwurf; a plan or blueprint.</term> stem the metals, the salt, and all earthly elements which, at all times, are meant to renew and preserve everything that will be necessary for the inhabitants of the earth. One can clearly see that He created them to be indestructible, so that there would never be a lack of any of these things.

Yet, although the earth is already provided with these magnificent elements, it is nevertheless not yet fit to receive the human being who is to inhabit it. The sun may already be shining—or perhaps it is yet to be created—but the earth is still nothing more than a <term>waste and a void: Wüste und Einöde; a reference to the Hebrew "Tohu wa-bohu" from Genesis 1:2.</term>. It is a waste, for not a single blade of grass yet grows upon it. It is a void, for there is as yet nothing living within it. Heat and rain could make grass grow if it were already formed; but God alone can provide the seed. This heavy work is reserved for His power alone, just as the world itself was.

But His will, which makes and arranges everything with wisdom, reveals itself everywhere we look. It is His will that, in order to create a space for the inhabitants, raised the earth above the sea and created a chamber large enough for all the water contained within it.

All parts of this world work so collectively for man's benefit, and are so interconnected, that we cannot doubt for a moment: He who specifically willed one part, willed them all in general, and arranged each one specifically so that they should form a whole.

We find, therefore, in the layout of all parts of this world and their general harmony in the service of man, the convincing mark of a Wisdom which has intentionally chosen and determined the nature and use of each and every thing. # Book III.

The Earth, bared by the receding water, adorns itself with countless plants full of foliage, blossom, fruit, and seed. Could the moisture left behind by the water have caused this? Yes, if one added fermentation to this moistening, and truly understood the meaning of this great word; if one combined with this moistening and fermenting the sun, which does not yet exist; if to all these active causes one added attraction and repulsion, central forces and gravitation; even then, all these forces would not produce a single plant. # Book III.

Our ancient philosophers <note>original: "Weltweisen," literally "world-wise ones." The moderns, who generally (and this is laudable) have learned more geometry, often use this geometry to explain through lines and calculations how attraction and repulsion, or central and eccentric forces, produce an ovary in the animal, an egg in the ovary, and seed in the egg; or how, in the brain of an animal, they effect the secretion of the animal spirits <note>original: "Lebensgeister"; early modern scientists believed these were subtle fluids that traveled through the nerves to control movement and sensation.</note> and the precise, rapid movements of the muscles. However, if the Creator, who made the basic elements and all living creatures, deemed that their **use** and not the **knowledge** of their inner nature would be beneficial to us in our present state, then it follows evidently that Moses taught us what we need to know and omitted only what does not concern us. On the other hand, a system of philosophy <note>The author uses "philosophy" here to refer to "Natural Philosophy," the precursor to modern physics and science.</note> that loses sight of God’s purposes and the harmony of all the world's creatures toward a single ultimate end, and instead tries to show us the "reason" for all things by deriving them from a mass of clay <note>original: "Thone," referring to the mechanistic view that the universe can be explained purely through the movement of matter or "atoms."</note> set in motion, seeks in a ridiculous way to break through the limits God has set for us, and finds only contradiction throughout all of nature.

# Book III. Moses' Natural Science.

Who then could have taught the Hebrew lawgiver <note>original: "hebräischen Gesetzgeber"; referring to Moses.</note> such fruitful principles, so beneficial to good morals, and such a singular yet intelligible natural science, which agrees so closely with all of nature since it has been better observed? Or even from his own rightly-thinking intellect? One may choose what one wishes. I begin and honor Moses as the most venerable teacher, even before I have examined the proofs of his mission.

# The History of the Heavens
## Book Four.
### Conclusions of the History of the Heavens.

From the comparison conducted thus far between the thoughts of the ancients regarding presumed heavenly powers, the opinions of philosophers of all ages concerning the origin of all things, and what Holy Scripture <note>original: "die heilige Schrift"</note> and experience teach us about the origin of the world and the destiny of man, we now recognize sufficiently how much perversity has existed in the opinions of men, and how much futility in their investigations. The Creator of all things led them, as if by the hand, toward their proper object, in that He refused to satisfy their insatiable desire or to resolve their questions regarding the foundation <note>original: "Grund"</note> of His works; instead, He blessed the labor of their hands and their efforts in practical experiments with successful progress from day to day. 

But they did not remain peacefully within the order of their station nor within the limits of their capacity; rather, they all thought to attain lofty knowledge and a special state of bliss <term>Glückseligkeit; in 18th-century thought, this refers to a state of supreme happiness or spiritual well-being</term>; yet in their instability, they grasped at nothing but shadows, and lost the profound pleasure which comes with modest— <note>The text ends mid-word here. To be sure, it bids us to contemplate the beauty of God’s works and the wonders of His providence. Look, it says, at the grain of wheat that is sown into the earth. Look at the birds under the heavens, and how they live. Consider the lilies of the field and their glory.

But what is the intention behind this effort? To what end? What is the final purpose of this commanded attention? Are we meant to distinguish ourselves through this deep wisdom? Perhaps to attain a precise knowledge of the *nature* of all visible things? No; all the teachings the Savior gives us are intended to ensure that we work with perfect confidence in the providence of the heavenly Father and stand by one another as brothers.

# IV. Book. Conclusions

There is also this yet common error among those who apply themselves to the fine arts <term>schöne Wissenschaften; a 18th-century term for the humanities or "belles-lettres," including literature, poetry, and rhetoric</term>, and a consequence of the previous point, that they use concepts from the poetic world and the names of the mythological gods either in the language of common conversation or in what are called works of wit <note>original: "Werke des Witzes"; creative or literary works demonstrating intellectual cleverness and stylistic flair</note>: and from this grows a harm for us that is greater than one might think.

This, however, is the misuse regarding the history of the poetic heavens <note>a reference to the mythological stories of the Greek and Roman gods</note>, that many among men, who nonetheless wish to be thought to possess reason, taste, and religion, delight themselves throughout their entire lives in the refuse of paganism <note>original: "Wuste des Heidenthums"; literally the "waste" or "chaos" of heathenry, suggesting moral or intellectual clutter</note>, and weaken their reason, as they find taste in no other style than the so-called language of the gods. They know all the classes of the gods and the long series of their adventures. The transformations <note>original: "Verwandelungen"; likely referring to the myths found in Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*, a popular source for art and garden design</note> are the usual decoration of their gardens and halls: they demand to see or read nothing that is not adorned with some features from pagan antiquity. From their indifference toward everything else, one must conclude that they believe if one leaves Rome and Athens behind, or departs from the concepts of Homer <note>the legendary Greek author of the *Iliad* and the *Odyssey*</note> or Ovid <note>Publius Ovidius Naso (43 BC–17 AD), a Roman poet famous for his works on mythology</note>, no more grace, sound wit, or anything pleasing is to be found anywhere. But do they well know that they thereby create a very unfavorable impression of their religion, their wit, and their taste?

If such adornment is already false and improper in paintings, because one should not please the eye by disregarding sound reason; how much more must it be ill-suited in poems? ### Book IV. Conclusions

Meanwhile, there are indeed cases where it is permitted for poetry, and even more so for painting, to employ allegorical images. For example, in public festivities and celebrations of great events; there, one must not present decorations to the people that have no connection among themselves. Since one is compelled to choose the individual parts of the presentation so that they constitute a whole—for otherwise nothing can please—one devises a moral being <note>The author uses "moralisch Wesen" to describe a personification—a human figure representing an abstract concept like "Justice" or "Peace."</note> and gives it a body, a purpose, and an action; for example: Peace, Justice, Europe, or the Spirit of Commerce. One attributes to them a resolve, an entourage, equipment, and conquests, and brings everything together with probability, by which one intends to please and engage the people.

There are other occasions where one must employ not only allegorical persons but even the deities of fable <note>The "deities of fable" refers to the gods of Greek and Roman mythology.</note>. If a painter or poet wishes to represent an action from Antiquity, he must necessarily let his characters speak and act according to their education and way of life, and according to the nature of the times and places. These actions are then not worthy of blame, for they are grounded in sound reason. However, if one represents a modern general in the old guise of a Hercules or of Mars the Liberator <note>original: "Martis Liberatoris"</note>, and attributes a Greek religion to Christians, it is truly far more ridiculous than if one were to deploy cannons before Troy, or

And thereafter they call "clarity" that which they have found from entirely uncertain premises, collected, and, as far as possible, brought into a coherent connection. However, this new method, which elevates the advantages of clarity so high and wishes to apply it everywhere, gives birth to nothing but systems of error and eternal strife. In the hope of clearly and certainly perceiving the elements, the causes, and the effects, we must not begin to study philosophy; for of what do we indeed have certainty? Can we indeed flatter ourselves to clearly recognize what God, the soul, the body, lead, or clay might be?

We perceive quite clearly, and must perceive it even against our will, that the essence within us—which thinks, wills and does not will, rejoices and grieves, distinguishes good and evil—is not the same as the body, which sleep and death render incapable of everything. ### # of the History of the Heavens.

... [mankind] is always the same in the order of the truths of salvation and natural truths. Both are equally inscrutable to our understanding. This method—preferring to derive everything from experience and experiments rather than from a clear insight into the interior of nature—and resting in the fact that we reflect modestly on how best to apply what experience [teaches]...

Many among us who had distinguished themselves in the study of the fine sciences tried for a while to maintain their honor in logic; in the end, however, some sooner and others later, chose to read more pleasant things instead of this labor, or to give up studying altogether.

### IV. B. Consequences of the History of Heaven.

Moses, and the whole of Holy Scripture <note>This completes the thought from the previous page: that the most thorough and useful minds are in agreement with the biblical tradition.</note>: and yet it seems as if the great systems of **natural science** <term>Naturlehre; an early modern term for the study of the physical world, encompassing what we now call physics and the natural sciences</term> intentionally want to lead us away from it, by raising us so high that we leave our own element and occupy ourselves with something that can be neither understood nor put to use.

# First Elucidation
## On the Origin of **Idolatry** <term>Abgötterey; literally "off-godliness," referring to the worship of idols or false gods in place of the biblical Creator.</term>

I am compelled to answer an objection that has been repeated several times. "This man," it is said, "will not tolerate any system, and yet he makes one himself concerning the origin of idolatry."

A **system** <note>In the 18th century, a "system" was an all-encompassing intellectual framework that tried to explain everything through a single set of principles—often criticized by the author for being too speculative.</note> actually has the inner construction of the world as its object. For the arrangements devised by **Ptolemy** and **Copernicus** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (2nd century CE) argued the Earth was the center of the universe, while Nicolaus Copernicus (1473–1543) argued the Earth revolved around the Sun.</note>, according to which the planets move, are—if one is to speak precisely—not systems; they are well- or poorly-made observations on the position of the stars. **Reason** <term>Vernunft; the human capacity for logical thought and understanding.</term> clearly recognizes this. Nothing can be called a system except the formation of the elements and the connection of the whole; and since this creation far exceeds all our powers, I thought it wise to spare philosophy from it.

Collecting a series of reliable events and comparing them to one another in order to clarify an important matter is never forbidden to humans, and for all I care, one can call that a system. On that basis, every **treatise** <term>Abhandlung; a formal written work dealing systematically with a subject.</term> is a system; and so I too have made a system, of which I am not ashamed. For, on the one hand, it is laudable and very reasonable to investigate how man fell so far as to become idolatrous; and moreover, the most prominent events I have used in explaining such a pleasant subject are reliably certain.

<page-num>392</page-num>
<header>On the Origin</header>

I will not dwell on how much it matters to us to recognize the origin of the senseless **idolatry** <term>Götzendienst; the worship of idols or false gods.</term> from which **Christianity** has delivered us; for that is obvious. But as for the reliability of the events from which I have derived this origin: one may judge that from the following.

The Ram, and the Bull, the **Sphinx** consisting of a Lion and a Virgin, the Erythraean Sibyl, the Virgin with the red ear of grain <note>This refers to the constellation Virgo and its brightest star, Spica (the "ear of grain"), which marked the harvest season.</note>, the Ruler of Heaven, the fruitful Mother adorned with the fruits of every season, the beloved Child, the Dog that closes one year and begins another; even that Dog-head which commands one to step forward—all of these are symbolic animals and instructive images. Various scholars have now clearly stated what they were intended to mean. However, these animals and images were also worshipped and consulted for advice. It is therefore clear that these misunderstood signs gave birth to the most prominent gods, the strange veneration of sacred animals, the most famous oracles, and the peculiar metamorphoses. With an origin so simple and yet so productive in its application, it does not matter much if one doubts or even errs in the explanation of any particular figure.

It is provable that symbolic figures were already in use in **Babylonia** before the dispersion of the peoples <note>A reference to the biblical story of the Tower of Babel, after which humanity was said to have split into different languages and nations.</note>, and remained with the famous colonies of the **Chinese**, **Egyptians**, and **Syrians**. These images and all the signs required for the communities changed from people to people and from time to time. However, the same desires and the same lack of understanding perverted everything.

<page-num>393</page-num>

# Of Idolatry #

Even though we derive all the specific excesses from which pagan religion is composed from a single source—and this very simplicity is itself a hallmark of truth—we must nonetheless admit that once error had arisen in the world, it underwent many diverse changes. The delight in fables and new deities became universal. It was not enough to deify the presumed founders of a nation or a colony. Every province, indeed every family, wanted to have its own deities. A father comforted himself over the loss of a beloved daughter by dedicating a temple to her as if she were a goddess. A princess believed she could soothe her grief over her widowhood by immortalizing the memory of her husband and establishing an annual festival in his honor. The Greeks defined the overly broad concept of the "Twins" <note>Referring to the constellation Gemini.</note> by assigning them the names **Castor** and **Pollux**; the astronomers in Alexandria named a star-cluster that had no name after the hair which **Berenice** <note>Berenice II of Egypt; the constellation is known as Coma Berenices (Berenice's Hair).</note> had cut off upon the return of **Ptolemy Euergetes**. I do not wish to deny the historical origin of these newer, well-known deities at all; despite all of this, history can take nothing away from the deities of the old lineage—these were signs and nothing more.

I raised a difficulty for myself, and upon reviewing this history of the heavens once more, I have answered it. As I have since learned, it was presented before a learned society and can be found in the *Memoirs of Trévoux* <term>Mémoires de Trévoux; an influential academic journal published by French Jesuits from 1701 to 1782.</term>. It is only fair to present it here in its full light. "It is indeed true," it will be said,

-># On the Origin #<-

How much it matters to us to recognize the origin of the senseless idolatry <note>original: "Götzendienstes"</note> from which Christianity has freed us, I shall not dwell upon; for that is self-evident. But as for the reliability of the events from which I have derived this origin: that can be judged from the following.

The Ram <note>The zodiac sign Aries.</note>, and Bull <note>The zodiac sign Taurus.</note>, the Sphinx consisting of a Lion and a Virgin <note>A common 18th-century theory held that the Sphinx represented the transition between the zodiac signs of Leo and Virgo, marking the Nile's flood.</note>, the Erythraean Sibyl, the Virgin with the red ears of grain <note>The constellation Virgo, often depicted holding wheat (the star Spica).</note>, the Sign of Heaven, the fruitful Mother adorned with the harvests of every season, the beloved child, the Dog who concludes one year and begins another; the very Dog-head <note>A reference to Anubis or the star Sirius, the "Dog Star," which heralded the Egyptian new year.</note> which commands preference—all these are symbolic animals and instructional images. Various scholars have clearly stated what they are meant to signify. However, these animals and images were also worshipped and consulted for advice. It is therefore clear that these misunderstood signs gave birth to the most eminent gods, the strange worship of sacred objects, the most famous oracles, and the peculiar rituals. Given such a simple origin, which is yet so fertile in its application, it does not matter much if one doubts the explanation of any particular figure or even misses it entirely.

It is provable that symbolic figures were already in use in Babylonia before the dispersion of the nations <note>A reference to the biblical story of the Tower of Babel.</note>, and remained in use among the famous collectives of the Chinese, Egyptians, and Syrians. These images and all the signs required for the communities changed from people to people and from time to time. But the same passions and the same ignorance <note>original: "Lüste und einerley Unverstand"</note> distorted everything.

<header>### on Idolatry ###</header>

Even though we derive all the particular excesses of which pagan religion is composed from a single source—and this simplicity itself is a hallmark of truth—we must nevertheless admit that once error had arisen in the world, it branched out into many forms. The delight in fables and new deities became universal. It was not enough to deify the supposed founders of a nation or a colony. Every province, indeed every family, wanted to have its own deities. A father consoled himself over the loss of a beloved daughter by dedicating a temple to her as if she were a goddess. A princess believed she could soothe her grief over widowhood by immortalizing the memory of her husband and establishing an annual festival in his honor. The Greeks defined the overly broad concept of the Twins <note>The constellation Gemini.</note> by assigning them the names <term>Castor</term> and <term>Pollux</term> <note>In Greek mythology, the twin half-brothers who were transformed into the constellation Gemini.</note>; the astronomers in Alexandria named a nameless cluster of stars after the hair that <term>Berenice</term> <note>Queen Berenice II of Egypt.</note> had cut off upon the return of <term>Ptolemy Euergetes</term> <note>Her husband, Ptolemy III; the constellation is still known as Coma Berenices, or Berenice's Hair.</note>. I do not wish to deny the historical origin of these well-known newer deities at all; however, despite all this, history cannot take anything away from the deities of the ancient lineage; these remain signs and nothing more.

I have raised a difficulty for myself, and upon reviewing this "History of Heaven" once more, I have answered it. I later learned that this matter was presented to a learned society and can be found in the <term>Memoirs of Trévoux</term> <note>A prominent 18th-century Jesuit journal of literature, science, and theology.</note>. # On the Origin #

How important it is for us to recognize the origin of that nonsensical idolatry from which Christianity has liberated us is something I will not dwell upon; for it is quite obvious. However, regarding the reliability of the events from which I have derived this origin, one may judge from what follows.

The Ram and the Bull <note>The zodiac signs Aries and Taurus.</note>, the Sphinx consisting of a Lion and a Maiden <note>The author suggests the Sphinx represents the transition between the zodiac signs Leo and Virgo.</note>, the Erythraean Sibyl <note>An ancient prophetess; the author likely views her here as a personification of a seasonal or astronomical sign.</note>, the Virgin with the red ear of grain <note>The star Spica in the constellation Virgo, which traditionally marked the harvest.</note>, the Regent of Heaven, the fertile Mother adorned with the fruits of every season, the beloved Child, the Dog that closes one year and begins the next <note>A reference to the "Dog Star" Sirius, whose rising predicted the flooding of the Nile and the Egyptian New Year.</note>; even the Dog’s Head <note>Likely referring to the Egyptian god Anubis.</note> which commands one to step forward—all these are symbolic animals and teaching images. Various scholars have quite clearly stated what they are intended to mean. However, these animals and images have also been worshiped and consulted for counsel. It is therefore clear that these misunderstood signs gave rise to the birth of the most prominent gods, the strange veneration of sacred animals, the most famous oracles, and the peculiar transformations <note>original: "Verwandelungen"; a reference to the myths of gods changing shape or being placed in the stars.</note>. Given such a simple and, in its application, fruitful origin, it matters little if one doubts or even errs in the explanation of any particular figure.

It can be proven that these symbolic figures were already in use in Babylonia before the dispersion of the nations, and they remained with the famous colonies of the Chinese, Egyptians, and Syrians. The images and all the signs required for the communities changed from nation to nation and from time to time. Yet, the same desires and the same lack of understanding perverted everything.

<meta>catchword: Der</meta>

...[those who] wish to inform us <note>The text begins mid-word, likely "belehren" (to instruct or inform), continuing from the previous page's discussion on ancient authorities.</note> report that the Egyptians in the remotest antiquity began their year not when the sun entered the first degree of **Cancer** <note>The Crab.</note>—which the ignorance of those times did not permit them to determine—but rather when the sun was in the middle of the sign, making the entire constellation of **Cancer** invisible, and rose at the same time as the **Dog Star** <note>Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky.</note>. With the sight of this star, which separated itself from the sun after one month, began all the observations that related to the flooding of the **Nile** and the fertility of the year. From this arises the custom—which becomes ridiculous in other places—*) to observe the movement of the air at the visible rising of this star, in order to conclude from it what would happen throughout the entire year.

And in this matter, all other points arise from a single one. If we know for certain that the beginning of the ancient Egyptian year coincided with the **summer solstice** <term>Sommerwende: the point in the year when the sun reaches its highest point in the sky, marking the beginning of summer.</term>, when the sun joins with **Cancer** and arrives at the horizon alongside the **Dog Star**, then **Cancer** is the first sign of summer. Now, the sun needed a month to reach the middle of **Leo** <note>The Lion.</note>, which was therefore the second sign, and so forth. If, then, the **Dog Star** and **Cancer** rose together with the sun at the **summer solstice**, then **Aries** <note>The Ram.</note> necessarily began the spring in the ancient Egyptian year; and **Taurus** <note>The Bull.</note> and **Gemini** <note>The Twins.</note> were the two other **spring signs** <term>Lenzzeichen: archaic term for the constellations marking the spring season.</term>.

# On Egyptian Plants.

one can sail about in boats on the Nile water under the shadow of this forest. From the center of the flower rises a pod, in the shape of an inverted little bell. It was called the calyx <note>original: *Kelch*</note>, and it contained about thirty grains like small beans, which are good to eat both fresh and dried. The calyxes, when empty and without fruit, served as drinking bowls. From dried leaves, all sorts of other vessels were woven. The root of the plant had a magnificent flavor. The plant **Nelumbo** <note>the sacred lotus, *Nelumbo nucifera*</note> in Ceylon, India, and China has all these properties. The root is ground down to make bread. The Chinese cultivate them in vessels full of water to preserve the flower; and there can be little doubt that it is the **Lotus**, whose leaves, blossoms, and bells are found among the Egyptian figures. When the leaves are rolled together, they are seen emerging from a vessel on the head of a figure. The unfurled leaves are often on a throne that seems to have a connection to the sun; and the fruit or the closed flower often serves as a support for the image of **Osiris**, as well as an ornament for him and others. This flower bears another name, which we shall soon discuss, in addition to the names **Lotus**, **Ciborium**—that is, a food-casket <note>original: *Speisekästlein*; referring to the seed pod's shape</note>—and the "Egyptian bean."

4. A plant was also cultivated in Egypt that had come there from Arabia, named **Colchas** or **Colocasia** <term>Taro; a tropical plant grown for its edible starchy corms</term>. This was a plant whose root was a bulb and was good to eat.

# On Egyptian Plants.

Although in Egypt it very rarely bore a flower—much like the German pepper **Arum** <note>*Arum maculatum*, a plant with a distinctive ear-shaped bract</note>—it was oblong like a donkey's ear, with the fruit emerging from its center. One finds it occasionally on Egyptian monuments. It can also be seen in an image of **Harpocrates** <note>the Greek name for the child-god Horus, often depicted with his finger to his lips</note> in the works of **Cuper** <note>Gisbert Cuper (1644–1716), a Dutch scholar of antiquity</note>. However, this is not the common ancient **Colocasia** <note>Taro</note> so frequently mentioned by ancient authors. That *Colocasia* bears flowers that were commonly used at festivals, as well as fruits which, like the root, were a staple food for the people; this does not match the *Colchas* of which we are speaking, because the latter bloomed very little in Egypt and thus even more rarely bore fruit. All ancient authors agree that they called the fruit of the *Colocasia* sometimes **Lotus**, sometimes **Ciborium** <note>original: *Ciborium*; referring to the cup-shaped seed vessel</note>, and sometimes the **Egyptian bean**. Thus, what initially seemed to present a difficulty becomes a clear proof of the truth, and it is impossible to doubt that the Indian **Nelumbo** <note>the sacred lotus</note> is the second species of **Lotus** with the red flower.

5. The fifth distinctive Egyptian plant is the **Persea** <term>an evergreen tree, likely *Mimusops laurifolia*, held sacred in ancient Egypt</term>, which various writers and translators groundlessly confuse with the *Persica* (the peach). It is a beautiful evergreen tree whose leaves resemble laurel and have a spicy fragrance. The pear-like fruit is good to eat and has a pit shaped like a heart. 6. The sixth plant known in Egypt throughout all ages is the <term>Banana</term> or the **Musa**; I will not repeat its description here. Since such a **banana tree** bloomed and produced some fruit in the botanical garden in 1741, Mademoiselle **Basseporte** <note>Madeleine Françoise Basseporte (1701–1780), a prominent French botanical illustrator at the Royal Garden in Paris</note> drew it from nature, and we have had it engraved. **)

These are the plants whose foliage is commonly found accompanying the symbolic circle above the heads of Egyptian figures. The circle signified God and served to define everything concerning religion. This circle, either plain or set with rays, was afterwards attributed to the kings of the East out of flattery. This is the origin of their crowns; for previously, they wore only a <term>diadem</term>, which is to say, a headband. The solar circle—that magnificent and innocent sign of what belongs to God—is evidently the origin of the radiant glow (<term>halo</term> or <term>nimbus</term> <note>original: *Limbus* or *Nimbus*</note>) which has been preserved to this day around the heads in images of holy persons.

# On Egyptian Plants.

From this presumably arises the custom in pagan antiquity of adding certain leaves to some images and assigning to every god a preferred dedication of a plant particularly dear to him.

Our uncertainty regarding the true significance of these plants, however, does not in the least weaken the validity of the principle of <term>symbols</term> <note>original: *Sinnbilder*; visual emblems or allegorical representations common in Enlightenment-era studies of mythology</note>. It is impossible to doubt that Osiris relates to the sun, Isis to the earth and the annual festivals, Horus to agriculture, and Anubis to the <term>Dog Star</term> <note>Sirius; the brightest star in the night sky, whose heliacal rising signaled the beginning of the Nile's flood in ancient Egypt</note>. And if the main figures indeed signify something, then this applies to the secondary details as well, even if we remain uncertain of their specific interpretation.

**Truths**, physical, of a perfect clarity 358 ff.

### Z.
